Our results indicated that, relative to Shannon and Simpson indices, AWM_PC1 exhibited distinct patterns both in spatial variation across airports or habitat types and in spatial association with distance from airport. Spatial associations of AWM_PC1 were positive across habitat types at Zhongchuan, indicating that fast-lived species are more prevalent near the airport whereas slow-lived species become more abundant farther from the airport, while no such spatial trend was observed at Lintao and habitat-specific patterns were observed at Wuwei. Spatial associations of Shannon and Simpson indices followed a quadratic pattern at Zhongchuan and a linear pattern at Lintao, while no significant pattern at Wuwei. Our findings suggest that the strength and direction of community-level responses vary with both frequency- and distance-related disturbance gradients, and that life-history type-based indicators can effectively complement conventional diversity indices for interpreting these responses.

title: Plant size drives divergence in leaf economic spectrum of tropical forest understory herbaceous species
abstract: Herbaceous plants represent an understudied component of tropical forest understory diversity, and the role of plant size in mediating leaf trait variation remains unclear. In this research, we analyzed plant height (PH), leaf length (LL), and 10 leaf traits associated with the leaf economic spectrum across 23 tropical forest understory herbaceous species to explore trait responses to size and adaptation strategies. The results showed that PH significantly influenced photosynthetic nitrogen use efficiency (PNUE) and area-based nitrogen content ( N area ), with PNUE increasing and N area decreasing with height. Compared to PH, LL explained a greater number of leaf traits and a larger proportion of interspecific variation among these understory herbs. Leaf thickness ( L t ), leaf area (LA), and PNUE increased as LL increased, whereas leaf mass per area (LMA) and N area decreased with increasing LL. We further demonstrated that LL drove leaf trait variation along principal component 1 (PC1), identified as the leaf nitrogen economic spectrum (LNES), orthogonal to the carbon economic axis (PC2). The extremes of LNES were characterized by species with high PNUE, thick leaves, large area, high chlorophyll, low N area , and low LMA (long-leaved N-efficiency species) versus nitrogen-conservative strategies (short-leaved N-inefficiency species). Notably, PH and LL were unrelated to leaf carbon economics. Our results revealed that, compared with PH, LL was a more effective classifier of leaf adaptation strategies in tropical forest understory species. These findings provide novel insights into nitrogen acquisition-conservation trade-offs in forest understory ecosystems and improve mechanistic understanding of leaf trait economics in understory herbaceous plants.

title: Scene-dependent associations between G–C–I corridor morphology and mixed-surface aggregated LST within Beijing's fifth ring road
abstract: Although the thermal associations of street geometry, vegetation, and development intensity have been widely investigated, existing evidence remains fragmented across individual indicators, spatial scales, and isolated seasonal or diurnal scenes. Consequently, planning-relevant corridor-scale frameworks that jointly classify these dimensions, examine their scene-dependent associations with mixed-surface aggregated land surface temperature (LST), and quantify adjusted thermal differences between representative corridor types remain underdeveloped. To address these gaps, we used the high-density built-up area within Beijing's Fifth Ring Road as a case study and integrated four selected ECOSTRESS overpass scenes—summer daytime, summer nighttime, winter daytime, and winter nighttime—with multi-source data on three-dimensional urban form and vegetation. A Geometry–Cover–Intensity (G–C–I) typology was developed to characterize street-adjacent corridor units, and CatBoost combined with SHAP was used to identify dominant predictors, nonlinear response patterns, and interactions across scenes and corridor types. Covariate-adjusted contrasts were then estimated for representative type pairs under comparable observed conditions. The results showed clear scene dependence in the associations between corridor morphology and aggregated LST. The winter scenes were included not to propose winter cooling measures, but to examine whether morphology–LST associations persisted or reversed under cold-season background conditions. Under the selected summer daytime scene, vegetation-related variables, especially street fractional vegetation cover and canopy-structure metrics, showed the strongest cooling-related associations. Under the selected nighttime scenes, building height, interface morphology, and development intensity showed greater relative importance. Candidate turning ranges varied across corridor types, indicating that the thermal associations of a given morphological attribute depend on the joint configuration of geometry, cover, and intensity. In addition, contrasts between low- and high-greening types generally indicated lower aggregated LST for the higher-greening types under the selected summer daytime scene, whereas contrasts involving higher development intensity were predominantly warming-oriented. Overall, this study provides a reproducible workflow for diagnosing scene-dependent morphology–LST associations and translating G–C–I type differences into differentiated management cues. The findings should be interpreted as mixed-surface, corridor-scale aggregated LST patterns observed under selected background scenes, rather than as universal thresholds, pure road-surface temperature, or direct evidence of pedestrian-level thermal exposure.

title: Enhanced NSGA-III-IntPLUS multi-objective framework for optimizing ecological restoration strategies in the Triangle of Central China
abstract: The Triangle of Central China, defined as an interprovincial region in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, encompasses Hubei, Hunan, and Jiangxi provinces, with Wuhan, Changsha, and Nanchang as its principal urban centers. Rapid urban expansion in this region has increasingly encroached upon ecological spaces, threatening ecosystem health and the sustained provision of ecosystem services. Climate change and land-use change are widely recognized as key drivers affecting ecosystem service functions. This study introduces the NSGA-III algorithm to seek a Pareto-optimal balance between ecological protection and economic growth under the Economic and Ecological Balance (EEB) scenario. Additionally, we integrate climate-sensitivity zoning with land-use response zoning to construct a combined “climate risk–human interference” zoning framework. Western and northern Hubei form a “Climate Buffer Zone,” where Water Yield (WY) and Soil Conservation (SC) are largely driven by precipitation (approximately 33%). Central and northern Jiangxi—classified as the “Stable Conservation Zone” and “Fluctuating Gain Zone”—are dominated by evapotranspiration (approximately 50%). Under the EEB scenario, precise spatial allocation of urban construction and ecological protection is achieved through the NSGA-III algorithm, avoiding significant ecological trade-off hotspots. Huanggang and Jingmen are priority areas for future ecological restoration. Under the Economic Development (ED) scenario, Wuhan and Nanchang exhibit a trend of contiguous degradation, which urgently necessitates cross-regional collaborative governance, with the aim of promoting the effective extension of research outcomes from theoretical cognition to decision support.

title: Scale dependence and nonlinear threshold effects of recreation service supply–demand coupling in large river basins
abstract: The matching of recreation service supply and demand affects regional sustainability and human well-being, yet the multi-scale coupling mechanisms and threshold effects of driving factors remain unclear. Taking the Yellow River Basin, this study developed a “grid–county–city” three-scale framework and integrated the MaxEnt model, coupling coordination degree model, random forest permutation test, and segmented threshold identification algorithm to analyze the scale-dependent patterns and driving thresholds of the coupling coordination degree of recreation ecosystem service supply and demand (CCD_RES). Results showed that: (1) Spatial heterogeneity of CCD_RES decreased with increasing scale, ranging from 0.985 at grid and county scales to 0.722 at the city scale; its pattern shifted from scattered in the southern basin (grid scale) to clustering around Xi'an and Zhengzhou (county scale), stabilizing over these core cities (city scale). (2) Driver importance transitioned from “natural constraints” to “social support”: at grid scale, slope (increase in MSE ≈ 100%) and fractional vegetation cover (≈150%) dominated; at county scale, road network density (≈40%) and GDP (≈35%); at city scale, population density (≈25%) and GDP (≈25%). (3) Key drivers showed nonlinear threshold effects: population density thresholds were 208.89 people/km 2 (city) and 206.53 people/km 2 (county), and fractional vegetation cover threshold at grid scale was 0.8. This study reveals scale dependence and nonlinear thresholds of CCD_RES drivers, offering a scientific basis for differentiated spatial management in large river basins.

title: Simulation of non-point source pollution response to extreme rainfall and agricultural activities using the LSPC model: the case of the Zhegao River Basin, a tributary of Lake Chaohu, China
abstract: The intensification of precipitation extremes, owing to global climate change, has significantly altered hydrological processes and pollutant export characteristics in watersheds, exacerbating non-point source (NPS) pollution in agricultural watersheds. This study aimed to clarify the dynamic response mechanisms of NPS pollution in agricultural watersheds to precipitation extremes, focusing on the Zhegao River Basin. Using the LSPC model, a dynamic NPS pollution response model was constructed for the watershed and seven extreme rainfall scenarios (S0–S7) were simulated. The results showed that the timing of extreme rainfall events significantly regulates hydrological intensity and pollution responses in the watershed. Notably, a 1.38-fold increase in rainfall during the non-flood season (S3) resulted in a 1.52-fold increase in runoff, and heavy rainfall events during the flood season (S2) increased total nitrogen (TN) loads by approximately five fold relative to the baseline value, implying differences in rainfall impacts across temporal scales. Further, the temporal coupling of fertilisation and heavy rainfall considerably altered pollutant fluxes. Specifically, heavy rainfall before fertilisation during the flood season (S4) increased NH₃-N load by 350%, while heavy rainfall after fertilisation during the flood season (S5) increased TN loads by 233.3%, reflecting synergistic effects between pollutant sources and rainfall runoff. Therefore, extreme rainfall coupled with agricultural activities exerts a nonlinear amplification effect on watershed NPS pollution, and overall, a multi-level “source control—process interception—systematic governance” adaptive management strategy taking into account the impacts of rainfall and fertilisation is required for the case study watershed.

title: A transferable environmental responsibility framework for provincial water footprints: Production–consumption interaction patterns and inequality in China
abstract: Spatial separation between production, consumption, and environmental burdens complicates responsibility allocation in water footprint assessment. This study developed a transferable environmental responsibility framework and used China's 31 provinces as an empirical case to assess blue, green, and grey water footprints from production and consumption perspectives. By integrating top-down and bottom-up accounting with a water footprint extended multi-regional input-output model, we quantified production-side external contribution, consumption-side external dependence, and their relative balance. Provinces were classified into four interaction pattern groups, and environmental inequality was evaluated using the Theil index. Virtual water flows formed a pronounced interprovincial network in which southeastern coastal provinces acted as major demand hubs, whereas many northeastern and northwestern provinces served as net suppliers of embodied water use and pollution burdens. The environmental responsibility coefficient showed strong validity, exhibiting significant positive correlations with provincial net transfer roles. The weighted Theil index indicated a moderate level of national inequality. Blue water footprint inequality was consistently dominated by between-group differences, grey water footprint inequality by within-group heterogeneity, and green water footprint inequality showed relatively balanced between-group and within-group contributions. Robustness tests based on median- and mean-based thresholds preserved the main conclusions for blue and grey water footprints, while indicating greater threshold sensitivity for green water footprints. The framework and findings provide transferable insights for multi-regional systems where production, consumption, and environmental burdens are spatially decoupled.

title: Unraveling eco-environmental responses and critical thresholds to urban expansion in a dryland region: Evidence from Kashgar, northwestern China
abstract: Accelerated urbanization in drylands under regional development strategies intensifies ecological pressures; however, the non-linear coupling thresholds within fragile oasis–desert ecotones remain poorly understood. This study quantifies the spatiotemporal synergy between Ecological Environmental Quality (EEQ) and Urbanization Level (UL) in Kashgar Prefecture, China, from 2005 to 2021. Utilizing the Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform, we developed a tailored Desert Remote Sensing Ecological Index (DRSEI) to filter severe soil background and salinization noise, pairing it with a multidimensional Comprehensive Urbanization Index (CUI). A Coupling Coordination Degree (CCD) model, dual-constraint boundary analysis, Generalized Additive Models (GAM), and GM(1,1) grey forecasting were integrated to analyze non-linear dynamics, identify critical threshold effects, and project future trends. The results reveal that: (1) the DRSEI followed an inverted “N”-shaped trajectory, wherein riparian ecological gains effectively counterbalanced urban-induced marginal degradation; (2) the regional CCD steadily upgraded from “mild imbalance” to “intermediate coordination,” driving a widening “core-periphery” rift between the monocentric growth pole (Kashgar City) and lagging peripheral counties; and (3) dual-constraint boundary analysis and GAM verification confirm significant non-linear interactive effects of EEQ and CUI on the CCD, identifying a stringent “dual-optimum” threshold window required to achieve highest-level coordination. Furthermore, grey forecasting projects a steady, overall upgrading of the regional CCD from 2023 to 2029, with peripheral counties undergoing sequential echelon transitions toward systemic, high-level synergy.

title: Soil nitrogen mineralization explains seasonal uncertainty of gross primary production estimation for a deciduous broadleaf forest by a light use efficiency model
abstract: Nitrogen is an essential nutrient for plant growth and plays a critical role in photosynthesis and gross primary productivity (GPP). The light use efficiency (LUE) models are perhaps the most classical and widely used to estimate GPP. However, large uncertainties remain in seasonal GPP estimation, partly due to neglecting the effect of nitrogen on ecosystem GPP. Here, we firstly evaluate the error source of LUE model at 89 FLUXNET sites worldwide and found that the large seasonal errors in model estimates were primarily attributable to model structure, particularly the omission of soil nitrogen constraints. We then examined the relationships between soil nitrogen content and tower GPP over the seasonal scale for deciduous broadleaf forests. We found soil nitrogen mineralization, a process for determining soil available nitrogen, closely matched and exhibited strong correlation with observed GPP at daily scale (R 2 = 0.66, p < 0.01), monthly scale (R 2 = 0.74, p < 0.01) and seasonal scales (R 2 = 0.67, p < 0.01). We further found that incorporating soil nitrogen into the estimation of GPP can improve the explained variance of GPP up to 18%. Our results demonstrated that the significant positive impact of soil nitrogen mineralization on GPP cannot be ignored in terrestrial ecosystem GPP estimation by LUE models. Our finding highlights the potential of soil nitrogen mineralization in the estimation of GPP by LUE models for deciduous broadleaf forests.

title: Mapping priority conservation areas for China's rice terraces: an integrated framework for identification and spatial prioritization
abstract: In the Anthropocene, traditional rice terraces have emerged as exemplary sustainable agro-ecosystems due to their dual functions in ecological conservation and cultural heritage. Systematically identifying the spatial distribution of Priority Conservation Areas (PCAs) is a prerequisite for mitigating abandonment risks and enabling effective conservation planning. Focusing on China's rice terraces, this study first developed a national 30 m resolution database by integrating multi-source geospatial data; then established a comprehensive evaluation framework encompassing six dimensions—livelihood, landscape, biodiversity, eco-service, culture, and social values; and finally employed the systematic conservation planning tool Marxan to identify the PCAs under 18 scenarios, with subsequent evaluation using multiple indicators. The results revealed that: (1) The total area of rice terraces in China is approximately 19.1 Mha, primarily distributed south of the Qinling–Huaihe Line, with the highest concentration in the Sichuan Basin. (2) The spatial patterns of PCAs vary across scenarios: cost-excluded scenarios lead to a more concentrated distribution, whereas cost-included scenarios result in a more dispersed pattern with a distinct eastward shift. The core PCAs are primarily clustered in several key regions: southern Zhejiang–northern Fujian, southern Anhui–northern Jiangxi, the Fujian–Guangdong–Jiangxi–Hunan junction, the Guizhou–Hunan–Guangxi junction, and southwestern Yunnan. (3) Regional analysis shows that Yunnan contains the largest number of PCAs, while Sichuan and Chongqing encompass the greatest total rice terrace area within these areas. Furthermore, Zhejiang and Fujian exhibit the highest share of rice terraces designated as PCAs relative to their provincial totals. This study maps China's rice terrace PCAs and demonstrates how regional heterogeneity and value orientation shape conservation outcomes, providing scientific guidance for tailored protection and restoration strategies.

title: Divergent carbon sink resilience and response mechanisms across three forest management types under compound drought–heatwave events in China
abstract: Forest carbon sinks play a pivotal role in global climate change mitigation, yet their stability is increasingly threatened by compound drought–heatwave (CDHW) events. However, the resilience of forest carbon sinks to CDHW events and its differentiation across forest management types remain poorly understood. This study identified CDHW events across China during 2001–2020 and quantified the resistance (Rt), recovery (Rc), and resilience (Rs) of carbon sinks for three forest types: unmanaged natural forests, managed natural forests, and planted forests. An XGBoost-SHAP framework was employed to disentangle the contributions and nonlinear response mechanisms of CDHW attributes and climate legacy effects. Results revealed that: (1) CDHW events annually affected 3.74% ± 2.29% of the study area, with spatial coverage increasing from 3.47% (2001−2010) to 4.01% (2011−2020). (2) Managed natural forests exhibited the strongest overall resilience (Rs = +0.079), achieving supra-recovery following CDHW events. Planted forests displayed the weakest resistance (Rt = −0.050), while unmanaged natural forests showed a pronounced recovery deficit (Rs = −0.084). (3) The preceding-year standardized NEP dominated all resilience models (22.15%–53.36%), followed by CDHW event characteristics (16.70%–35.82%). CDHW severity exhibited forest-type-specific thresholds: 1.45 °C for unmanaged natural forests and planted forests versus 1.87 °C for managed natural forests, with opposing response directionalities: below their respective thresholds, severity suppressed resistance in unmanaged natural and planted forests but promoted it in managed natural forests, while above the thresholds the directionality reversed. The thermal acclimation window of managed natural forests was broader than that of unmanaged natural forests. These findings indicate that managed natural forests provide the most stable carbon sink capacity under compound extremes, and that silvicultural management interventions can extend the thermal tolerance range of forest carbon sinks; accordingly, managed natural forests should be prioritized as a climate-adaptive forestry strategy. This study provides critical evidence for formulating differentiated forest management strategies that simultaneously enhance carbon sequestration and stabilize sink functioning.

title: Macrophyte-based assessment of European rivers: Status, gaps, and a practical checklist for improvement
abstract: Aquatic macrophytes are key indicators of ecological status in European rivers and are recognised as biological quality elements under the EU Water Framework Directive (WFD). Following the adoption of the Water Framework Directive (2000), twenty-nine national macrophyte-based assessment systems have been implemented and intercalibrated across the European Union (EU). These systems have been shown to respond to ecological degradation, with the strongest evidence relating to nutrient enrichment. However, their application has generated contrasting perspectives: while macrophyte indices are widely regarded as effective indicators, they have also been criticised as lacking ecological interpretability or explicit links to human pressures. A balanced evaluation of these perspectives is hindered by the limited accessibility of methods, many of which remain unpublished or are available only in grey literature, and the absence of a comprehensive, integrative overview. Here, we present the first synthesis of 29 macrophyte-based assessment systems across EU Member States and associated countries, explicitly addressing these contrasting perspectives and providing a coherent framework for their interpretation. We examine these systems with respect to their taxonomic scope, metrics, target pressures, pressure–response relationships, and boundary-setting approaches. Most systems rely on indices combining taxa-specific indicator values with abundance data and show strong relationships with nutrient concentrations. Nevertheless, substantial differences persist, including wide variation in taxonomic coverage (40–450 taxa) and methodological design, while the ability to distinguish among multiple pressures remains limited. Invasive alien species (IAS) are inconsistently incorporated into the assessment systems. Emerging tools such as environmental DNA (eDNA) offer promising opportunities to complement traditional assessment approaches but require further development. We identify key gaps and propose a practical checklist to improve accessibility, strengthen ecological interpretation, and guide future development of macrophyte-based assessment systems in the context of climate change and emerging environmental challenges.

title: Interpretable deep-learning assessment of environmental indicators of global marine plastic pollution across ocean basins and climate zones
abstract: Marine plastic pollution has emerged as a pressing global environmental issue and poses a significant threat to both oceanic ecosystems and human well-being. Nevertheless, the patterns of its dispersion and the environmental associations underlying its distribution remain inadequately characterized on a worldwide scale, primarily due to the limitations of traditional monitoring and modeling techniques. In this study, we introduced an interpretable deep learning (DL) framework to predict the plastic pollution level across global oceans and to elucidate the model-attributed environmental associations. Multiple global datasets of plastic pollution concentrations and relevant environmental variables from 2018 to 2022 were integrated. A total of 1193 surface-ocean records were initially compiled. After harmonization and quality control, 1155 records were retained for model development, including 916 training samples and 239 samples in a held-out internal test set. The predictive performance of the FCNN was benchmarked against several widely used machine-learning models. Although XGBoost achieved the highest predictive accuracy and was identified as the best-performing benchmark model, the FCNN demonstrated competitive predictive performance and was retained as the focal deep-learning architecture for evaluating the proposed interpretable neural-network framework. The FCNN model demonstrated moderate predictive performance under random internal validation based on 13 environmental predictor variables spanning geographic, biological, biogeochemical, physicochemical, physical-dynamic, and transport-related categories, achieving a mean five-fold cross-validation R 2 of 0.608 and a held-out internal test-set R 2 of 0.612. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis identified DTC, dissolved oxygen, net primary productivity, and phytoplankton concentration as the main environmental indicators contributing to model predictions. Stratification analysis further revealed distinct regional differences in model-attribution patterns and predictor importance across the four major ocean basins (Atlantic, Pacific, Indian, and Arctic) and climate zones (tropical, temperate, and polar), thereby emphasizing the necessity for region-specific management strategies. This interpretable DL framework provides a data-driven approach for large-scale marine plastic pollution assessment and regional monitoring support within the range of environmental conditions represented by the available data.

title: Coastal protection and inland flood mitigation values provided by priority wetland sites in the East Asian-Australasian Flyway
abstract: The East Asian–Australasian Flyway connects breeding and wintering grounds for migratory waterbirds across East Asia, South-East Asia and Australasia. Wetlands along the flyway buffer coasts against storm surges, store floodwaters, and sustain globally significant biodiversity. Yet the extent to which sites of biodiversity importance protect people remains unclear. We assessed 41 wetlands in Bangladesh, Cambodia, the Philippines, and Thailand identified as biodiversity priority sites. Using global datasets and hydrological models, we quantified nine biophysical and economic metrics of hazard mitigation, including coastal risk reduction, flood storage, downstream beneficiaries, and economic value of avoided infrastructure damage. Results show that priority sites deliver substantial benefits relative to their extent. Coastal wetlands, especially mangroves in Bangladesh and the Philippines, consistently exceeded national averages for ecological efficiency (% risk reduction and per-hectare avoided damages), though beneficiary numbers varied with settlement patterns. Philippine sites accounted for 12% of the national annual flood-protection value while covering only 3% of the mangrove area, and Bangladeshi sites yielded nearly nine times higher per-hectare values than other mangroves. Inland wetlands showed more variable outcomes: Agusan Marsh and Bueng Boraphet contributed substantial flood storage, while others fell below national averages due to hydrological configuration. Across all metrics, priority sites exceeded national averages in 14 of 36 metric-country combinations, were lower in nine, and did not differ in the remainder. This study provides the first multi-country assessment of how wetlands prioritised for biodiversity contribute to hazard mitigation, using a standardised indicator framework to support integrated conservation and climate adaptation planning.

title: Ecological–economic spatial mismatch and nonlinear drivers in ecologically fragile counties of the upper and middle reaches of the Yellow River: insights from XGBoost–SHAP
abstract: Ecologically fragile regions often face difficulty in improving ecological environmental quality and economic development in a synchronized way. However, most previous studies emphasize overall coordination and pay less attention to spatial relationship types, transition patterns, and their drivers. Focusing on ecologically fragile counties in the Upper and Middle Reaches of the Yellow River (UMYR), China, this study constructed an Ecological Index (EI) and an Economic Development Index (EDI), and combined local bivariate Moran's I with an interpretable XGBoost–SHAP framework to identify EI–EDI relationship types, their transitions, and nonlinear driver effects in 2012, 2017, and 2022. Ecological quality remained broadly stable, whereas economic development became increasingly concentrated in the east. The non-significant type consistently accounted for the largest share, the LL type expanded in north-central arid counties, and the LH type contracted in western ecological protection areas, indicating that ecological–economic relationships did not evolve linearly toward coordination. XGBoost–SHAP further showed marked type-specific nonlinearities: primary-industry share reflected structural heterogeneity, population density exhibited a segmented turning pattern, and slope and annual precipitation showed clearer threshold-like responses. Overall, ecological–economic relationships in ecologically fragile counties of the UMYR are better understood as a process shaped by typological differentiation, spatial reorganization, and nonlinear driver effects. These findings provide empirical support for differentiated territorial spatial governance.

title: Using interpretable machine learning to reveal carbon storage responses associated with rapid development in a “mountain-plain-hill” metropolitan area: Marginal patterns and interactions
abstract: Rapid urbanization reshapes land use and carbon storage, yet nonlinear explanatory patterns and planning implications in mountain-plain-hill metropolitan areas remain insufficiently understood. This study selected the Chengdu Metropolitan Area to construct a comprehensive “past-future” analytical framework. By coupling system dynamics (SD), the Patch-generating Land Use Simulation (PLUS) model, the Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Tradeoffs (InVEST) model, and interpretable machine learning (IML), we quantified the spatiotemporal evolution of carbon storage and explored the marginal patterns and nonlinear interactions among the main explanatory factors. The results indicate that: (1) carbon storage decreased by 6.28 Tg from 2000 to 2020, with spatial changes mainly occurring among cropland, woodland, and building land. By 2050, carbon storage is projected to increase by 52.19 Tg and 39.47 Tg under SSP126 and SSP245, respectively, but decrease by 23.16 Tg under SSP585. (2) Elevation (DEM), slope (SLOPE), and population density (POP) were consistently identified as the main explanatory factors associated with carbon storage in the model. DEM and SLOPE showed positive marginal associations with carbon storage, whereas POP showed a negative marginal association. (3) Clear SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based nonlinear interactions were detected among the main explanatory factors. These findings suggest that carbon storage management should follow topographic gradients. Low-elevation plains should prioritize compact urban growth, cropland protection, and green network construction, whereas mid- and high-elevation areas should strengthen woodland conservation and ecological restoration.

title: Topography-human activities-climate jointly shape the multi-scale spatiotemporal patterns of alpine ecosystem services: Evidence from the Zoige Plateau, China
abstract: Alpine ecosystems serve as critical bulwarks for regional ecological security and provide irreplaceable ecosystem services (ESs). However, the multi-scale interactions among ESs and their coupled natural-human driving mechanisms remain poorly understood, hindering targeted improvements and collaborative management of ecological functions. This study quantified the spatiotemporal dynamics, trade-offs/synergies, and bundles of four key ESs (carbon storage (CS), habitat quality (HQ), soil conservation (SC), and water yield (WY)) across different scales in China's Zoige Plateau. XGBoost-SHAP machine learning and structural equation modeling (SEM) were used to explore the impacts of topography, climate, and human activities on ESs and their driving pathways. The results revealed the following: (1) Across the three observation years, WY and SC were higher in 2020 than in 2000, whereas CS and HQ showed lower values in 2020. Spatially, WY was higher in the south and lower in the north; high values of CS and HQ were concentrated in the marsh wetlands and forests. (2) Significant trade-offs and synergies existed among ESs. HQ showed synergistic relationships with CS and SC, while WY exhibited trade-offs with CS and HQ, with evident scale effects. Multi-scale ES bundles displayed clear spatial differentiation. (3) Machine learning identified precipitation (PRE) dominated changes in WY, slope significantly promoted SC, and elevation (DEM) contributed the most to CS and HQ. SEM further indicated that DEM directly influenced PRE, potential evapotranspiration (PET), and the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), thereby establishing the natural supply base for ESs. Meanwhile, gross domestic product (GDP) acted as an intermediate regulatory factor, significantly mediating the conversion efficiency of these three variables into ESs. This study reveals a nonlinear coupling mechanism in which topography, climate, and socio-economic regulatory factors synergistically shape ESs, providing scientific support for differentiated zoning, synergistic optimization, and sustainable management of alpine ecosystems.

title: Characteristics and dynamic evolution patterns of drought-flood abrupt alternation events based on three-dimensional identification
abstract: Drought-flood abrupt alternation (DFAA) events, as a unique hydrometeorological disaster, remain poorly understood in terms of their dynamic evolution characteristics and nonlinear mechanisms. This study introduces a daily-scale Dry-Wet Abrupt Alternation Index (DWAAI), which is constructed from daily SPEI data derived from the China Meteorological Forcing Dataset. The DWAAI integrates multi-timescale (30-, 90-, and 360-day) SPEI values through a weighted scheme that explicitly accounts for cumulative effects of antecedent drought or flood conditions. By identifying DFAA patches and applying spatial connectivity rules, temporal overlap criteria, and patch-merging procedures, we innovatively develop a three-dimensional (longitude-latitude-time) identification framework that enables continuous spatiotemporal tracking of DFAA patches. By incorporating event migration and severity transitions into the assessment framework, we systematically analyze the spatio-temporal evolution of DFAA events. The main findings are as follows: (1) Based on DWAAI, DFAA events are classified into four severity levels (mild, moderate, severe, and extreme), with mean severity, duration, affected area, and intensity all increasing progressively with event level. Moderate events occur most frequently and exhibit the most concentrated within-group distributions. (2) Spatially, event frequency shows an east-high and west-low pattern, with the South China Humid region serving as a hotspot. Over the past four decades, both drought to flood and flood to drought events have shown fluctuating increases, with the most significant increase observed in the Northwest Inland Arid Region. (3) Approximately 51.28% of events exhibited expanding affected areas during their evolution, with about half accompanied by changes in event severity, and four primary evolution patterns were identified. (4) VPD and NINO were identified as common influencing factors across all four regions, indicating that DFAA events are jointly regulated by both region-common and region-specific factors. This study incorporates the dynamic evolution dimension into DFAA assessment, deepens the understanding of DFAA evolution mechanisms, and provides a new analytical framework for risk prevention and control.

title: Opportunity or challenge? Exploring the impact of artificial intelligence on climate change adaptive capacity
abstract: Climate change is expected to negatively impact countries worldwide, but the adaptive responses of different nations to this threat vary significantly. Efforts to enhance adaptive capacity to climate change have been largely insufficient. This paper aims to explore how to make use of artificial intelligence to enhance the adaptive capacity to climate change by using a dataset spanning 66 countries. This paper first finds a positive link between artificial intelligence and climate change adaptive capacity, showing that artificial intelligence significantly boosts adaptive capacity to climate change. Furthermore, artificial intelligence enhances climate change adaptive capacity across all areas, from infrastructure adaptability to ecosystem services adaptability. Third, this paper confirms a significant moderating effect of climate aid. Climate aid amplifies artificial intelligence's effectiveness in enhancing climate change adaptive capacity, highlighting a synergistic interaction. Fourth, we identify natural disaster losses and productivity as major channels through which artificial intelligence impacts climate change adaptive capacity. In addition, impact channels vary by income levels: in low-income countries, artificial intelligence facilitates the development of energy infrastructure, whereas in high-income countries, artificial intelligence supports energy transition, leading to higher climate change adaptive capacity levels. Based on these findings, we propose several policy implications to enhance AI-driven climate adaptation, scale up climate aid effectiveness, and tailor energy pathways according to country income levels.

title: Soundscape as a proxy for seagrass meadow condition and anthropogenic activity
abstract: Soundscape analysis has emerged as a relevant tool in functional marine ecology. However, how habitat-specific variables, environmental and biological components, and external pressures influence acoustic metrics requires further validation. This study investigates how soundscape structure and dynamics are influenced by seagrass meadow conditions, seasonal patterns, and anthropogenic disturbance. To this aim, the soundscape of P. oceanica meadows in 16 sites across two Mediterranean Marine Protected Areas was analysed (over 6,600 5-min recordings). The results revealed a multifaceted and highly site-specific soundscape. Diel cycles were the primary driver of the soundscape, with a significant nocturnal increase associated with fish sounds and the snapping rates of invertebrates. Meadow density and intermediate coverage positively influenced many acoustic metrics, suggesting that more structured meadows supported a more heterogeneous acoustic environment. However, denser meadows exhibited a reduction in low-frequency Sound Pressure Levels, indicating that the canopy acted as an acoustic attenuator. Furthermore, meadows on sandy substrates negatively influenced almost all acoustic metrics compared to those on rocky substrates, which provided more niches for soniferous species and acted as a reflective surface. Boat noise was pervasive and acted as the primary driver of low-frequency Sound Pressure Levels while significantly reducing acoustic complexity and diversity metrics. In conclusion, acoustic metrics reflected the dynamic interactions between habitat structure, biological processes, and human activity. These findings confirmed that soundscape analysis is a powerful complementary tool for assessing the functional state of P. oceanica meadows and that soundscape should be integrated into conservation strategies as a key functional attribute.

title: Species–Community Contextual Fit Index (SCCFI): a word embedding-derived ecological indicator from co-occurrence data
abstract: Ecological indicators derived from standard biodiversity surveys are needed for monitoring community change where functional trait and environmental data are incomplete. Here, we propose the Species–Community Contextual Fit Index (SCCFI), an embedding-derived indicator that quantifies how well a species fits the ecological context represented by its local community. Inspired by the distributional hypothesis in natural language processing, we treated species as words and local communities as sentences, and used Word2Vec to learn species embeddings from neighbourhood co-occurrence patterns. SCCFI was calculated as the cosine similarity between a focal species embedding and the leave-one-out embedding of its surrounding community. We evaluated the framework in two forest dynamics plots: Dinghushan, China, and Barro Colorado Island, Panama. Species embeddings predicted functional traits and species-level environmental associations, indicating that contextual similarity in the embedding space captures ecological resemblance among species. Community embeddings reconstructed soil nutrient and topographic gradients more accurately than weighted averaging and count-based approaches, supporting their use as representations of local ecological context. SCCFI was positively associated with local abundance and negatively associated with mortality for most species in both forests. These results show that SCCFI translates co-occurrence-derived embeddings into an interpretable indicator of species–community contextual fit. Because SCCFI requires only co-occurrence data, it provides a scalable tool for biodiversity monitoring, early warning of population decline and conservation prioritisation in data-limited ecosystems.

title: A decade of Sentinel-2 observations for Water Framework Directive assessment in an anthropized coastal lagoon: The Berre Lagoon (France)
abstract: Coastal lagoons are productive yet vulnerable ecosystems exposed to strong anthropogenic pressures. The Berre Lagoon (southern France) illustrates this vulnerability, having undergone long-term degradation from large freshwater, nutrient and sediment inputs. Using a decade of calibrated and validated Sentinel-2 satellite observations (2015–2025), this study demonstrates the value of Earth Observation (EO) for Water Framework Directive (WFD) assessment and operational lagoon management. Satellite-derived chlorophyll-a concentration ([chl-a]), suspended particulate matter ([SPM]) and Secchi depth (Zs) were used to derive WFD-consistent indicators: the phytoplankton biomass Ecological Quality Ratio (EQR B ), an SPM-based hydropower discharge indicator, and a Zs-derived Potential Seagrass Habitat (PSH). Results show that eutrophication assessed from satellite is more severe than suggested by the current WFD monitoring network, which fails to capture major phytoplankton blooms occurring from late summer to early winter. Satellite-derived [SPM] time series also reveal a shift in hydropower operation from near-continuous discharges (2016–2021) to winter-restricted releases after 2022. This transition increased summer water transparency and expanded light-suitable seagrass habitat by about 15% (PSH ≈ 26 km 2 ), exceeding the 15 km 2 threshold required for “good” macrophyte status. Overall, this study shows how satellite observations can diagnose changes in anthropogenic pressures, monitor management-driven recovery, and provide actionable indicators for WFD implementation in coastal lagoons.

title: Community shifts across canopy composition: Threshold responses of forest floor vegetation indicate overstory change in temperate beech forests
abstract: Introducing new and more tree species to species-poor forest canopies is seen as a key measure of silviculture to adapt temperate forests to climate change by distributing the risk of climate-related mortality and disturbance events across multiple tree species. In Central Europe, this strategy meets forests that would naturally be dominated by European beech ( Fagus sylvatica ), which excludes most of its competitors by shade-casting. Analyzing a dataset of native and non-native alternative tree species that are candidates to partly replace beech in managed forests, we posed the question how this strategy would affect the species richness and species composition of forest floor vegetation. We selected beech stands in southwestern Germany with canopy fractions of <10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and > 90% of other tree species, including Douglas fir ( Pseudotsuga menziesii ), silver fir ( Abies alba ), sessile oak ( Quercus petraea ), red oak ( Quercus rubra ), and mixtures of several native broadleaves. Where appropriate, we differentiated between stands on acidic and base-rich soils. We found increases in species richness with increasing canopy fractions of Douglas fir, silver fir, sessile oak only on base-rich soil, and mixed broadleaves compared to the naturally species-poor beech forests. These increases were consistent with increased light availability with reduced share of beech in the canopy and to better nutrient availability from non-beech litter on base-rich soil. Species richness did not change with the introduction of red oak and sessile oak on acidic soil. Species composition also changed, with several species characteristic of closed beech forests showing early declines along some canopy gradients of other tree species, whereas more generalist, nitrophilic, or light-demanding species increased mainly at higher admixture levels. Our results suggest that partial displacement of beech by other tree species causes significant changes in the ground vegetation. These threshold responses indicate that even low admixture levels can alter characteristic beech forest vegetation and should be considered when balancing climate-adaptation and conservation objectives.

title: Corrigendum to “Long-term multi-source remote sensing reveals region-specific driving mechanisms of forest fire spatiotemporal patterns across floristic sub-regions in mountainous Yunnan, China” [Ecol. Indic. 189 (2026) 115239]
An interactive data tool for ecosystem service value assessment in the Great Barrier Reef
abstract: SYNTHESEAS (System for iNTegrating Human dimensions, Ecosystem Services and Economic Assessment for Sustainability) is an interactive R Shiny application developed by Commonwealth Scientific Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) to catalogue and share metadata on datasets related to ecosystem service values in the Australian Great Barrier Reef (GBR) region. Designed primarily for environmental managers, policy-makers, and researchers, the platform supports more informed decision-making by providing a structured overview of data describing the uses, benefits, and values associated with GBR ecosystems. SYNTHESEAS users can explore and filter datasets by ecosystem service category (Provisioning, Regulating, Cultural), specific service types (e.g. recreational fishing), and major beneficiary groups (Government, Households, Industry, and First Nations Peoples). The tool also enables filtering along key components of the Ecosystem Service Value Chain (ESVC), including types of use, methods of quantification or qualification, economic multipliers, and derived values. By integrating diverse data sources and making them accessible through an intuitive interface, SYNTHESEAS facilitates transparent, inclusive, and spatially nuanced assessments of ecosystem service values that pertain to marine social-ecological systems.

title: Crucial role of conditionally rare taxa in preserving bacterioplankton community stability in a large reservoir during seasonal water level fluctuations
abstract: Bacterioplankton are core drivers of biogeochemical cycles in reservoir ecosystems, playing a vital role in maintaining water quality and ecosystem functioning. However, the response mechanisms and functional logic of sub-communities with varying abundances under intense hydrological fluctuations remain poorly understood. This study investigated the community dynamics and assembly processes of rare taxa (RT), conditionally rare taxa (CRT), and conditionally rare and abundant taxa (CRAT) across different hydrological periods in the Danjiangkou Reservoir. Results showed that microbial species richness and evenness peaked during high-water periods but decreased significantly during drawdown and low-water phases due to hydrological shifts. Network topology analysis revealed that rare taxa preserved latent diversity during stable water levels, while conditionally rare taxa (CRT) consistently served as the core topological backbone, facilitating community structural reorganization through species replacement after disturbances. Functional annotation confirmed that CRT possess remarkable metabolic plasticity, ensuring the continuity of key nutrient cycles through functional compensation under environmental stress. Hydrological fluctuations primarily regulated the succession pathways and functional homeostasis of sub-communities by altering the vertical distribution of physicochemical factors and nutrient availability. These findings highlight the important ecological role of CRT in maintaining microbial network robustness and community organization under hydrological fluctuations, providing scientific support for adaptive reservoir management and ecological assessment of strategic water resources under climate change.

title: Multi-scale evapotranspiration and evaporative stress as indicators of vegetation health and drought response – an application in central Missouri, USA
abstract: Satellite estimates of evapotranspiration (ET) based on thermal infrared retrievals of land-surface temperature enable monitoring of vegetation water use and health/stress at sub-field to global scales. The information content of these products varies with pixel size, reflecting dominant drivers of land-surface fluxes at different scales as well as tradeoffs in satellite spatial vs. temporal coverage. This study evaluates the performance and utility of multi-scale ET and Evaporative Stress Index (ESI) products at 4-km (GOES), 500-m (VIIRS-M band), and 30-m (Landsat+ECOSTRESS+VIIRS-I5 band, spatially sharpened) resolutions across a heterogeneous agricultural-ecological landscape in central Missouri, USA. At 30-m, the modeling framework combines multiple Landsat-like thermal and optical datasets to improve temporal sampling at that critical agricultural management scale. Daily ET and weekly ESI are compared with eddy covariance fluxes, PhenoCam observations, drought classifications, and crop condition data collected over the Central Missouri River Basin from 2017 to 2023, a period including significant drought events. A rotation-correction methodology applied to the 30-m ESI reduces crop-rotation artifacts and improves timing and magnitude of stress detection relative to standard pixel-based approaches. Together, the multi-scale products reveal complementary drought-response signals: coarse ESI captures regional drought signals with good temporal response, whereas 30-m ESI resolves local drivers of stress, management actions, post-disturbance recovery, and landcover-specific drought sensitivity. A strong correlation is identified between 30-m ESI and corn and soybean crop condition at harvest, suggesting potential value for yield prediction. These findings support operational implementation of 30-m ESI within a cloud platform such as OpenET and highlight the growing value of multi-sensor thermal constellations for field-scale drought monitoring and agricultural decision-support.

title: Analysis of evolution characteristics of water resources development and utilization in Shaanxi Province based on emergy theory-based water footprint
abstract: To address critical water resource challenges in Shaanxi Province, this study integrates emergy analysis with the ecological water footprint (EWF) approach to develop an emergy-based water resources ecological footprint (EEF) model. The framework was employed to quantify the emergy-based ecological footprint, emergy-based carrying capacity, and sustainability status of water resources from 2013 to 2024. Both the EEF and carrying capacity exhibited fluctuating upward trends; however, the carrying capacity consistently remained below the ecological footprint, resulting in a persistent ecological deficit. Agricultural water use dominated the total footprint, accounting for 63.47%, while ecological and environmental water use contributed the smallest share (4.15%). The water resources ecological pressure index exceeded 1.0, indicating a sub-optimal security status, and the ecological-economic coordination index remained below the theoretical optimum of 1.414. These findings underscore that the ecological security of water resources in Shaanxi remains precarious. Enhancing comprehensive water use efficiency represents the principal strategy for advancing sustainable water resource management in the region.

title: Landscape ecological risk assessment and multi-scenario simulation in the Kaidu-Kongque River Basin
abstract: Landscape ecological risk assessment (LERA) is of key importance for maintaining the stability of natural systems and guiding land spatial optimization. However, quantifying landscape ecological risk (LER) in arid river basins remains challenging because of fragile ecosystems, rapid land-use transitions, and increasing human disturbances. Taking the Kaidu-Kongque River Basin as a typical region, this study integrated land-use transition analysis, PLUS simulations, LERA, and XGBoost-SHAP to systematically examine land-use evolution, spatiotemporal patterns of LER, and associated predictors. Based on validation using 2020 land-use data, future LER distributions were further estimated under multiple development pathways for 2030. Results showed that (1) During 2005–2024, the regional landscape was overwhelmingly characterized by barren land and grassland, together covering over 90% of the basin. Cropland increased by 2046.60 km 2 , while barren land decreased by 1353.55 km 2 . Grassland experienced a total outflow of 3512.74 km 2 , mainly converted to cropland and barren land. (2) LER exhibited an overall downward tendency, with the high- and highest-risk areas decreasing by 3387.79 km 2 . Global Moran's I remained significantly positive from 2005 to 2024, ranging from 0.776 to 0.803, indicating persistent spatial clustering of risk. (3) The XGBoost-SHAP framework demonstrated relatively good predictive performance under five-fold spatial block cross-validation. Among the selected predictors, natural and river-proximity variables exhibited higher model-based predictive contributions to LER variation than the socioeconomic variables. (4) Scenario simulations for 2030 indicated that the LER distribution would largely maintain the historical pattern, but with varying risk levels and class structures. Relative to 2024, the natural development (ND) scenario reduced the combined area of high- and highest-risk classes by 5936.92 km 2 . Relative to the 2030 ND scenario, the ecological protection (EP) and economic development (ED) scenarios further reduced this area by 5773.84 km 2 and 2568.52 km 2 , respectively. These changes can be interpreted through four coupled land-process pathways: oasis agricultural redistribution, grassland-buffer degradation, aquatic-patch fragmentation, and desert-margin disturbance. These findings provide landscape-index-based evidence for spatially targeted land management and pattern-based ecological risk control in arid basins.

title: Assessing the impact of natural environment and human activities on the ecological environmental quality based on RSEI in Inner Mongolia from 2000 to 2020
abstract: The ecological environment quality of Inner Mongolia is a fundamental pillar for sustaining regional environmental health and safeguarding human well-being. Despite its critical importance, the region has faced escalating ecological challenges in recent years, yet the dynamics of its ecosystems and the underlying drivers of change remain largely underexplored. This study aims to assess the ecological environment quality in Inner Mongolia and investigate the impacts of a total of seventeen natural and human factors using remote sensing data and machine learning. The remote sensing ecological index (RSEI) was used to reveal the ecological environment quality and its spatiotemporal variation from 2000 to 2020 was analyzed. An interpretable machine learning framework, integrating Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) with eXtreme Gradient Boosting Trees (XGBoost), was then employed to uncover the complex driving mechanisms influencing the ecological environment quality. The results reveal a slight but clear improving trend in the ecological environment quality over the two decades, accompanied by pronounced spatial heterogeneity. Notably, net improvement is characterized by significant expansion of moderate and good areas, alongside contraction of poor and worst areas. The XGBoost-SHAP model identifies climatic factors as primary drivers, with precipitation as the most influential positive factor (exceeding 273.79 mm), while temperature variables act as dominant negative factors (suppressing the ecological environment quality beyond 3.02 °C and 11.71 °C). Relationships are predominantly nonlinear with critical thresholds. Interaction analysis further indicates that any single factor's effect highly depends on other factors. Crucially, these findings demonstrate that the overarching regional vegetation recovery is fundamentally a climate-driven process, wherein anthropogenic restoration efforts play a secondary role. By elucidating these nonlinear and threshold-dependent mechanisms, this study provides a robust, transferable basis for targeted ecological restoration and management strategies, offering critical insights for arid ecosystems in Inner Mongolia and globally.

title: Corrigendum to “The utility of different acoustic indicators to describe biological sounds of a coral reef soundscape” [Ecol. Indic. 124 (2021) 107435]
Response of vegetation ecological water requirement to landscape evolution: From non-linear regulation to critical sensitive zones
abstract: The intensification of global environmental change has accelerated the reorganization of terrestrial landscapes. Such structural variations inevitably alter local climatic conditions and ecosystem functions, thereby governing the spatiotemporal distribution of ecological water requirement (EWR). However, the non-linear constraining effects of landscape spatial configuration on vegetation EWR remain underexplored. This study characterized landscape pattern evolution in the Ziya River Basin (ZYRB) and applied a SHAP-interpreted random forest model to decouple its regulatory effects on EWR. Furthermore, a comprehensive framework for sensitivity analysis was developed to identify critical thresholds and sensitive zones. Results indicated a distinct trend toward landscape fragmentation and diversification from 1990 to 2023. The increased patch fragmentation, shape complexity, and diversity, particularly the Fractal Dimension Index ( r = −0.73) was associated with reduced EWR, whereas heightened structural connectivity amplified water demand. Spatially, climatic factors dominated the heterogeneity of EWR, accounting for about 64% of the total importance. Among the landscape pattern indices, the Fractal Dimension Index (FRAC) and Patch Cohesion Index (COHESION) emerged as the leading modulators, with each explaining approximately 9% of the total variance. The response of EWR to landscape drivers exhibited the U-shaped or fluctuating trends rather than simple linearity. The meteorologically sensitive zones identified based on the thresholds were predominantly concentrated in mountain-plain ecotones and groundwater over-exploited regions distributed along a northeast-southwest strip extending across eastern Shijiazhuang and central Handan City. Landscape -sensitive zones coincided with regions of high structural complexity, which were clustered in the western parts of Shijiazhuang and Xingtai City, as well as in Yangquan City. These insights underscore the critical role of landscape complexity in buffering water stress and provide the spatially explicit scientific basis for formulating water regulation measures and land management strategies. The proposed framework possesses broad applicability for diagnosing constraint mechanisms and delineating critical zones in diverse ecological contexts.

title: From composite resilience assessment to indicator-based structural fragility diagnosis in the Lower Yellow River Basin
abstract: Composite resilience indices summarize observed conditions in river-basin social-ecological systems, but they rarely reveal whether administrative units are structurally linked through similar responses to shared pressures. Here, we extend composite resilience assessment into an indicator-based diagnosis of structural fragility in the Shandong section of the Lower Yellow River Basin, China. A harmonized county-level dataset covering 25 counties and six benchmark years from 2000 to 2022 was used to construct a 34-indicator resilience assessment across social, economic, ecological, and water-resource domains. We first identified recurrent dominant drivers using Geodetector and estimated domain-specific driver coefficients. These coefficients were combined with county-level driver values to construct response attributes, response-similarity networks, and random and targeted node-removal stress tests. Composite resilience increased overall from 2000 to 2022, but its spatial hierarchy persisted: higher values remained concentrated in central and eastern counties, whereas several western counties repeatedly fell into the lower-value group. The response-similarity networks showed that state-based rankings did not necessarily correspond to structural embeddedness. Counties with moderate or lower composite scores could be more strongly embedded in response networks than some higher-scoring counties. At the node level, residual structural cohesion identified recurrent cross-domain dependence more clearly than functional retention. Four county nodes repeatedly appeared in the residual-cohesion upper tail across multiple networks, revealing cross-domain structural relevance that was not visible from composite scores alone. Progressive node-removal tests confirmed this structural sensitivity. Random removal produced gradual degradation, whereas targeted removal of structurally central counties caused earlier and sharper losses in normalized global efficiency and structural cohesion. These findings show that composite resilience scores alone are insufficient for diagnosing structural fragility in regulated and resource-constrained basins. The framework separates counties with weak observed conditions from counties that disproportionately maintain response-network performance, offering a clearer basis for basin management priorities and cross-county coordination.

title: Multidimensional variations in lateral hydrological connectivity and nonlinear ecological thresholds for vegetation in regulated floodplains
abstract: Lateral hydrological connectivity (LHC) is crucial for maintaining the health of floodplain ecosystems; however, its evolutionary mechanisms under the dual stressors of large hydraulic engineering and climate variability remain poorly understood. Focusing on the Jingjiang reach, a critical response zone in the middle Yangtze River, this study comprehensively analyzed the spatiotemporal evolution of its river network from 2000 to 2022 using long-term remote sensing and hydrological data. The evaluation was conducted across three dimensions: topological efficiency (graph theory α index), geomorphological structure (river network density), and hydraulic function (water surface ratio). To overcome the limitations of traditional linear weighting, an R-Vine Copula joint probability framework was employed. This approach accurately captured the non-Gaussian and tail dependence characteristics among variables, facilitating the construction of a highly robust Connectivity Index (CI). Results indicate that over the past two decades, the river network topology underwent a four-stage, irreversible transition from a naturally braided baseline to a channelized locked state. Furthermore, long-term evolutionary analysis revealed a distinct “trend decoupling” phenomenon: while runoff increased due to climate variability, flood-season LHC divergently decreased. This confirms that LHC relies heavily on flood peak pulse intensity rather than total annual runoff, underscoring the functional decoupling induced by the “peak-shaving” operations of the Three Gorges Dam. Ecologically, floodplain vegetation, represented by the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), exhibited a typical saturated nonlinear response to LHC. We statistically estimated a potential eco-hydrological transition interval (CI: 0.45–0.55), suggesting a shift in the role of LHC from “resource provisioning” to “physiological stress.” Ultimately, this research elucidates how the physical structure of river networks dictates hydrological functions, which in turn nonlinearly drive vegetation health in regulated floodplains. By unpacking these cascaded interactions, this study provides robust methodological support for the scientific operation of large cascade reservoirs and wetland ecological restoration.

title: Assessing the interactive effects of land use and climate change on species assemblages of giant panda and its sympatric large- and medium-sized terrestrial mammals
abstract: Land use and climate change are currently two most important drivers of biodiversity loss worldwide. Although the effect of these two drivers on species assemblages has been widely assessed both in isolation and in combination, their interactive effects (i.e., additive, synergistic, or antagonistic) are still poorly understood. Here, we used MaxEnt algorithm to project the potential distribution of 23 large- and medium-sized terrestrial mammals in the giant panda range for three model configurations in the 2070s: ( i ) current land use conditions and future climate conditions; ( ii ) future land use conditions and current climate conditions; and ( iii ) future land use conditions and future climate conditions. Then, we assessed the single and combined effects of land use and climate change on four diversity indices (i.e., changes in species richness, species gains, species losses and Sørensen similarity) and their interactive effects on species losses and species gains. Our results showed that land use change effects were substantially weaker than climate change effects and their interactive effects were additive in most cases. Moreover, both the climate change impacts and land use change impacts are spatially highly variable, with the greatest impacts in Xiaoxiangling mountains. These findings highlight the necessity and importance of assessing the interactive effect of land use and climate change on species assemblages and therefore provide new insights for adopting effective local climate and land use management polices to cope with global change.

title: Imperfect detection and sampling effort shape ground beetle (Carabidae) diversity indicators in large-scale monitoring
abstract: Soil biodiversity indicators are increasingly used to inform environmental assessment and policy, yet their robustness is often constrained by heterogeneous sampling designs and imperfect species detection. Surface-active arthropods, such as ground beetles (Carabidae), are widely monitored using pitfall-based methods, but differences among trapping protocols and sampling effort complicate comparisons across sites and programmes.Using data from the French Soil Quality Monitoring Network (RMQS-Biodiversity), we analysed how sampling protocol and trapping intensity shape species detectability and how these effects propagate to inventory completeness and taxonomic diversity estimates. We applied species-level occupancy models to explicitly estimate detection probabilities as functions of sampling protocol, effort and species traits, and propagated these estimates to community-level diversity metrics using coverage-based standardisation.Detection probability varied strongly among protocols and increased non-linearly with sampling effort, reaching saturation only at high trapping intensity. Directional pitfall traps exhibited intermediate detectability compared to conventional pitfall designs with equivalent nominal effort. Species traits explained only a limited fraction of residual variation in detectability once effort was accounted for, indicating that protocol effects primarily operate through baseline detection processes rather than trait-specific filtering. At the community level, standardising diversity estimates by inventory coverage substantially reduced protocol-dependent differences, particularly for diversity metrics dominated by common species. However, species richness remained sensitive to protocol choice even at comparable coverage, highlighting persistent biases in the representation of rare species.Our results demonstrate that differences among sampling protocols primarily reflect observation processes rather than ecological variation alone. We show that harmonising biodiversity indicators based solely on sampling effort is insufficient, and that detection-aware frameworks combining explicit detectability modelling and coverage-based standardisation are required to ensure comparability. This approach provides a practical basis for integrating heterogeneous sampling protocols into large-scale soil biodiversity monitoring and for improving the reliability of soil biodiversity indicators in environmental assessment frameworks.

title: Cross-scale hotspot transition and scale-dependent drivers of urban bird richness
abstract: Biodiversity conservation has become a major challenge in rapidly urbanizing regions, where environmental heterogeneity reshapes ecological patterns across spatial and seasonal dimensions. However, most studies have focused on identifying a single optimal scale while overlooking how biodiversity responses vary across scales. In this study, we developed an integrated framework combining multi-scale analysis, explainable machine learning, and seasonal simulations to investigate urban bird diversity patterns in Shenzhen, China. More than 215,000 citizen-science bird records and environmental variables were analyzed across spatial scales ranging from 300 m to 2000 m. The results revealed strong scale dependency in both model performance and environmental responses. Among all scales, 1000 m achieved the highest predictive accuracy and ecological interpretability, representing the optimal scale for modeling urban bird diversity. Cross-scale hotspot analysis identified stable, attenuated, and emergent hotspot transition patterns, indicating that biodiversity-supporting conditions undergo persistence, attenuation, and spatial reorganization during scaling processes. Environmental drivers exhibited hierarchical shifts across scales, transitioning from fine-scale habitat regulation to broader climatic, topographic, and anthropogenic control, accompanied by widespread nonlinear threshold responses. Seasonal simulations further revealed substantial temporal shifts in hotspot distributions and driver dominance associated with species phenology. Overall, this study provides a scale-adaptive framework for understanding urban biodiversity responses and offers practical implications for ecological monitoring, biodiversity conservation, and spatial planning in rapidly urbanizing landscapes.

title: Soil wind erosion and its driving forces in the three-north region, China
abstract: The Three-North Region hosts the world's largest and longest-running artificial afforestation project. Systematic research in this area is not only an ecological imperative but also a key strategic instrument for alleviating China's forest resource shortages and their associated economic burdens. To elucidate the magnitude and trajectory of soil wind erosion over recent decades, this study applied the Geodetector method and the RWEQ model to quantify the contributions of natural and anthropogenic factors to erosion risk, aiming to provide theoretical and empirical support for ongoing shelterbelt initiatives. Results indicate that over the study period, the retention rate of windbreak and sand-fixation measures rose from 12.97% to 13.22%, while total soil wind erosion exhibited a fluctuating yet downward trend from west to east, with a mean erosion modulus of 724.57 t/km 2 . High-erosion areas were concentrated in Northwest and North China (24.61% of the total area), whereas the Northeast Plain sustained lower intensity. Slight erosion was dominant, severe erosion occupied the smallest proportion, and destructive and very severe erosion were confined to the Tarim Basin, Junggar Basin, Gonghe Basin, major deserts and sandy lands, and the Qilian Mountains. Slight and moderate erosion mainly occurred in the Northeast Plain, accounting for 62.42% of the erosion-affected area, while tolerable erosion was largely restricted to the Turpan Basin. Among all factors, soil type and temperature emerged as primary drivers of temporal changes, while spatial patterns were predominantly governed by interactions among wind speed, vegetation cover, elevation, precipitation, and soil type.

title: Mainstreaming genetic diversity indicators through the IUCN Red List process: A national-scale assessment of South African mammals
abstract: Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity are required to report on progress towards the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), which for the first time includes two population genetic indicators to track the maintenance of populations and their effective population size, addressing Goal A (reducing threats to biodiversity) and Target 4 (halting extinctions and safeguarding genetic diversity). Operationalising these indicators at national scale, particularly for complete taxonomic groups, remains challenging. Here, we present the first comprehensive, national-scale assessment of these genetic indicators for all South African mammals ( n = 320 taxa). Leveraging regional Red Listing processes, published and non-public datasets, and expert elicitation, we conducted 320 genetic assessments, achieving coverage of 96% for the Populations Maintained indicator and 45% for the Ne 500 indicator. Nationally, most mammal populations are maintained (∼98%), and ∼ 75% exceed the Ne 500 threshold, indicating generally strong genetic status. However, disaggregated analyses based on threat status revealed substantial heterogeneity, with some Least Concern, Vulnerable and Near Threatened taxa having low Ne 500 values, highlighting populations at risk of undetected genetic erosion. Differences among taxonomic orders likely reflect life-history traits, population structure, and management contexts. Accounting for transboundary populations increased Ne estimates, highlighting the importance of biologically meaningful population delineation. These findings demonstrate that broad taxonomic coverage, structured data mobilization, and integration with existing assessment frameworks enable practical, policy-relevant genetic monitoring. Our study provides a scalable approach for operationalising genetic indicators, informing conservation prioritisation, and supporting national commitments under the KMGBF.

title: Drone-measured canopy spectra can be a complementary predictor of belowground arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi variations in urban community gardens
abstract: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) form essential symbioses with plant roots, improving nutrient uptake, plant health, and soil function. However, assessing AMF abundance in urban ecosystems remains challenging. Drone-based multispectral imaging can estimate canopy functional traits, raising the question of whether variation in aboveground canopy metrics can serve as an ecological indicator of belowground AMF abundance. We sampled five community gardens over two growing seasons, combining quadrat-level plant surveys, soil sampling for AMF abundance, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) multispectral imagery, and point clouds. From the UAV, we derived vegetation indices, spectral diversity and texture metrics, and from the point clouds we extracted canopy height metrics. We related these traits to log AMF abundance using LASSO cross-validated regression and piecewise structural equation modelling (SEM). Our analyses showed that drone-derived canopy traits captured part of the aboveground variation associated with belowground AMF abundance, particularly through canopy greenness and image texture patterns. Higher AMF abundance was associated with greener and more vertically heterogeneous canopies. UAV-derived canopy texture features explained up to ∼38% of the variance in AMF abundance. Piecewise SEM indicated that AMF abundance was associated with a non-linear climate response, represented by the quadratic climate term (β = 0.25) and a positive vegetation-index pathway (β = 0.21). The AMF abundance SEM model had a marginal R 2 of 0.62, suggesting that seasonal climatic conditions and canopy greenness jointly structured AMF variation. Overall, UAV-derived canopy traits represent a scalable ecological indicator of relative AMF abundance in urban gardens, supporting non-destructive assessment of relative AMF variation and spatial targeting of field sampling. Establishing this link provides a baseline for developing stronger urban ecological indicators by integrating UAV data with soil measurements, garden management, and higher-resolution remote-sensing approaches.

title: Modified remote sensing ecological index (MRSEI) reveals spatiotemporal coupling of eco-environmental quality with traditional villages in Red River Basin
abstract: The Red River Basin (RRB) in Southwest China serves as a critical transboundary ecological barrier and a hotspot for multi-ethnic cultural heritage. Monitoring the spatiotemporal dynamics of eco-environmental quality (EEQ) is essential for regional sustainability. However, conventional remote sensing indices often suffer from spectral saturation and soil background interference in high-sediment basins and dry-hot valleys.
