Attribution analysis identified the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and human footprint (HFP) as the primary spatial drivers of both indicators, but their driver patterns diverged across stages. For CS, the dominant limitation shifted from vegetation recovery and human activity toward hydroclimatic factors, especially potential evapotranspiration (PET) and mean temperature (Tavg). For HQ, expanding human disturbance and southward-strengthening thermal stress, particularly maximum temperature (Tmax) and Tavg, became increasingly important. These findings highlight the stage-dependent nature of ecosystem-service indicators and provide spatially explicit evidence for differentiated restoration and adaptive management in the Yellow River Basin.

title: Environmental heterogeneity shapes divergent assembly processes and network stability of plankton communities along a tropical island coast: Evidence from Hainan Island
abstract: Understanding how plankton communities respond to environmental heterogeneity is essential for assessing tropical island coastal ecosystems and supporting region-specific management. Based on data from 59 environmental monitoring stations, including 16 stations with plankton samples, this study investigated the spatial differentiation, assembly processes, network characteristics, and environmental response pathways of phytoplankton and zooplankton communities along the coast of Hainan Island. We integrated analyses of community diversity, β-diversity, community assembly, co-occurrence networks, and piecewise structural equation modelling (piecewise SEM). The results showed marked heterogeneity in salinity, nutrients, chlorophyll a , suspended solids, and dissolved oxygen among coastal sectors. Regional differences in both communities were weak at higher taxonomic levels. In contrast, genus-level β-diversity showed significant sectoral effects in both groups, with stronger spatial differentiation in phytoplankton than in zooplankton (PERMANOVA: R 2 = 0.65, P = 0.002; R 2 = 0.58, P = 0.001). At the α-diversity level, zooplankton showed clearer regional differentiation, whereas phytoplankton α-diversity did not differ significantly among sectors. Community assembly analysis suggested that phytoplankton deviated more strongly from neutral expectations and was jointly influenced by environmental filtering and spatial processes, whereas zooplankton showed a greater contribution of stochastic processes, with dispersal limitation and undominated processes playing more important roles. Co-occurrence network analysis and piecewise SEM further identified region-specific network organization and variation in network-derived stability metrics, with statistical associations between environmental gradients and network properties being predominantly indirect and involving community composition and diversity. These findings reveal hierarchical responses of coastal plankton communities to environmental heterogeneity along a tropical island coast and provide ecological evidence for coastal ecosystem assessment, biodiversity evaluation, and region-specific management.

title: Combined active-passive remote sensing inversion of grassland aboveground biomass on the Qinghai-Tibet plateaus and exploration of its driving mechanisms with optical-radar-meteorological systems
abstract: The grasslands of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau constitute the world's highest and most extensive high-elevation grassland ecosystem. Aboveground biomass (AGB) is a key indicator of grassland ecosystem structure and function and is highly sensitive to climate variability. Existing studies primarily focus on improving AGB inversion accuracy, whereas the underlying relationships between AGB and climatic drivers remain insufficiently explored. We employed Sentinel-1/2 imagery from 2018 to 2024 to evaluate the performance of GBDT, RF, and SVM in estimating AGB for three grassland types on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau: alpine grassland, alpine meadow, and temperate grassland. We subsequently applied shapley additive explanations (SHAP) to identify AGB-sensitive features, constructed phenological curves, and assessed significant AGB trends using the Mann–Kendall test and Theil–Sen median estimator. Furthermore, optical metrics, SAR features, and ten meteorological variables were integrated into a partial least squares path modeling (PLSPM) framework to elucidate the driving mechanisms linking environmental systems and grassland AGB. The results indicate that: Bai and Cotrufo (2022) (1) Incorporating SAR features improved AGB estimation across all three grassland types, reducing RMSE by 3.55–8.10 g/m 2 and increasing R 2 by 0.05–0.08. GBDT exhibited the strongest inversion performance, with average RMSE values 4.105–16.357 g/m 2 lower and R 2 values 0.036–0.169 higher than those of SVM and RF; Balzter et al. (2007) (2) the AGB of the three grassland types ranked from high to low as alpine meadow, temperate grassland, and alpine grassland, all showing significant declines; Bernardino et al. (2024) (3) phenological curves derived from the atmospherically resistant vegetation indices and excess green index revealed that grassland growing season length first shortened and then lengthened; Bueso et al. (2023) (4) PLSPM results demonstrate that a negative statistical pathway between the regional meteorological system and grassland productivity. Temperature, precipitation, and soil moisture were associated with negative path coefficients for AGB, whereas wind speed showed a positive path coefficient. Optical features respond most sensitively to changes in the AGB, whereas SAR backscatter features have relatively limited explanatory power. These three types of systems could provide an effective framework for monitoring grassland productivity on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau.

title: Economic spectrum of desert ephemeral plants along a precipitation gradient in the Gurbantungut desert: aboveground and belowground functional traits determine productivity
abstract: Precipitation is a pivotal factor regulating ecosystem patterns and processes in arid and semi-arid regions and plays a significant role in plant community development. This study aims to elucidate the variation patterns of above-ground and belowground functional traits in herbaceous plant communities along natural precipitation gradients, as well as the specific mechanisms through which shifts in community-weighted mean trait values influence productivity. Six sampling points were established along a precipitation gradient (115, 120, 125.8, 135, 137.5, and 160 mm) in the Gurbantunggut Desert. Species diversity, biomass, and leaf and root functional traits were measured to investigate their trends and interrelationships. Results indicate that increasing precipitation enhanced community cover and biomass, both of which exhibited rising trends, whereas community richness did not follow a similar pattern. Above- and belowground functional traits varied in accordance with the plant economic spectrum: under lowest precipitation, stands exhibited a high-turnover strategy characterized by high specific leaf area and specific root length; Under comparatively higher precipitation, a high-investment strategy prevailed, featuring larger individual size and thicker root diameter. Structural equation modeling (SEM) revealed that variations in herbaceous plant functional traits and soil total nitrogen content were the primary pathways influencing above- and belowground biomass. Specifically, specific leaf area (SLA) was negatively correlated with aboveground biomass, while belowground root diameter (RD) was positively correlated with belowground biomass. This study contributes a scientific basis for predicting how desert ecosystems may respond to future precipitation pattern changes and for understanding community succession mechanisms. It also holds important implications for functional trait–based ecological management strategies and biodiversity protecting.

title: Historical climate stability and anthropogenic refugia jointly shape the biogeography of old trees in the central part of the Yellow River Basin of China
abstract: Old trees are affected by natural drivers (climate, topography, and soil) and protected by cultural factors (temples, ancestral halls, and legends). However, our knowledge of how the presence and growth status of old trees might be maintained by intertwined climatic, soil, and cultural forces is remains limited. To decouple their relative significance on the spatial presence and maximal growth (diameter at breast height) of the top ten old tree species, we utilized a novel historical baseline (1989 pre-urbanization census) in the central Yellow River Basin, China to eliminating the confounding effects of recent rapid urbanization. We combined four cultural drivers (human footprint, and distances to temples, ancestral halls, and legends) and seven natural drivers (elevation, temperature seasonality, precipitation stability, aridity index, soil pH, soil bulk density, and soil fertility Principal Component Analysis), independently evaluating their effects using Ensemble Species Distribution Models (SDMs) and XGBoost- SHapley additive explanation machine learning. We found that distances to temples and ancestral halls are the important decisive factors for the spatial presence of old trees, exhibiting strict distance-decay thresholds. Specifically, religious sites favored evergreen conifers, with 84.34% of Platycladus orientalis and 62.92% of Pinus tabuliformis populations concentrated within a < 3 km core radius. The presence probability dropped sharply beyond specific cultural boundaries: 0.6 km for P. orientalis , 0.7 km for both Sabina chinensis and Sophora japonica , and 1.2 km for P. tabuliformis and Ulmus pumila . In contrast, the maximal growth of old trees is driven by a dual-refuge mechanism relying heavily on historical climate stability (precipitation stability) and soil micro-environments. Our findings have significant ramifications for conservation: (1) preserving historic structures and old trees in tandem to establish holistic biocultural units; (2) leveraging traditional clan networks as essential community-based conservation sanctuaries; and (3) implementing targeted management strategies that optimize soil physical properties while buffering against climate aridity to ensure precise conservation.

title: Green space dynamics in a rapidly urbanizing landscape: A multi-temporal remote sensing assessment and CA-Markov modelling of Jashore, Bangladesh
abstract: Urban green space is disappearing faster than planning frameworks can track, particularly in secondary cities like Jashore Sadar Upazila, Bangladesh, where monitoring capacity is limited and population growth is rapidly converting green space into built-up land. This study analyzes spatio-temporal LULC change in Jashore Sadar Upazila (2017–2023), focusing on green space loss, built-up expansion, urban heat island effects, and projected scenarios for 2029 and 2032. Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8/9 imagery were analyzed using Cellular Automata-Markov (CA-Markov) modelling. Multi-directional and gradient-based analysis showed conversion concentrated within 10 km of the CBD and along major transportation corridors. The spatiotemporal study found a loss of 6336.81 ha (52.4%) of green space during this period, accompanied by a significant increase in built-up areas, growing 107.16%. The UHI index, computed as a standardized LST anomaly ( Z -score), ranged from +3.12 to −1.92 Z-score units in 2017 and + 5.68 to −2.13 Z-score units in 2023, indicating progressive thermal polarization, significantly correlated with green space conversion ( r = 0.087, p < 0.001). CA-Markov validation yielded class-level FoM of 31.71% (built-up) and 16.57% (green space); the overall FoM (35.71%) reflects landscape persistence rather than change-prediction skill. The projected LULC maps for 2029 and 2032 indicate a continuation of these trends, with a projected loss of 1634.77–2874.44 ha by 2032, reflecting sensitivity to calibration and residual spatial uncertainty (FoM: 16.57%). These findings underscore the need for proactive urban planning, stricter zoning enforcement, and targeted green space conservation to mitigate future environmental impacts.

title: Watershed viability: A novel threshold-integrated pressure-state-response framework
abstract: This study proposes a new framework to operationalize watershed viability by quantifying the buffer capacity of a watershed, which refers to the relative position of current conditions within the dynamic resilience and release thresholds. The framework has been developed in line with the Pressure-State-Response (PSR) model and local indicators, enabling an actionable, diagnostic assessment for watershed managers. Accordingly, a new type of watershed viability is proposed, which uses a 10-point scale ranging from inviable to viable. It is operationalized using the PSR model and applied to the Shazand Watershed in Iran. Statistically refined key criteria were determined using field surveys and normalized criteria to identify dynamic resilience and release thresholds. The viability index was then calculated by comparing the prevailing conditions to these thresholds. Findings showed that the mean viability index of the Shazand Watershed is 43.46% (±6.58%), indicating moderate viability with a negative trend. The industrial area (7.85%), specific sediment yield (9.32%), and employment ratio (14.13%) were the most important contributing variables to the P, S, and R indices, respectively. Sub-watersheds 10 and 11 were top-prioritized for being closest to their release thresholds. The research concludes that the viability measure provides essential and practical insights for managers to direct their interventions, prevent further degradation, and focus on restoring the ecosystem, especially in watersheds under significant anthropogenic strains.

title: Unraveling long-term trends and drivers of fish biodiversity change using eDNA metabarcoding of archived samples
abstract: Abstract Long-term biodiversity data are critical for assessing, understanding, and predicting ecosystem change globally, but are often limited by their availability. We present the longest eDNA metabarcoding time series for freshwater fishes based on archived suspended particulate matter (SPM) from Germany’s Environmental Specimen Bank, covering 17 years (2005-2021) across six major European river systems (Rhine, Danube, Elbe, and their tributaries). From 211 annual samples collected according to highly standardized procedures at 13 sites, we detected 63 fish and lamprey species and traced their spatio-temporal trajectories. eDNA metabarcoding captured significantly declining trends at multiple sites with no recoveries. Common and sensitive species declined at nearly half of sites while invasive species spread. Site occupancy and relative read abundance trends were correlated, providing semi-quantitative indicators. Alpha and beta diversity shifted over time and Bayesian hierarchical models revealed that 19% of species showed significant declines in relative read abundance. The eDNA-derived trends showed strong concordance with long-term regulatory fish monitoring data, validating the patterns across methodological approaches. Random forest models and multivariate analyses identified multiple anthropogenic pollutants, measured from the same SPM samples, as drivers of biodiversity patterns. Pesticides, heavy metals, temperature, and fine sediment negatively affected species richness, with site-specific stressor combinations explaining 29% of community variation. Our results demonstrate that archived SPM, originally collected for chemical monitoring, provides a reliable, dual-purpose monitoring matrix integrating pollution and biodiversity trend assessments simultaneously. This approach enables holistic monitoring of global freshwater ecosystem change and can provide an early warning framework supporting evidence-based environmental management.

title: Drivers of ecological network quality change and multi-scenario simulation and optimization in fragile alpine regions: a case study of Lhasa
abstract: Confronting the resilience depletion of ecological networks in alpine fragile regions under the synergistic pressures of urbanization and climate change, this study elucidates the historical evolution and driving mechanisms of the ecological network in Lhasa and explores optimization pathways for ecological security patterns under diverse future scenarios.An integrated "structure-function-species" identification framework was developed by coupling MSPA, InVEST, and MaxEnt models. The "scale-structure-function" evaluation system was employed to quantify spatio-temporal fluctuations in network resilience. Furthermore, the OPGD model was utilized to reveal the underlying driving mechanisms, while the SD-intPLUS model simulated ecological network responses under various Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) for 2040. The result shows that: (1) From 1980 to 2020, Lhasa’s ecological network exhibited a dramatic transition from "degradative contraction" to "restorative expansion," with ecological sources evolving from eastern aggregation toward a pan-regional equilibrium and corridors shifting from "long-distance high-risk" to "short-distance stable-state" patterns. (2) The network evolution is driven by the profound coupling of biophysical baselines and anthropogenic disturbances; specifically, intensified grazing pressure emerged as the primary catalyst for source degradation and resistance elevation, while mid-altitude zones (4793–5050 m) functioned as "safety windows" for ecological flow. (3) Future resilience responses demonstrate pronounced path dependency: under the SSP126 scenario, source area and ECA increased by 34% and 36.7% respectively, whereas the SSP245, SSP370, and SSP585 scenarios exhibited varying degrees of functional retrogression, particularly in SSP585 where source areas contracted by 46%. (4) Linear fragmentation by transportation networks and persistent climatic shifts were identified as pervasive threats, prompting the proposal of management strategies based on the precise remediation of obstacle points. The proposed "identification-evaluation-attribution-simulation" framework offers a novel paradigm for deciphering the evolution of ecological networks in alpine fragile regions, providing theoretical robust support and spatial references for the resilient planning of Lhasa’s ecological security.

title: Investigating ecological network resilience to cascading failures in drylands under multi-hazard attack simulations: A case study of the northern slope area of the Tianshan Mountains, Xinjiang, China
abstract: Ecological networks in arid regions face dual pressures from climate-driven hazards and inherent fragility. Traditional purely topological resilience assessments are inadequate under complex disturbances. Hence, we developed a “topology-hazard” coupled simulation framework, within which we used circuit theory to construct the ecological network and Python NetworkX to conduct node-removal attack simulations, and then employed random forest to identify the dominant drivers of resilience decay. Results show that: (1) the network comprises 141 ecological sources and 344 corridors, with high-importance nodes clustered in the southern Tianshan and core ecological source areas to the west and northeast, forming dual vulnerable zones highly susceptible to cascading failures; (2) topology-targeted attacks have a much lower collapse threshold (40.9%) than hazard-topology coupled attacks (74.5%), indicating that purely topological approaches underestimate resilience under simulated scenarios; (3) low-temperature stress yields the lowest collapse threshold (84.7%), whereas compound hazard stress yields the highest (98.5%), indicating that hazard action modes modulate resilience responses; (4) network density decay contributes 53.2% of resilience decline and transmissibility decay 26.3%, together accounting for 79.5% and confirming density loss as the dominant driver. Based on these findings, we propose a three-tier protection strategy that prioritizes “dual vulnerable units” to enable precise resource allocation for multi-hazard collaborative prevention and network optimization. This study innovatively constructs a “topology-hazard” coupled simulation framework, which advances quantitative resilience assessment for arid regions and offers a practical pathway for multi-hazard collaborative prevention and ecological network optimization.

title: A spatial downscaling framework for vegetation optical depth based on geographically weighted stacking ensemble learning
abstract: Vegetation Optical Depth (VOD) is an important microwave remote sensing parameter that reflects vegetation canopy water content and aboveground biomass. However, the relatively coarse spatial resolution of existing VOD products restricts their application in regional ecological and environmental studies. To generate high-spatial-resolution VOD data, this study selected the Yangtze River Economic Belt as the study area and used multi-source high-resolution variables related to vegetation, meteorology, and topography as model inputs. Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) were employed as base learners, while Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) was adopted as the meta learner to develop a Geographically Weighted Stacking Ensemble (GWSE) downscaling model. Using this framework, VOD data were downscaled from 0.1° to 0.01° spatial resolution. The results indicate that the GWSE model achieved better downscaling performance than the individual RF, XGBoost, and LightGBM models, with an R 2 of 0.702, an RMSE of 0.180, and an MAE of 0.124. After downscaling, the spatial correlations between VOD and NDVI, EVI, LAI, and GPP were enhanced. At the significance level of P < 0.001, the correlation coefficient increased from 0.362 to 0.442 for NDVI, from 0.210 to 0.240 for EVI, from 0.305 to 0.424 for LAI, and from 0.277 to 0.362 for GPP. In addition, the monthly mean VOD time series before and after downscaling remained highly consistent across different land cover types and showed significant positive correlations ( P < 0.001). The strongest correlations were observed in grassland, cropland, and the overall vegetation cover area, with correlation coefficients of 0.993, 0.992, and 0.997, respectively. Overall, this study provides a feasible approach for generating regional high-resolution VOD products and offers data support for vegetation dynamics monitoring and ecological environment assessment. The generated high-resolution VOD data can further improve the understanding of vegetation responses to environmental changes and support ecosystem monitoring at regional scales.

title: Developing a biodiversity–health–services nexus to reveal how external pressures influence ecosystems: Evidence from Sanjiangyuan National Park
abstract: The cascading relationships among biodiversity (BD), ecosystem health (EH), and ecosystem services (ES) are critical for understanding how external pressures, such as climate change and human activities, influence ecosystem processes. However, such relationships remain rarely explored. To address this, we developed a new BHS (biodiversity–health–services) nexus framework for Sanjiangyuan National Park (SNP), chosen for its pristine and complete ecosystems. This research integrates Generalized Convergent Cross Mapping, network analysis, structural equation modeling, and Zonation to examine the cascading relationships and response mechanisms of the ecosystem to external pressures. The results show significant bidirectional causal relationships among biodiversity, ecosystem health, and ecosystem services in SNP, with BD→EH→ES as the dominant pathway. The BHS nexus maintained a stable positive network structure, with ecosystem health as the key hub. Notably, climate change and human activities influence the BHS nexus primarily through biodiversity, affecting the system through the −BD−ES and −BD−EH−ES pathways. Climate change exerted a dominant negative effect, while the impact of human activities shifted from negative to positive after the implementation of the national park system. Spatial priority analysis identified overlaps between high-pressure areas and high-value BHS regions, leading to the development of targeted sustainable management strategies. This study emphasizes that focusing on biodiversity sensitivity and the central role of ecosystem health can facilitate precise ecosystem management. The framework enhances our understanding of the internal relationships and external driving mechanisms within the BHS nexus, providing scientific insights for ecosystem management in national parks located in similar ecologically sensitive regions.

title: Spatiotemporal heterogeneity and multi-scenario simulation of vegetation carbon sinks under the influence of ecological engineering: a case study in the Three-River Headwaters Region, China
abstract: Clarifying the impact of ecological engineering on vegetation carbon sink (VCS) and predicting future VCS under ecological protection constraints is of significant importance for formulating ecological protection policies and addressing climate change. This study uses Net Ecosystem Productivity (NEP) as the core indicator and establishes a multi-scenario coupled simulation framework of “ecological engineering effects—SSP-RCP scenarios—PLE-SEM driver decomposition” by dynamically linking the effects of ecological engineering implementation at different stages. Taking the Three-River Headwaters Region (TRHR) in China as an example, this study reveals the phased differences in VCS during different ecological engineering periods (2000−2022) and the evolution patterns of their source-sink distribution, and also predicts the VCS under various scenarios for the carbon peak year (2030) and the carbon neutrality year (2060). The results show that from 2000 to 2022, vegetation NEP in the TRHR exhibited a fluctuating upward trend with a multi-year average of 32.3 gC·m −2 ·a −1 . The boundary between carbon sources and sinks was distinct, with the southeast functioning as carbon sinks and the northwest as carbon sources; the carbon sink area was 1.38 times that of carbon source area. During ecological engineering implementation, the increasing trend of vegetation NEP was significantly higher than before and after implementation, with the second phase showing a more pronounced increase than the first phase. However, ecological engineering had limited influence on the source-sink pattern, which remained dominated by stable carbon sources and sinks. For 2030 and 2060, the spatial distribution characteristics of vegetation NEP under the three SSP-RCP scenarios showed obvious similarity to the historical period. Notably, mean NEP differed significantly across scenarios: SSP5-8.5 exhibited the highest NEP, while SSP1-2.6 showed the lowest. From 2030 to 2060, NEP increased across all three scenarios, with SSP1-2.6 demonstrating the largest increment (∼7.83 gC·m −2 ) and strongest carbon sink potential, whereas SSP5-8.5 showed the smallest increment (∼0.95 gC·m −2 ) with limited carbon sink potential. Ecological constraints generated positive carbon sink benefits across all scenarios, enhancing carbon sequestration by 8.65 gC·m −2 ·a −1 (SSP1-2.6), 4.65 gC·m −2 ·a −1 (SSP2-4.5), and 3.72 gC·m −2 ·a −1 (SSP5-8.5) in 2060, with the constraint effect exhibiting an inverse relationship with baseline NEP levels. PLE-SEM analysis indicated that vegetation factors had the strongest direct effect on NEP, while topography dominated through indirect effects via climate and vegetation. These findings provide important references for optimizing regional ecological protection and restoration strategies and formulating carbon sequestration enhancement pathways.

title: Seasonal dynamics of cross-trophic interactions and bottom-up effects: Implications for biodiversity conservation in dam-regulated Rivers
abstract: Mega-dams fragment rivers and alter hydrological regimes, yet the manner in which such perturbations cascade through food webs to restructure multi-trophic communities remains poorly understood in freshwater ecology. Whether bottom-up control varies systematically across seasons and trophic levels was tested along the environmental gradient of the Xiangjiaba–Three Gorges Dam cascade (upper Yangtze River). To this end, microscopy-based plankton surveys and eDNA metabarcoding of fish were integrated during the 2024 wet and dry seasons, and distance–decay models, NST, co-occurrence networks, and PLS-PM were employed to disentangle assembly mechanisms and cross-trophic interactions. The results revealed a pronounced seasonal reversal in food-web dynamics. During the wet season, a random forest model, evaluated via out-of-bag prediction (OOB-R 2 ) indicated that environmental factors, phytoplankton diversity, and network topological metrics together explained 81.5% of the variation in fish beta diversity, with network topology acting as the key mediator between phytoplankton and fish communities. In the dry season, bottom-up control weakened sharply, giving way to environmental filtering and intrinsic fish population dynamics. Network complexity displayed a spatial reversal, peaking in the downstream reservoir during the wet season but shifting upstream to the riverine reach in the dry season. Notably, network topological metrics (e.g., average degree and modularity) and beta diversity were more sensitive to seasonal hydrological shifts than traditional alpha diversity or species abundance alone, indicating their potential as early-warning indicators in dam-regulated rivers. These results thus establish that bottom-up control in regulated rivers is a seasonally gated, dam-modulated process, emphasizing the importance of season-specific, network-informed conservation strategies.

title: Assessing ecosystem service values responses to livelihood transitions in an Arid Mountain–Oasis–Desert system
abstract: Balancing ecological conservation and rural livelihoods represents a critical challenge in arid social-ecological systems. Livelihood transitions among agropastoral households strongly influence the area allocated to different land-use types, thereby shaping regional ecosystem service values (ESV)，yet this decision-to-ecosystem pathway remains insufficiently represented in arid mountain–oasis–desert systems (MODS). To address this gap, a livelihood transition framework with an agent-based model (ABM) was integrated to simulate land-use change and evaluate ESV responses under three scenarios in a typical MODS of northern Xinjiang, China. Three livelihood transition scenarios—natural development following existing livelihood and land-use trends, profit oriented emphasizing income-driven livelihood choices, and ecological regulation prioritizing ecosystem conservation—were designed to explore future trajectories. The model was validated through historical back-casting and used for comparative scenario analysis. Relative to the ESV in 2020, total ESV was projected to decline under all three scenarios by 2030, with reductions of 33.3, 7.0 and 6.1 billion CNY under the natural-development, profit-oriented, and ecological-regulation scenarios, respectively. The ecological-regulation scenario showed the smallest decline in total ESV, while its main advantage over the profit-oriented scenario was reflected in relatively higher regulating and supporting service values associated with greater grassland retention. These findings deepen the understanding of the MODS as an integrated social–ecological system in which livelihood strategies, land-use allocation, and ecosystem-service responses are closely interconnected. This perspective provides a theoretical basis for coordinated ecosystem management and sustainable livelihood-transition research in arid agropastoral regions.

title: A data synthesis and comparative review of rainfall partitioning: Drivers and management implications in fruit crops
abstract: Rainfall partitioning, the redistribution of gross rainfall into canopy interception (Ic), throughfall (TF), and stemflow (SF), is a critical ecohydrological indicator governing water acquisition, soil water availability, and yield in fruit crops. Although studies in various climates have quantified rainfall partitioning across different fruit crops, a concerted effort to quantitatively synthesize such data is still lacking. To address this gap, data from previously published studies on 13 fruit crop species across 13 experimental sites were compiled and analyzed to better understand how these indicators respond to environmental drivers, plant morphological attributes, and artificial management practices. A boosted regression tree (BRT) model was employed to quantify the relative importance of rainfall event characteristics and meteorological factors in driving Ic, TF, and SF. The results indicated that the mean per-event Ic, TF, and SF were 2.2 mm, 12.7 mm, and 0.6 mm, respectively, corresponding to average event-based partitioning ratios of 25.4%, 73.0%, and 4.3%. TF was the primary rainfall partitioning pathway, characterized by the strongest positive linear dependence on gross rainfall (R 2 = 0.96, p < 0.01) and minimal sensitivity to variations in leaf area index. The BRT model revealed that, among environmental drivers, rainfall amount and wind speed predominantly governed TF flux, Ic flux, and the Ic ratio, collectively accounting for 94.5%, 83.5%, and 92.6% of the relative importance, respectively. Notably, despite incorporating data from various fruit crops, these findings may be biased toward the data-dominant species (apple). Plant morphological attributes and management practices significantly altered these components: evergreen fruit crops exhibited a much higher mean Ic ratio (38.0%) than deciduous crops (20.6%) due to perennial leaf coverage. Tree-type crops showed distinctly lower TF and SF ratios compared to bush- or vine-type crops. In tree-type crops, increased planting density enhanced the Ic and SF ratios; conversely, bush- and vine-type crops were more susceptible to competition-driven inhibition at high densities, which weakened their canopy interception function. These findings provide a basis for the hypothesis that hydrological complementarity could be harnessed through layered mixed-cultivation systems combining evergreen and deciduous species. Because tree-type crops constitute a large proportion of fruit crops, optimizing their planting density is of vital importance. Future research could verify the practical effectiveness of two specific strategies: applying medium planting densities in high-rainfall areas to reduce evaporation losses, and adopting high planting densities in low-rainfall areas to enhance localized soil-water storage.

title: Climate-driven modeling and future projection of grassland aboveground biomass on the Qinghai-Xizang plateau using an interpretable Transformer framework
abstract: Grassland aboveground biomass (AGB) on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau is highly sensitive to climate change, yet existing studies lack fine-scale characterization of month-to-month climate forcing dynamics and their cumulative cross-month effects on AGB. This study proposes an interpretable Transformer framework that mitigates the opacity of black-box prediction by making the model's internal climate-driving contributions traceable. Monthly AGB data spanning 2003–2023 (9123 sampling sites) were used as training labels, and three interpretability methods including occlusion experiments, integrated gradients (IG), and attention weights were cross-compared to identify dominant drivers and key time windows. Both occlusion experiments and IG identified precipitation as the dominant driver, with April precipitation reaching the highest attribution across the entire variable-month matrix (mean |IG| = 1185 kg DW/ha), refining spring-lag effects from the seasonal scale to the individual-month scale. Cross-comparison revealed that attention weights diverged substantially from both methods, cautioning against their use as proxies for climate driver importance. The final model driven by monthly precipitation and maximum temperature (R 2 = 0.6330, RMSE = 331.38 kg DW/ha) was coupled with CMIP6 ensemble projections to simulate potential AGB trajectories through 2060 under a climate-only driving assumption that excludes grazing, land-use change, and other non-climatic drivers. Plateau-wide annual maximum AGB rose by 6.58%, 9.09%, and 11.65% under SSP126, SSP245, and SSP585, respectively, with the high-emission scenario producing sharply divergent projected outcomes: alpine grassland, alpine desert, and alpine desert grassland all exceeded 30% gains, whereas mountain meadow and marsh declined, reflecting competing warming and moisture-deficit effects across grassland types.

title: Interpretable machine learning reveals contrasting drivers of streamflow droughts in regulated and natural river systems
abstract: This study investigates the spatial, temporal, and process-based dynamics of streamflow droughts across the Godavari River basin using daily discharge records from multiple gauging stations. A multivariate framework integrating drought duration, intensity, and deficit was employed to characterize event severity through a joint probability approach. Two composite indices, the Short-Duration Drought Index (SDDI) and Long-Duration Drought Index (LDDI), were derived to distinguish between rapid, high-intensity droughts and prolonged, cumulative-deficit events. Random Forest models and one- and two-dimensional partial dependence analyses were applied to identify dominant drought characteristics and nonlinear interactions among hydrological characteristics across high human-influence (HHI) and low human-influence (LHI) regions. Results reveal a pronounced hydro-anthropogenic dichotomy: HHI sub-basins, heavily regulated by major reservoirs, exhibit long-duration but moderate droughts controlled primarily by operational persistence that alters the natural flows, while LHI catchments display shorter yet more intense events governed by climatic forcing. The analyses further show that in HHI regions, flow intensity dominates short-term drought dynamics, whereas in LHI regions, duration and cumulative deficit are the key controls on long-term drought propagation. Extreme event analysis (>80th percentile) confirms this contrast, highlighting regulation-induced moderation in HHI basins and climatic amplification in natural systems. The findings emphasize that drought management in the Godavari basin must adopt region-specific strategies, improving adaptive dam operations to maintain critical environmental flows in regulated areas and enhancing climatic and ecological resilience in natural basins. The framework offers a transferable approach for diagnosing drought behaviour and associated environmental risks in other large, human-influenced river systems.

title: Topography-dependent nonlinear predictive relationships of water conservation revealed by explainable machine learning in the Three-River headwaters region
abstract: Understanding the nonlinear predictive relationships of water conservation (WC) in alpine “water towers” is critical for realizing ecosystem adaptive management under global climate change. As “Water Tower of China”, the hydrological processes of the Three-River Headwaters Region (TRHR) are undergoing profound reshaping under warming and wetting climates, yet the nonlinear characteristics of predictive relationships and their topographic dependence remain unclear. This study constructed an analytical framework integrating the InVEST model and explainable machine learning (XAI), utilizing XGBoost to capture complex nonlinear dependencies among high-dimensional variables, and introducing the SHAPley Additive Explanation model to decompose model outputs into feature contributions, so as to realize the quantitative analysis of nonlinear predictive relationships and accurate identification of model-derived transition points to systematically quantify the spatiotemporal dynamics of WC in the TRHR from 1990 to 2020, and further explores the differentiation patterns of related features across topographic gradients. The main conclusions are as follows: (1) The WC capacity of the TRHR exhibited a significant increasing trend over the past 30 years (0.261 mm/yr), with 1995 identified as a critical turning point, which coincided with changes in climate conditions, underlying surface properties, and the implementation of ecological engineering projects. (2) In the XGBoost model, Soil Organic Matter (SOM) showed the highest explanatory contribution (29.5%), reflecting its strong statistical association with WC services. When SOM was below approximately 6.92%, its SHAP contribution increased rapidly with increasing SOM; thereafter, the increase in contribution weakens significantly, while Leaf Area Index (LAI) exhibits a model-derived statistical transition point at 0.46, beyond which its SHAP predictive contribution to WC shifts from positive to negative, suggesting a model-derived pattern that is consistent with the potential for a “greening paradox” under water-limited conditions. (3) Environmental features exhibit pronounced nonlinear predictive relationships with WC, and these relationships vary systematically across topographic contexts. The contribution of LAI peaks in the subalpine zone (2000–4000 m), yet shifts to negative inhibition above 4000 m due to intensified evapotranspiration; aspect mediates a complete reversal of predictive relationships from universal inhibition on sunny slopes to positive promotion on semi-shady slopes. These findings verify the non-stationarity of explanatory features regulating WC in the TRHR and indicating that topographic context provides an important framework for differentiating feature–WC predictive relationships. This research provides vital scientific guidance for developing spatially explicit adaptive management strategies for Water Tower of China and other high-elevation ecosystems worldwide.

title: Mainstreaming nature-based solutions in human-dominated landscapes: from isolated interventions to evidence-based landscape governance
abstract: The editorial of the Special issue “Strategies for Mainstreaming Nature-based Solutions (NbS) for Holistic Mangement of Human-Dominated Landscapes” synthesizes 34 articles. The special issue identifies six major themes: Urban NbS; Risk reduction and adaptive restoration; Ecosystem services, prioritization and ecological compensation; Soil carbon, biogeochemical processes and restoration; Biodiversity, forest ecosystems and conservation evidence; and Socio-ecological coupling, human-land governance and policy. The synthesis collectively demonstrates that mainstreaming NbS should be evidence-based and should address the challenges of human-dominated landscapes with focus to ecological functions, social needs, spatial planning and governance institutions.

title: Scale-sensitive river water quality indicators reveal spatially heterogeneous drivers across China
abstract: River water quality degradation poses a critical challenge to water security, yet one-size-fits-all management approaches often overlook region-specific pollution sources and drivers, thereby constraining effective water quality improvement. To address this issue, we conducted a multi-scale analysis of river water quality drivers and management priorities under different regional contexts, using observations from 725 monitoring stations across China and a framework integrating Bayesian hierarchical modeling, machine learning, pathway analysis, and exploratory change-point analysis. Results revealed that eutrophication remained the primary constraint on nationwide water quality improvement. Total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), and permanganate index (COD Mn ) were the principal indicators of water quality degradation. Water quality exhibited marked spatial heterogeneity, with poorer conditions in northern rivers than in southern rivers. Indicator responses varied by scale and region: TN, TP, and COD Mn were best explained at riparian buffer scales, whereas the eutrophication index and water quality index were better explained at the sub-basin scale. Landscape composition dominated in both regions (41.40–43.40%), while natural factors contributed more in the north (14.05%) and socioeconomic factors in the south (17.80%). Pathway analysis suggested that riparian-scale drivers were more directly linked to pollutant indicators, whereas sub-basin conditions were more strongly associated with integrated water quality status. Exploratory change-point analysis identified distinct regional priorities, including reducing farmland dominance and atmospheric nitrogen pressure in northern China and limiting construction land expansion and population pressure in southern China. These findings support differentiated water quality management in China, while offering a transferable framework for water quality governance in other spatially heterogeneous regions.

title: Nonlinear thresholds in agricultural landscape fragmentation: A GWRF-SHAP diagnostic framework for differentiated rural land management
abstract: Agricultural landscape fragmentation (ALF) is a critical ecological constraint on rural sustainability, but conventional linear models fail to capture the nonlinear thresholds governing its response to rural development. This study proposes a GWRF-SHAP diagnostic framework to identify spatially explicit nonlinear driver-response relationships and operational thresholds along rurality gradients. Using Hunan Province as the study area, we classified six agricultural landscape types and stratified five rurality levels ranging from extreme rural to extreme non-rural using a three-dimensional rurality index. The GWRF model quantified local nonlinear associations while SHAP values interpreted factor contributions and threshold inflection points. Results demonstrated semi-natural production landscapes exhibit a unimodal fragmentation pattern peaking in transitional rurality zones, whereas constructed landscapes consistently maintain a relatively stable level of fragmentation. The proportion of forest land (Pfl), nighttime light index (NTL), topographic wetness index (TWI), plot distance to town center (Pdtc), and plot distance to road (Pdr) emerged as the dominant drivers of spatial variation in ALF. Together, these factors explained the observed fragmentation patterns and exhibited pronounced nonlinear threshold effects. Specifically, Pfl exhibited threshold values ranging from 0.48 to 0.68. Below this range, scattered forest patches embedded within farmland intensified edge fragmentation, whereas above the threshold, forests became the dominant landscape matrix and farmland was transformed into embedded patches, resulting in reduced fragmentation of production landscapes but increased fragmentation of natural landscapes. NTL showed threshold values between 0.45 and 1.02, reflecting distinct fragmentation processes under different stages of urbanization. Thresholds associated with Pdtc (2.49-6.28km) further distinguished human-dominated from terrain-dominated fragmentation processes in natural landscapes and separated compact urban cores from dispersed peripheral construction landscapes. These findings demonstrate that agricultural landscape fragmentation is governed by nonlinear threshold responses to rural development and provide a scientific basis for differentiated agricultural landscape governance and sustainable rural planning.

title: Integrated marine spatial planning for Chonburi Province, Thailand: Addressing pollution, blue carbon, and conservation
abstract: While Marine Spatial Planning (MSP) is globally recognized as a strategic tool for ocean governance, its implementation in tropical coastal regions faces distinct challenges stemming from fragmented governance and acute conflicts between traditional livelihoods and modern industries. To address these complexities, this study proposes an issue-oriented MSP framework designed for high-intensity development zones. Taking Chonburi Province, Thailand, as a representative case study, we integrated four thematic models—hydrodynamic pollutant diffusion, marine protected area optimization, blue carbon mapping, and coastal erosion risk assessment—to quantify the spatial compatibility between anthropogenic activities and sensitive habitats. Integrating spatial overlay analysis of thematic outputs with InVEST-HRA modeling, this study identifies anthropogenic maritime activities as the primary driver of habitat change across Chonburi Province. The assessment reveals pronounced spatial heterogeneity in risk across five key coastal zones: military activities exhibit a stable risk profile, coastal tourism demonstrates consistently low ecological impact, and fisheries and maritime transport emerge as the principal manageable variables—displaying a clear spatial gradient in risk levels. Through stakeholder engagement, this process culminated in a comprehensive zoning scheme comprising two primary zones—MPAs (9.47%) and Marine Development Areas (28.46%)—along with seven secondary sub-zones. This work demonstrates that issue-oriented, data-integrated zoning can effectively reconcile multi-sectoral trade-offs, offering a scalable pathway for bridging the gap between theoretical ecosystem-based management and practical administrative enforcement in the Global South.

title: Coding planktonic microbial community structure
abstract: Planktonic microbial community assembly is central to understanding biodiversity maintenance and nutrient biogeochemical cycling in aquatic ecosystems. However, the lack of directly quantifiable parameters to characterize community structure has constrained in-depth analysis of the underlying ecological processes. To bridge this gap, this study introduces a novel single-value index that characterizes community structure by assigning a unique rank to each possible theoretical community composition. The index was subsequently applied to a continental-scale dataset encompassing diverse planktonic microbial communities (phytoplankton, bacteria, archaea, fungi, and other eukaryotes) and associated environmental parameters to examine inter-taxa interactions and influencing factors. Based on this framework, bacteria and archaea appeared to occupy central positions in regulating planktonic microbial community dynamics. In addition, basic water physicochemical parameters (i.e., water temperature, pH, and dissolved oxygen) showed closer associations with community assembly compared to nutrients at the continental scale. The novel method developed in this work offers a robust tool for deeper exploration in microbial ecology and biogeochemistry.

title: Remote observations of particulate inorganic phosphorus concentration in three large waters of China over the past 25 years
abstract: Phosphorus exerts a critical biogeochemical effect in the eutrophication process, and particulate inorganic phosphorus concentration (C PIP ) is considered an important water quality indicator for evaluating human and environmental impacts on aquatic ecosystems. However, its monitoring remains challenging due to the lack of long-term recorded data. Using field measurements and image-matched data collected from three large lakes (Lake Taihu, Lake Hongze, and Lake Chaohu) of Eastern Plain of China, we calibrated and developed two new algorithms suitable for Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectrometer (MODIS) and Sentinel-3 Ocean and Land Color Imager (OLCI) data to estimate C PIP . Validations suggested that the developed models presented appreciable performance for estimating C PIP , with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) below 24%, root mean square error (RMSE) less than 0.025 mg/L, and normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) below 9.5%. Subsequently, the MODIS and OLCI data were utilized to reveal the 25-year spatiotemporal patterns of C PIP in three target lakes. Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope analyses demonstrated an overall increasing trend in C PIP of three observed lakes from 2001 to 2025 with significant spatiotemporal heterogeneity, which was driven by the distinct different effects of hydrological stresses and anthropogenic activities. Importantly, this study provides the first long-term recorded dataset of C PIP targeting inland water bodies, thereby offering an integrated approach and novel insights for advancing precise eutrophication control and efficient aquatic environmental management.

title: Methodological approaches to using bivalve gaping behavior as bioindicator
abstract: Bivalve mollusks are ecologically and economically important filter feeders which are considered useful bioindicators of environmental change. Their sedentary lifestyle integrates local conditions over time, while their continuous filtering activity makes them sensitive to changes in water quality. Their filtration and physiological status are potentially reflected in their shell opening behavior. This behavior can be measured by so-called valvometry, which has been applied across diverse research fields. Here, we summarize existing research on valve gaping to provide an overview over valve gaping behavior as ecological indicator across different species, habitats and applications. A systematic literature search was conducted, resulting in 196 studies on bivalve gaping behavior. For each study, we examined four categories of methodological decisions: species used, measurement approaches applied, employed methods for analyzing data, and study targets pursued. The screened studies covered 64 species from 9 taxonomic orders, with a strong bias towards marine species. Sensors directly attached to individuals without additional measurement units were the most commonly used measurement approach (72.4%). Study targets were highly diverse, resulting in a classification with two major groups (technology vs. biology) and several subgroups. For data analysis, seven biological endpoints were identified as the most commonly used bases, alongside various additional analytical approaches. We identified a lack of standardization in use of biological endpoints as a key challenge, and we propose the introduction of a minimum reporting standard for future studies. Additionally, we highlight interdependencies between methodological choices and discuss gaps and biases in the current literature, with the aim of connecting diverse research fields and supporting more cumulative scientific progress.

title: Applicability of eDNA metabarcoding for fish monitoring in high-sediment-laden rivers: a case study of the Lower Yellow River
abstract: Environmental DNA metabarcoding is widely adopted for aquatic biodiversity surveys, yet strong sediment adsorption and seasonal hydrological fluctuations introduce unquantified detection bias and unstable reliability in hyper-turbid, sediment-laden large rivers, which hinders the establishment of unified, standardized long-term fish monitoring workflows. We implemented synchronous paired seasonal field surveys covering summer and autumn of 2024 along the Lower Yellow River, to systematically compare four core monitoring dimensions-fish community composition characterization, sampling cost efficiency, spatial differentiation resolution, and low-abundance invasive species identification-between eDNA metabarcoding and conventional multi-mesh gillnets-traps capture approaches; all comparisons were quantified and validated via hierarchical clustering, non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS), Mantel test, redundancy analysis (RDA) and resampling-based species accumulation statistics. Obvious seasonal divergence in detection performance was detected across two survey periods: extreme high suspended sediment loads in summer significantly suppressed aqueous eDNA persistence and transport, leading to severe underestimation of benthic and herbivorous fish taxa by eDNA, with only 26 species detected versus 51 species captured by gillnets&traps, and a low Jaccard similarity of 0.24; in contrast, stable hydrology and reduced sediment concentration in autumn largely narrowed inter-method discrepancies, yielding comparable species richness (31 for eDNA, 35 for nets) and elevated community similarity (0.32). Conventional net sampling demonstrated prominent advantages in resolving fine-scale spatial partitioning of local fish assemblages across wandering, transitional and narrow river reaches, whereas eDNA signals, despite being blurred by long-distance downstream transport, better captured broad basin-wide environmental gradients and maintained lower stochastic variability under repeated sampling. These findings underscore that eDNA performance in high-sediment rivers is strongly modulated by seasonal hydrology and suspended sediment, calling for context-specific monitoring designs. Future work should integrate paired water-sediment eDNA sampling to validate sediment-mediated suppression and improve monitoring reliability in turbid large river systems.

title: Greening of the Taklamakan Desert: Effects of climate change and ecological water conveyance
abstract: Oases in the Taklamakan Desert exist in an extremely arid region. Persistent droughts in the late 20th century nearly caused ecosystem collapse in the Lower Tarim River region. Since the implementation of ecological water conveyance in 2000, groundwater levels have increased, vegetation has flourished, and a marked “greening” trend has occurred throughout the oases. However, a quantitative analysis of the drivers of these changes is lacking. This study integrates multi-source remote sensing data and field monitoring, using random forest modeling and Geographical Detector to monitor shifts in vegetation cover and their causes in the lower Tarim River and surrounding oases since 2000. In this period, groundwater has increased by approximately 0.07 m·yr −1 , surface-water areas have expanded, and regional air temperatures, particularly in winter, have increased markedly. Oasis vegetation cover has also increased significantly, while cropland has expanded markedly. Although natural vegetation has generally improved, cropland growth has encroached on desert riparian forests, intensifying interspecific competition within these communities and increasing potential ecological risks. Moreover, groundwater recovery and cold-season warming are key influencing factors associated with oasis greening, while recurrent droughts and interactions between climatic and hydrological variables further shape vegetation growth. Cumulatively, this study shows that effective water management supports oasis greening in arid areas, while highlighting the ecological risks of over-farming. Overall, this study provides new insights into how arid ecosystems respond to coupled climatic and anthropogenic drivers, and offers scientific support for ecological water-delivery regulation, agricultural water-use optimization, and riparian habitat conservation.

title: Grazing systems select leaf number as an indicator of ecosystem responses to climatic variability in salinized meadows
abstract: The degradation of salinized meadows under environmental change calls for reliable functional indicators to support adaptive grazing management. However, while plant functional traits mediate grazing effects, identifying those that can robustly indicate the coupling between environmental factors and productivity across different grazing systems remains unresolved. Through a four-year controlled grazing experiment in a salinized meadow, we evaluated whether grazing systems select leaf number (LN) as a functional indicator of environment-productivity linkages. By integrating structural equation modeling and random forest analysis, we disentangled the cascading network connecting climate, grazing, traits, diversity, and ecosystem functioning. Our results showed that rotational grazing enhanced community productivity through increased LN, whereas continuous grazing shifted the system toward a height-avoidance strategy. Air temperature emerged as the dominant climatic driver, promoting LN and productivity under rotational grazing, while precipitation played a secondary role. Across all grazing systems, LN was the most important predictor of aboveground biomass (relative importance: 18.4%), surpassing plant height and stem length. LN also showed a synergistic relationship with the Shannon-Wiener index ( P < 0.01). These results demonstrate that grazing acts as a selector of ecological pathways rather than merely an intensity gradient. We therefore propose LN as a practical indicator linking grazing management to ecosystem responses under the interannual climatic variability, providing a trait-based tool for forecasting salinized meadow functioning.

title: Connectivity, aggregation and structure: Exploring the effects of landscape fragmentation on ecosystem health in national parks — A case study of Huangshan National Park
abstract: Assessing the impact of human activities on ecosystem health is essential for balancing conservation and development within national parks. Current research often examines human-induced landscape fragmentation through a single perspective, overlooking its non-linear relationship with ecosystem health. Taking Huangshan National Park as a study area, this study adapts the Vigor-Service-Resilience (VSR) assessment model and a three-dimensional (connectivity, aggregation, and structure) landscape fragmentation index to the national park context. On this basis, Boosted Regression Trees (BRT) were employed to identify the heterogeneous and non-linear effects of tourism-driven fragmentation on ecosystem health. The results indicated that: (1) During the study period, ecosystem health in Huangshan National Park showed a steady upward trend, while landscape fragmentation exhibited relatively small fluctuations overall. Spatially, ecosystem health displayed a “high in the core, low in the periphery” pattern, whereas landscape fragmentation showed the opposite “low in the core, high in the periphery” distribution. (2) Ecosystem health was significantly negatively correlated with all three fragmentation dimensions in both space and time, positively correlated with indicators of patch integrity and aggregation, and negatively correlated with indicators of patch isolation and fragmentation. (3) Different fragmentation dimensions exerted significant non-linear threshold effects on ecosystem health, with the connectivity dimension exhibiting stepwise threshold effects and increasing marginal returns, the aggregation dimension displaying bidirectional responses with post-threshold stabilization, and the structural dimension showing sensitive thresholds with response lags. Despite the 30 m resolution constraint, this study elucidates the multi-dimensional, non-linear mechanisms through which tourism-driven fragmentation affects ecosystem health, providing a scientific basis for optimizing landscape patterns and adaptive management in national parks.

title: Ecological quality is overestimated in fragmented urban landscapes: Evidence from the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration
abstract: Ecological indices derived from satellite observations are widely used to monitor environmental quality in rapidly urbanizing regions. However, most existing approaches primarily capture ecosystem state while neglecting landscape configuration, which may introduce systematic bias in fragmented landscapes. Here, we investigate whether landscape fragmentation constrains ecological quality assessment using the Yangtze River Delta Urban Agglomeration as a case study. Using the Landscape Division Index (DIVISION), we demonstrate that fragmentation represents an independent structural dimension of ecological quality, with IRSEI showing substantial divergence from conventional RSEI (ρ = 0.67), while remaining highly consistent with the intermediate nRSEI framework (ρ = 0.93). Our results reveal that traditional remote sensing-based indices tend to overestimate ecological conditions in highly fragmented urban environments, particularly in suburban and intercity transition zones where vegetation greenness does not necessarily reflect ecological integrity under fragmented conditions. To address this limitation, we incorporate landscape fragmentation into an improved assessment framework and show that accounting for spatial configuration reduces overestimation and provides a more spatially consistent representation of ecological quality. Spatiotemporal analysis further revealed pronounced spatial heterogeneity, although the proportion of areas classified as Poor and Fair declined from 37% in 2001 to 28% in 2022 across the region, persistent degradation remained concentrated in highly fragmented urban cores. These findings highlight that landscape fragmentation plays a critical role in shaping ecological assessment outcomes and should be explicitly considered in satellite-based environmental monitoring and regional sustainability evaluation.

title: Multi-scenario optimization of land use and net carbon effects under China's dual-carbon goals: Evidence from Hubei Province, China
abstract: The disorderly expansion of construction land is encroaching upon ecological carbon sink spaces at an unprecedented rate, transforming the land-use system from a carbon balancer into a key driver of regional carbon budget imbalance. In response to the lack of a unified analytical framework integrating the carbon sequestration of non-construction land, carbon emissions from construction land, and land-based economic benefits at the provincial scale, this study takes Hubei Province as the research area and develops a net carbon effect assessment framework encompassing these three dimensions. Linear trend projection, multi-objective programming (MOP), and the GeoSOS-FLUS model were jointly employed to establish four scenarios, namely BAU, EDP, LDS, and EEB, and to simulate land-use allocation and associated net carbon effects in 2030 and 2060. The results indicate that from 2000 to 2020, land-use change in Hubei Province was characterized by the contraction of agricultural space, the expansion of construction space, and the relative stability of the ecological substrate. The spatial pattern of net carbon effects exhibited a clear structure of “carbon sinks in the west and north, and carbon sources in the east and south.” Multi-scenario comparisons further reveal that the EEB scenario provides a representative economic–carbon compromise under equal weights assigned to normalized economic and carbon objectives, subject to ecological and development constraints. These findings provide decision-making support with both planning guidance and policy interpretability for provincial territorial spatial optimization and low-carbon transition under China's dual-carbon goals.

title: Process-dependent wetland degradation and ecological resilience in Northeast China revealed by a zone-weighted regional wetland composite index
abstract: In Northeast China, wetland degradation has intensified under climate change and human activities, disturbing the stability of the system. However, due to the spatial heterogeneity in dominant degradation processes, the applicability of conventional indicators and fixed weighting schemes appears to be limited. To address this issue, this study developed a dominant-process-based zonal weighting framework by distinguishing wetlands in Northeast China into a salinization-dominated zone (SDZ) and a hydrology-dominated zone (HDZ), and constructed a zone-weighted Regional Wetland Composite Index (RWCI). Moreover, environmental and socioeconomic factors were analyzed in relation to long-term mean RWCI. The results show that RWCI effectively characterized wetland habitat changes (POA = 91.65%, Kappa = 0.9008). During 2000–2023, increasing RWCI trends were observed in 69.73% of the baseline wetland pixels in the SDZ, whereas decreasing trends occurred in 50.28% of the pixels in the HDZ. Low and medium resilience wetlands of 54.76% and 41.17%, respectively suggesting the recovery trend in partial regions, while the ecosystem stability was still insufficient. Moreover, the driving contributions also differed between zones. In the SDZ, long-term mean RWCI was mainly associated with hydrothermal factors, especially precipitation (33.2%). Conversely, long-term mean RWCI in the HDZ was more strongly associated with human activity, especially population density (26.3%). Overall, this paper indicates the regional heterogeneity of wetlands in degradation, stability risk and their drivers, offering scientific support for zoned management, risk warning and wetland conservation in Northeast China.

title: Evaluating functional connectivity in urban aquatic ecosystems using environmental DNA: A case study on eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) habitats in Daegu, South Korea
abstract: The integration of aquatic environments into urban ecosystems for biodiversity conservation has gained attention, yet the ecological functions of constructed aquatic habitats remain underexplored. This study characterized Eurasian otter ( Lutra lutra ) occurrence across urban water-body types, evaluated biotic and abiotic factors, and identified connectivity-informed restoration priorities. We surveyed 32 sites across rivers, streams, tributaries, reservoirs, and ponds in Daegu, South Korea, using qPCR to detect otter eDNA and metabarcoding to characterize fish communities. Otter eDNA was detected at 26 sites (81.3%), with detections particularly frequent in reservoirs and ponds and in Sincheon Stream. In the MaxEnt model, ecosystem type had the highest percent contribution, whereas distance from water had the highest permutation importance. Predicted suitable areas occurred across both natural and artificial environments; however, predictions in transportation and residential areas may reflect proximity to aquatic habitats or movement constraints rather than direct habitat preference. Otter eDNA signals were not significantly associated with fish diversity or community dominance, suggesting that prey biomass, body size, and accessibility may be more informative than taxonomic diversity alone. Using a cloglog threshold of ≥0.1, we identified 85 core habitat patches of ≥5 ha. Connectivity analysis highlighted stream–river confluences as central network hubs, constrained connectivity through the densely developed Jung-gu area, and potential stepping-stone functions of constructed aquatic habitats. These findings demonstrate that fine-scale eDNA occurrence data can be integrated with habitat suitability and connectivity analyses to identify spatially explicit conservation and restoration priorities for urban otters.

title: A dynamic calculation model for river ecological flow based on variable intervals
abstract: Conventional ecological-flow assessments often rely on fixed thresholds or static hydrological indices, limiting their ability to capture hydrological variability, ecological-service demands, and reach-scale water losses. To address these limitations, this study develops a dynamic ecological-flow calculation and adaptive regulation model based on variable ecological-flow intervals, in which ecological flow is represented by lower and upper limits rather than a single fixed value. Hydrological shifts are identified using change-point detection, and variable ecological base-flow and incremental-flow intervals are derived by integrating multiple hydrological methods and ecological-service demands. River seepage and water-surface evaporation are further incorporated to derive the final ecological-flow intervals. A guarantee-level-based adaptive regulation mechanism is developed to adjust ecological-flow allocation under different hydrological conditions. The model was applied to the Shaanxi reach of the Wei River mainstream. The results show that ecological-flow intervals generally increase from upstream to downstream and are higher during the flood season than during the non-flood season. The dominant contributors to ecological-flow requirements differed between upstream and downstream reaches, with environmental-protection demand accounting for 64.6%–78.6% of the upper ecological-flow limits at upstream sections and sediment-transport demand accounting for up to 98.0% downstream. Under moderately dry conditions, lower ecological-flow limits generally achieved high guarantee levels, whereas upper ecological-flow limits associated with ecological-service demands showed greater seasonal variability. Under extremely dry conditions, the reliability of upper ecological-flow limits decreased, particularly in downstream reaches, although adaptive regulation improved the guarantee levels of high-priority ecological-service demands. Compared with conventional fixed-threshold ecological-flow approaches, the proposed model provides a more adaptive representation by integrating hydrological regime shifts, ecological-service demands, and reach-scale water losses, thereby supporting ecological-flow management in regulated and water-scarce river systems.

title: Diurnally asymmetric warming and hydroclimatic stress structure alpine ecosystem vulnerability in the Three-River headwaters region
abstract: Day-night asymmetry in alpine warming is increasingly pronounced, yet how it affects ecosystem vulnerability under hydroclimatic extremes remains poorly resolved. Here, we quantified functional ecosystem vulnerability across the Three-River Headwaters Region (TRHR) during 2001–2022 by integrating productivity-derived ecosystem sensitivity and adaptive capacity with temperature- and precipitation-extreme indices. Moderate-to-severe vulnerability covered 60.86% of the TRHR and increased from the humid southeast to the cold-arid northwest. Alpine grasslands were the dominant vulnerability hotspots, with 70.42% of alpine steppes and 56.88% of alpine meadows classified as moderately to severely vulnerable areas. The climatic associations also differed between these ecosystem types. Vulnerability in water-limited alpine steppes was associated mainly with precipitation availability and precipitation–temperature interactions, whereas vulnerability in alpine meadows was more closely linked to cold extremes and contrasting day- and nighttime temperatures. These results indicate that water limitation and thermal constraints jointly shape regional vulnerability and provide a spatial basis for climate-adaptive restoration.

title: Characteristics of seasonal snow cover variations and their effects on soil moisture and vegetation dynamics in Xinjiang
abstract: Snow cover acts as a critical regulator of the hydrological cycle and ecological stability in arid and semi-arid regions. Focusing on Xinjiang, this study integrated multi-source data from 2000 to 2023, including spring snowmelt (SSM), snow depth (SD), climatic factors (spring temperature, ST; spring precipitation, SP), spring soil moisture (SM), and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI). By combining trend analysis, correlation analysis, XGBoost, and structural equation modeling (SEM), we systematically investigated the spatial patterns of spring snow under climate change and their relationships with SM and NDVI. The results indicate that both SSM (−0.44 mm/year) and SD (−2.80 mm/year) in Xinjiang exhibited a declining trend. Increasing spring temperature was identified as a major factor associated with snowpack thinning, and its negative effect weakened the positive replenishment effect of spring precipitation on spring snow conditions. Spring snow exhibited a relatively stable positive linkage with soil moisture (SM), with positive correlations accounting for more than 70% of the study area; however, this moisture linkage was not synchronously reflected in increased vegetation greenness. XGBoost-SHAP analysis showed that spring precipitation had the highest relative importance in predicting SM, whereas NDVI prediction was mainly influenced by climatic factors and SM, with lower relative contributions from SSM and SD. Furthermore, SEM results indicated a strong positive pathway between SSM and SM (path coefficient = 0.43), while the direct pathway between SSM and NDVI was relatively weak (−0.02), suggesting that the relationship between spring snow and vegetation dynamics may be largely associated with SM mediation. Meanwhile, spring temperature exhibited a strong direct positive pathway with NDVI. Over the past 24 years, SM and NDVI in Xinjiang have exhibited a “decreasing water, increasing greenness” divergence, which may be attributed to warming that, on the one hand, promotes earlier vegetation green-up, while on the other hand advances snowmelt and enhances evapotranspiration, thereby reducing SM. This study systematically revealed the associations and asynchronous responses among climate factors, snow variables, SM, and NDVI in Xinjiang. These findings provide a scientific basis for ecological security early-warning and adaptive water resource management in arid regions.

title: Asynchronous convergence of annual satellite-derived forest productivity and within-year production allocation after fire: Counterfactual evidence from 7197 forest fires in China
abstract: Large-scale assessments of post-fire forest recovery commonly evaluate whether annual or growing-season productivity approaches a reference state, yet similar annual totals can arise from different within-year production patterns. For 7197 forest fires in China during 2005–2016, we matched burned forests with contemporaneous unburned controls and reconstructed 8-day counterfactual GPP trajectories through post-fire year 8 using MOD17 and PML-V2.2a. By post-fire years 6–8, annual GPP had approached the contemporaneous unburned reference, with mean relative effects (burned–control differences relative to control GPP) of −1.13% for MOD17 and +0.59% for PML-V2.2a. However, the burned–control relative effect during the early production phase remained 1.98 and 2.45 percentage points lower than during the core phase, respectively. This within-year allocation contrast declined by 77.7% and 73.2% from post-fire year 1 to year 8 but remained negative under four temporal definitions. Control-to-control randomization showed that the national-scale contrast exceeded design-internal variation. Timing differences were concentrated near the leading edge of the production window, and early-phase production amplitude was also lower than core-phase amplitude, although the 8-day data could not reliably separate their contributions. MOD17 and PML-V2.2a reproduced the direction and temporal location of the population-scale pattern, whereas cumulative 8-year GPP differences varied by up to 4.7-fold across MOD17, PML-V2.2a, and GLASS-GPP. These results show that annual satellite-derived productivity and within-year production allocation capture different but complementary dimensions of post-fire recovery.
