This study provides the first nationwide evidence that natural forests in Japan are undergoing defragmentation and highlights the potential role of conversion from planted forests to natural forests following clear-cutting in natural forest defragmentation.

title: Non-linear interactive thresholds of water use efficiency dictate precision ecological zoning across climatic gradients
abstract: Ecosystem water use efficiency (WUE ), the core metric of terrestrial carbon-water coupling, is increasingly studied, yet three gaps persist: nonlinear thresholds have been quantified mainly for single drivers, while thresholds of multi-driver interactions remain largely unquantified; basin-scale assessments rarely disaggregate broad climatic gradients, masking region-specific driver regimes; and identified thresholds are seldom translated into spatially explicit management zones. These gaps motivate a climate-stratified, interaction-aware assessment of WUE thresholds that can inform precision ecological zoning in water-limited basins. Taking the Yellow River Basin ( YRB ), a water-limited basin spanning arid to semi-humid climates, we quantified WUE dynamics from 2001 to 2020 and deciphered its drivers by integrating trend persistence analysis (Theil-Sen, Mann-Kendall, Hurst exponent, coefficient of variation) with an interpretable machine learning framework ( CatBoost / XGBoost-SHAP ). WUE exhibited three climate-mediated regimes: high-efficiency growth with moderate stability in the humid southeast, high fluctuation with low stability in the semi-arid center, and low-level, high-stability in the arid northwest. Dominant drivers reorganized systematically along this gradient, from vegetation-atmosphere interactions, through energy-vegetation co-limitation, to physical environment-moisture control under spatially heterogeneous nonlinear thresholds (e.g., PRES = 59.8 kPa in the Plateau Climate Zone; SWVL = 0.08 m 3 ·m −3 in the Middle Temperate Zone). By nesting four management zones within three climatic strata, the three-tier framework converts climate-regime-specific interaction thresholds into actionable, risk-based zoning; over half of the basin (55.6%) falls into early-warning zones. Coupling multi-driver interaction thresholds with climatic stratification, this framework supports a shift from uniform basin-wide policies to proactive, threshold-driven ecological management and is transferable to other water-limited regions.

title: Reservoir operation and irrigation drive contrasting responses in hydrological drought predictability across the Yellow River Basin
abstract: Against the backdrop of intensifying climate change, the predictability of hydrological drought—a devastating extreme event, is undergoing significant changes. However, the analysis of the spatiotemporal evolution laws of hydrological drought predictability and the quantitative contribution of human activities in existing research were still very limited. Here we developed a Mean Square Error Weighted Averaging Vine Copula (MSEWAVC) model to dynamically assess hydrological drought predictability in the drought-prone Yellow River Basin (YRB). The study showed: (1) Hydrological drought predictability exhibited marked spatial heterogeneity: the predictability of tributary areas was significantly better than that of main streams. The hydrological processes in the densely populated areas of water conservancy projects have become seriously “unnatural”. (2) Under different forecast periods, the overall hydrological drought predictability throughout the basin exhibited a weak upward trend, with rates of 0.0064/10w, 0.0080/10w, and 0.011/10w, respectively, possible enhancement of regional water regulation capacity. (3) Human activities exhibited contrasting effects on hydrological drought predictability across the Yellow River Basin: reservoir operation buffered the decline in the mainstream, while irrigation and land use change aggravated the decline in some tributaries. This study advanced the scientific basis for adaptive early warning of extreme hydrological drought and water resource zoning regulation in a changing environment.

title: Impact of forest cover change on mean and extreme surface temperatures in the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration, China
abstract: In recent years, global warming and frequent extreme weather events have prompted attention to the impact of land cover changes on surface temperature, especially the role of forest cover changes. While changes in forest cover influence local mean and extreme land surface temperature (LST) through radiative and non-radiative pathways, the mechanisms vary by latitude and remain contentious in mid-latitude regions. Focusing on the mid-latitude Yangtze River Delta (YRD) urban agglomeration, this study employs a space-and-time analysis and a corrected surface energy balance model to quantify the impact of forest change on mean and extreme LST (ΔTsm). Here, ΔTsm is treated as a diagnostic indicator of the overall thermal response to forest conversion. At the same time, the Non-Radiative Forcing Index (NRFI) serves as a complementary decomposition indicator of the relative non-radiative contribution. We find that afforestation was generally associated with cooling of daytime mean LST (−0.21 ± 0.11 °C), whereas deforestation was associated with warming (0.17 ± 0.07 °C), with effects amplified in spring and summer. At night, these effects reversed slightly. For extreme-high LST, afforestation was typically associated with lower values (−0.13 ± 0.14 °C), except for cropland conversion, which was associated with higher summer values. Conversely, deforestation was associated with higher extreme-high LST (0.20 ± 0.09 °C). Non-radiative effects associated with energy redistribution contribute substantially to the modeled LST responses under the reference correction factor c = 25%, with an overall mean NRFI of approximately 82.16%. Sensitivity tests across c = 10–25% show that the principal annual response patterns and the predominance of non-radiative effects are robust, although the magnitude of the modeled response varies with c . These findings highlight the seasonal and transition-specific effects of forest-cover change on regional LST and provide a scientific basis for sustainable land management and climate adaptation in urban agglomerations and similar regions.

title: Killing two birds with one stone: Exploring the dual impacts of National Urban agglomeration policy on carbon emissions and economic resilience in China
abstract: Urban agglomeration policies may reshape both carbon emissions and economic resilience, yet existing studies have largely examined these outcomes separately and at the city level, leaving their joint county-level effects insufficiently understood. This study treats China's national urban agglomeration policy as a quasi-natural experiment and evaluates its effects using panel data for 2129 counties from 2006 to 2023. A staggered difference-in-differences design is supplemented with heterogeneity-robust DID estimators, while mechanism tests and spatial Durbin models are used to examine possible channels and spatial spillovers. The results show that the policy lowers carbon emissions and strengthens economic resilience. These two improvements are particularly evident in eastern counties, those with medium-sized populations, and those with lower spatial concentration. Green innovation capacity and AI industry development emerge as potential channels. The spatial estimates further indicate that the policy is associated with lower carbon emissions and stronger economic resilience in geographically proximate or economically similar counties. These findings highlight the need for differentiated urban agglomeration governance that accounts for both local gains and cross-county spillovers, providing relevant evidence for developing and transition economies pursuing regional integration and low-carbon development.

title: Functional-space contraction and turnover reveal multiscale reassembly of benthic macroinvertebrates in the cascade-regulated Yalong River
abstract: Cascade hydropower development is transforming alpine river networks, yet conventional richness- and density-based metrics often obscure whether biological change reflects simple loss or broader community reassembly. We assessed benthic macroinvertebrate assemblages at 23 sites in the Yalong River, an alpine canyon tributary of the upper Yangtze River, spanning grassland, woodland and reservoir-influenced habitats. Taxonomic composition, density, nine functional-trait categories, alpha diversity, beta-diversity partitioning, elevation trends and environment-diversity relationships were integrated to diagnose multiscale responses to reservoir regulation. Thirty-six genus-level taxa from six higher taxonomic groups were recorded, with Insecta accounting for 75.0% of taxa. Richness declined from grassland (24 taxa) to woodland (21 taxa) and reservoir habitats (19 taxa), whereas reservoir assemblages retained all major groups and contained more slow-flow, depositional and lentic-tolerant taxa. Community composition differed significantly among habitats (PERMANOVA R² = 0.166, P = 0.001). Functional richness was lowest in reservoir habitats, indicating local contraction of trait space, while both taxonomic and functional beta diversity were higher and dominated by turnover rather than nestedness. Functional richness increased with elevation, whereas turnover generally decreased, demonstrating that reservoir filtering was superimposed on a strong alpine longitudinal gradient. These findings show that cascade regulation does not merely impoverish assemblages; it narrows local functional strategies while increasing regional taxonomic-functional replacement. The proposed indicator framework improves diagnosis of reservoir impacts and supports environmental-flow and habitat-restoration planning in alpine hydropower rivers.

title: Contrasting nutritional proxies and methylmercury exposure in zooplankton delivered by little auks across Greenland and Svalbard
abstract: Zooplankton forms a key trophic interface in Arctic marine ecosystems, transferring both nutritional resources and contaminants to higher consumers. Yet these dimensions are rarely evaluated together in the prey actually selected and delivered by predators under natural foraging conditions. We used little auks ( Alle alle ) as biological samplers of realized chick-provisioning diets and analysed 138 food loads collected across eight colony-by-year domains at six colonies in Greenland and Svalbard during 2022–2023. We quantified methylmercury (MeHg), total mercury (THg), carotenoids, molar carbon-to‑nitrogen (C:N) ratio, stable carbon and nitrogen isotopes, and taxonomic composition. We also combined standardized carotenoid, molar C:N ratio and MeHg measurements into a dataset-relative Nutrition–Toxicity Trade-off (NTT) score describing their joint configuration within individual diets. Diet chemistry differed markedly among the sampled domains, with particularly pronounced differences in MeHg, molar C:N and stable-isotope values. The component profiles showed that nutritional proxies and MeHg exposure did not necessarily covary: similar relative NTT scores could arise from different combinations of carotenoids, molar C:N and MeHg. Taxon-specific composites further showed that THg did not consistently track either MeHg concentration or the MeHg fraction and that these MeHg characteristics varied among locations within the same prey taxon and developmental stage. An exploratory domain-level analysis further showed a negative association between median dietary MeHg and sea-surface salinity. Where corresponding samples were available, variation in adult blood THg and astaxanthin broadly paralleled patterns observed in chick-provisioning diets. These results show substantial variation in the chemical characteristics of predator-selected zooplankton across contemporary Greenland and Svalbard foraging domains and demonstrate the value of jointly considering nutritional proxies and contaminant exposure when characterizing realized trophic conditions.

title: Spatial optimality of land use and land cover in three European capitals: Implementation of game theory
abstract: In European cities, landscape diversity plays a pivotal role in urban sustainability. This study defines local land use and land cover (LULC) optimality (LULCO) as a spatial compromise expressing the maximum relative representation of competing LULC types. We present a novel game-theoretic framework that operationalizes a self-contained, parameter-free stochastic model based on normal-form linear games to assess the spatial distribution of Nash Equilibrium (NE) probabilities. Applied across a hexagonal tessellation within the functional urban areas of three European capitals (Prague, Vienna, and Budapest) the framework models the local equilibrium among primary LULC types (forest, pasture, water, and arable land). The empirical results reveal that Prague exhibits the highest overall LULCO values, particularly in its southern region, followed by a slight reduction in Budapest, while Vienna displays the lowest relative optimality, concentrated across its northern sector. Crucially, historical structural depressions in landscape diversity, traditionally tied to 20th-century agricultural collectivization and land consolidation, are not actively apparent within these contemporary urban zones; instead, local optimality is driven by minor, highly localized changes. While spatial trends in LULCO align broadly with the information-theoretic Shannon index, the game-theoretic approach proves significantly more sensitive to subtle trade-offs in minor LULC categories like green and water spaces. This robust, universally applicable methodology provides a highly sensitive baseline of spatial equilibrium to identify localized structural disparities. It offeres a valuable diagnostic tool to inform targeted urban planning, zoning, and sustainable resource management policies.

title: Spatial aggregation induces asymmetric retention of ecosystem service bundles and reshapes their associations with social-ecological predictors: Evidence from the Loess Plateau
abstract: Ecosystem service bundles (ESBs) are widely used to identify recurring combinations of ecosystem services for spatial planning, but their representation and interpretation depend on analytical support. Although multiscale studies have shown that ESB patterns vary across scales, few have explicitly traced the retention, absorption, and reclassification of fine-scale bundle information during aggregation. This study examined aggregation-induced information filtering and scale-dependent predictor associations on the Loess Plateau, China. Five ecosystem services-water conservation, soil retention, carbon storage, habitat quality, and food production-were assessed for 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020 at 1000 m resolution. A unified ESB classification was applied across 1000 m grids, fine, mid, and coarse watershed units, and counties. Transition matrices and class-specific retention rates were used to quantify aggregation-induced reclassification, with particular attention to the composite/transition bundle. Random forest permutation importance was used to compare predictive associations between ESB types and social-ecological variables. The results showed that: (1) spatial aggregation selectively filtered fine-scale ESB information, producing asymmetric retention and directional reclassification among individual bundle types; (2) under the unified ESB taxonomy, carbon-habitat bundles gained representation across aggregated supports, while composite/transition bundles were frequently reassigned to carbon-habitat configurations, reducing the visibility of mixed service profiles; and (3) statistical associations between ESB types and social-ecological predictors varied across spatial supports, rather than showing a uniform shift toward either natural-context or human-pressure variables. These findings show that ESB maps are support-dependent diagnostic outputs. Watershed, county, and grid/fine-watershed supports should be used jointly for soil-water conservation planning, policy implementation, and the identification of local landscape heterogeneity.

title: Global forest aboveground biomass dynamics and disturbance attribution (2000–2019): A coordinated statistical framework for sustainable forest management
abstract: Reliable forest aboveground biomass (AGB) estimates are foundational for assessing the global carbon cycle, yet existing satellite products suffer from temporal gaps and spatial inconsistencies. Here, we coordinated three global AGB products (Liu, Xu, and Wigneron) covering 2000–2019 by combining random forest regression with pixel-level bias correction based on vegetation optical depth (VOD) observations. Spatiotemporal trends, structural break-points, and causal drivers were quantified using Theil-Sen slope estimation, Mann-Kendall tests, Pettitt change-point detection, and spatial overlay with Hansen global Forest change and MODIS fire datasets. Independent validation against 2019 spaceborne LiDAR (GEDI L4B) confirmed high consistency for the coordinated product ( R 2 = 0.71, RMSE = 14.96 Mg C ha −1 ), while ground VOD network validation yielded R > 0.7 across over 50% of monitoring sites. Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation revealed that parameter perturbation contributed ∼62% of overall uncertainty without time-dependent error accumulation. Global forest AGB exhibited a statistically significant net increase (slope range: +0.25 to +0.57 Pg C yr −1 , p < 0.01), with 56.89% of forested pixels exhibiting a significant upward trend ( p < 0.05). Pettitt tests identified a climate-driven structural break during 2009–2012 ( p < 0.05), coinciding with a strong El Niño–La Niña transition. Process-based attribution revealed a “growth-dominated gain, degradation-dominated loss” carbon dynamic: Forest growth drove 90%–92% (+0.51 to +2.64 Pg C yr −1 ) of global biomass gain, whereas persistent forest degradation accounted for 89% (−0.43 to −2.25 Pg C yr −1 ) of total loss—Substantially exceeding clear-cut deforestation. These findings highlight the necessity of incorporating degradation-centered monitoring into REDD+ policies and sustainable forest management

title: Integrating ecological supply–demand assessment and interpretable machine learning to reveal nonlinear mechanisms in the Central Yunnan Urban Agglomeration
abstract: Rapid urbanization and climate change have intensified conflicts between ecological supply and human demand, posing substantial challenges to sustainable development in urban agglomerations. This study focuses on the Central Yunnan Urban Agglomeration, China, and develops an integrated framework to characterize ecological supply–demand dynamics and nonlinear driving mechanisms during 2000–2024. Ecological supply was quantified by integrating ecological carrying capacity (ECC) and ecosystem services (ESS) into an ecological supply index (ESI), while ecological demand was assessed using a hazard–exposure–vulnerability framework to construct an ecological demand index (EDI). The ecological supply–demand balance (ESD) was calculated as the difference between ESI and EDI. Self-organizing maps (SOM) were used to classify ecological supply–demand regimes, and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) combined with Accumulated Local Effects (ALE) was used to identify nonlinear drivers and threshold effects. The results showed that ecological deficits dominated the study region, with a clear spatial mismatch between high-demand urban areas and high-supply mountainous regions. Four ecological supply–demand regimes were identified, revealing substantial spatial heterogeneity and temporal transitions. Road density, precipitation, elevation, and slope were the dominant drivers, and ALE analysis revealed nonlinear responses and critical ecological thresholds. Compared with conventional linear approaches, the proposed LightGBM–ALE framework improves the interpretation of complex ecological interactions and supports more robust ecological indicator development. This study provides a transferable framework for ecological assessment and spatially differentiated management in mountainous urban agglomerations.

title: Soil bacterial communities and co-occurrence patterns across soil types and land uses in a typical karst region of Southwest China
abstract: Soil microorganisms play a vital role in maintaining ecosystem stability in fragile karst landscapes. However, how edaphic properties and anthropogenic land use correspond to microbial assembly processes, network architectures, and functional potential remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluated the variations in soil bacterial communities across distinct soil types (limestone vs. red soil) and land-use systems (natural forest, eucalyptus plantation, citrus orchard, and paddy field) in a typical karst region of southwest China. Soil type accounted for 48% of the bacterial community variation, exhibiting a substantially stronger association with community structure than land use. Notably, Bacterial diversity and network complexity showed contrasting patterns: limestone soils harbored higher diversity, whereas red soils exhibited larger and more complex co-occurrence networks, reflecting divergent microbial community patterns across distinct edaphic contexts. These differences corresponded to contrasting community assembly processes, with homogenizing selection predominating in limestone soils and heterogeneous selection being more prevalent in red soils. Environmental modeling revealed that while pH, organic carbon, and calcium negatively correlated with network topology, available phosphorus stood out as the only parameter exhibiting a highly significant positive relationship with network connectivity ( p < 0.001), indicating that phosphorus availability is an important edaphic factor correlated with microbial network expansion in karst soils. Functionally, red soil bacterial communities were characterized by a higher relative abundance of pathways associated with cell motility and antimicrobial competition, whereas limestone soil communities showed higher representation of pathways related to specialized nitrogen turnover (nitrate reduction). Overall, these findings reveal that karst soil microbiomes and their co-occurrence networks are closely coupled with baseline geochemical characteristics, highlighting the importance of considering baseline soil types when designing ecosystem management and restoration strategies.

title: Global change factors diminish the contribution of soil fauna to litter decomposition: a meta-analysis
abstract: In terrestrial ecosystems, soil fauna communities play a crucial role in the decomposer community. Their feeding and shredding processes speed up the decomposition of litter and the release of nutrients, improving the soil's material cycling and energy flow. However, terrestrial ecosystems are continuously disrupted by increasingly severe global change factors (GCFs), and it is still unknown how much soil fauna's role in litter decomposition is evolving. To assess the effects of several GCFs (elevated CO 2 , hurricanes, drought, increased rainfall, nitrogen addition, warming, and multifactor combinations) on the contributions of soil fauna to decomposition, we performed a meta-analysis based on 734 observations from 32 studies. The results indicate that GCFs significantly reduced soil faunal litter decomposition contributions overall, with an average decrease of 23.72%. Forest ecosystems saw a decline of 34.48%, while the grassland and cropland samples observed were mainly distributed across East Asia, with declines of 26.19% and 26.10%, respectively. Apart from hurricanes and elevated CO 2 , due to the limited sample size, individual GCFs reduce the contribution of soil fauna to decomposition, while the combined effects of multiple factors result in an average decline of 53.8%, with the impact on cropland being particularly severe. Initial litter quality (25.05%) emerged as the key factor influencing the contribution of decomposition, although the dominant factors varied across the GCFs. GCFs primarily affected the contribution of decomposition through direct effects (−0.27), with indirect effects (0.08) being minor but involving multiple pathways. Overall, GCFs significantly reduced the contribution of soil fauna to leaf-litter decomposition, particularly under multifactor treatments. These findings suggest that GCFs may exert pressure on soil fauna and have important implications for material and energy cycling.

title: Indicators from fish habitat time series for climate change and environmental flows assessment
abstract: Mediterranean rivers are exposed to climate-driven hydrological change, yet environmental-flow assessment relies on static habitat metrics that poorly represent fish habitat variability over time. We developed a time-explicit framework that converts monthly weighted usable area (WUA) series into indicators of the magnitude, variability, duration, frequency and persistence of limiting physical habitat conditions. The framework was applied to a regulated reach of the Jucar River in eastern Spain, using bias-adjusted CMIP6 projections propagated through hydrological, water-resource system, hydraulic and physical habitat models. The indicators were calculated for critical life-stage periods derived from ecological evidence for Eastern Iberian barbel size classes and bleak, and compared between 1980 and 2014 (historical) and the near-term (2015–2040) and mid-term (2041–2070) horizons under three SSP scenarios, using Cliff's delta. Exposure was concentrated in juvenile barbel, whose summer window recorded no habitat deficit in any historical year, whereas a deficit occurred in 73% of years under mid-term SSP5–8.5, with large effects on the magnitude indicators. Adult barbel was already limited throughout its reproductive window, with four deficit months in 54% of historical years, leaving the threshold indicators near their ceiling. For fry barbel and bleak, the response did not extend beyond the driest month of the window. Therefore, the transition detected is from the absence of habitat deficit to its regular occurrence in the juvenile summer window, rather than from episodic to persistent limitation. These indicators provide a widely transferable and transparent physical-habitat diagnostic to support environmental-flow assessment and integrated river basin management under climate non-stationarity.

title: Quantifying synergies/trade-offs of biodiversity and ecosystem services across a tropical forest landscape
abstract: Tropical forests are the world's most biodiverse terrestrial ecosystems and provide critical ecosystem services that support global ecological sustainability. How to balance biodiversity conservation and ecosystem services provision is one of the challenges for natural resource management. Understanding landscape-scale relationships between indicators of biodiversity and ecosystem services is a key step for developing targeted management strategies tailored to specific site conditions. Here, based on investigation of 192 gird-based sample plots, we combined bivariate local Moran's I, root mean square deviation, composite index, and partial least squares path modeling to quantify spatial associations among four indicators, including two biodiversity indicators (species richness and functional richness) and two ecosystem service indicators (water yield and aboveground carbon storage), and examined their associations with key environmental factors across a tropical forest landscape. We found that synergies predominated across the study landscape, while trade-offs were restricted to scattered locations. Adequate precipitation supports the positive contribution of species richness to ecosystem services, whereas anthropogenic disturbance promotes synchronous degradation in low-value areas and intensifies trade-offs. Less accessible high-elevation areas are associated with greater supply capacity and multifunctionality. Integrating multifunctionality and trade-off intensity captured both overall ecological provision and internal functional imbalances, providing insights beyond pairwise correlations and supporting a more comprehensive interpretation of biodiversity–ecosystem service relationships and their associations with factors. Our study highlights the importance of incorporating biodiversity, ecosystem multifunctionality, their spatial associations and associated factors into landscape planning to support sustainable tropical forest management and biodiversity conservation.

title: A hydrological representation indicator for auditing wetland area targets across three river basins
abstract: Area-based wetland targets fix a total without specifying the hydrological settings and pressures represented by selected hectares. We evaluated a six-component Hydrological Representation Indicator (HRI) reference accounting rule across 2250 HydroBASINS level-8 units in the Mekong, Chao Phraya and Okavango–Makgadikgadi systems. We compared specification effects on screening labels and exact 30% portfolios, then tested whether fixed HRI retained endpoint information available in its components. We audited feature representation, river thresholds, native 10 m land cover, weights, aggregation and thresholds, and tested MODIS water, Sentinel-1 flooding, gauges and reach connectivity with spatial holdouts. A storage-only split nearly doubled wetland-feature records in 24 units while preserving wetland unions and class areas, demonstrating N's dependence on data representation. Native WorldCover processing covered all units. Under the A2 reference, high-area, low-HRI units contained 16.87%, 21.31% and 0.93% of wetland area. In the Mekong, matched geometric aggregation reduced this share to 8.70% and changed the focus set (Jset = 0.566), while exact portfolio overlap remained 0.995 by area. Area-ranked versus HRI-ranked portfolio Jarea was 0.410, 0.158 and 0.181 across the basins. For Mekong log loss, out-of-fold R 2 was −0.036 for fixed HRI, 0.327 for five components and 0.704 for early water; components added to early water yielded 0.706 without reliable incremental skill. Component models retained endpoint-specific skill for relative loss, flooding and reach connectivity. We therefore retain HRI as an auditable reference rule rather than a validated standard of wetland condition.

title: How far does greenness travel? Testing the domain-specific validity of remotely sensed greenness as an urban ecological indicator
abstract: Remotely sensed greenness is widely used as an urban ecological indicator, yet its validity is often assumed when vegetation signals are extended to thermal, habitat-structure, and biodiversity inference. This study tests domain-specific proxy validity across 100 public-space contexts in Seoul using Sentinel-2 vegetation and built-up indicators, Landsat 8/9 summer land-surface temperature, and effort-screened eBird complete checklists from 2023 to 2025. We develop a seven-module Greenness Proxy Validity Diagnostic (GPVD) to classify when greenness can be retained, qualified, or weakened as an ecological proxy. Greenness remained useful as a first-order screening signal but did not show uniform proxy validity. At the retained 500 m scale, built-up context was more strongly associated with land-surface temperature than greenness ( r = 0.878 vs. -0.589), while cooler-than-expected residual cases were concentrated in waterfront contexts, indicating that vegetation amount alone did not capture all thermal variation. Avian evidence was guild-specific and effort-sensitive: non-waterbird richness showed a strong bivariate association with greenness, but its adjusted estimate was less stable across subset and influence checks, whereas urban-generalist proportion was more consistent with built-up and hotter contexts. The study provides an operational diagnostic protocol for identifying where greenness remains useful as a first-order screening signal and where co-diagnostic evidence is required.

title: An internal–external coupling framework for multi-scale land use conflict analysis: Evidence from a mountainous urban agglomeration in Central Yunnan, China
abstract: Rapid urbanization in mountainous regions has transformed land use conflict (LUC) from simple land-type competition into complex functional–structural mismatches. However, existing identification paradigms often treat spatial units as closed systems and primarily focus on internal functional competition, leaving external spatial linkages and scale-dependent shifts in conflict mechanisms insufficiently addressed. To address these gaps, we propose a Multifunction–Structure–Scale (MSS) theoretical framework. We developed an Internal–External Double-layer Coupling Model to break the closed-system assumption of traditional methods and integrated the XGBoost-SHAP model to reveal non-linear driving mechanisms. Taking the Central Yunnan Urban Agglomeration (CYUA) as a case study, we found pronounced scale-dependent conflict patterns. At the grid scale, conflict intensity remained persistently high (median CI > 0.80), with mixed type conflicts accounting for over 95%. At the township scale, intensity decreased, while spatial heterogeneity peaked. At the county scale, intensity was the lowest, yet the external linkage deficiency type increased to 21.6%, indicating growing constraints from cross-unit coordination. Driving mechanisms also shifted systematically across scales: locational and topographic constraints dominated grid-scale conflicts; human activity effects became more prominent at the township scale; and natural background and resource–environmental constraints played a stronger role at the county scale. Key drivers exhibited clear non-linear responses, including thresholds for distance to settlement (4.35 km) at the grid scale and nighttime light intensity (33.79) at the township scale. These findings demonstrate that conflicts undergo structural transformation rather than linear attenuation across scales. Accordingly, differentiated governance should emphasize local risk identification and land-use expansion guidance at the grid scale, core–periphery functional coordination at the township scale, and regional coordination between development intensity and resource–environmental carrying capacity at the county scale. The internal–external coupling framework offers a transferable tool for diagnosing conflict sources and designing spatially differentiated land management in complex mountainous landscapes.

title: Decoupling of vegetation greening and resilience enhancing under a warming-wetting climate in coastal China over the past two decades
abstract: Divergent trends in vegetation greening and resilience create uncertainty about ecosystem sustainability. However, the spatiotemporal dynamics of this divergence and its climatic drivers remain poorly understood, particularly in climate-sensitive land–sea transition zones. We assessed spatiotemporal patterns of vegetation greenness and resilience across coastal China from 2000 to 2022 using the kernel normalized difference vegetation index (kNDVI) and lag-1 autocorrelation, AR(1), as indicators of vegetation greenness and resilience, respectively. We then identified the principal climatic correlates using multiple linear regression. Results revealed that vegetation greenness increased significantly, whereas resilience shifted from an increasing to a declining trend around an approximate breakpoint in 2012. This decoupling was primarily associated with temperature, vapor pressure deficit (VPD), and temperature variability. Specifically, in humid subtropical regions, rising temperatures and decreasing VPD were associated with reduced resilience, whereas in arid grassland regions, increased temperature variability mitigated the negative impacts of warming on resilience. Our findings show that vegetation greening does not necessarily indicate greater resilience. The nonlinear relationship between greening and resilience supports the inclusion of resilience indicators in ecological monitoring and may inform the sustainable management of coastal ecosystems under climate change.

title: Nonlinear and spatially differentiated assessment of visually perceived cultural ecosystem services in living heritage riverfronts
abstract: Large-scale living heritage landscapes require a CES perspective to understand the tension between heritage conservation and other cultural services. However, existing studies often represent heritage-related CES through recognized heritage resources, tourism hotspots, or aesthetic proxies. Taking the Grand Canal riverfront in southern Jiangsu as a case, this study examines whether ordinary municipal riverfront interfaces can provide heritage-related CES through visual perception. It evaluates two visually grounded CES dimensions—landscape aesthetic preference (HLP) and visual heritage value perception (HVP). A GPS-referenced image dataset was constructed from boat-based surveys, producing 1312 valid north-bank riverfront images with an average spacing of 31.4 m. OpenCLIP-based clustering and stratified sampling were used to select representative samples for face-to-face perception evaluation, and a fine-tuned deep-learning scoring model was then used to predict landscape aesthetic preference (HLP) and visual heritage value perception (HVP) across the full sample. XGBoost, SHAP, PDP, and GeoSHAP were further combined to identify key variables and interpret numerical and spatial nonlinearities. The results display that ordinary riverfront interfaces can provide heritage-related CES: 38% of samples outside heritage-concentration sections achieved above-average HVP scores. HLP and HVP are moderately correlated ( r = 0.675, p < .05). However, clear divergence emerges in industrial landscapes with limited greenery and in greenery-dominated scenes; With XGBoost models of both perceptions (validation R 2 values of 0.937 for HVP and 0.872 for HLP), SHAP results reveal that visual configuration variables dominate both perceptions (over 60%), while element proportions contribute more to HVP and landscape pattern indices contribute more to HLP. Nonlinear analyses further indicate that HLP is more sensitive to preferred ranges and compositional balance, whereas HVP responds more strongly to the visual prominence of specific elements. GeoSHAP results also reveal broader spatial variation in HLP effects, while HVP-related spatial effects are more concentrated in the center-eastern section. These findings suggest that heritage-related CES in living heritage landscapes cannot be inferred solely from heritage proximity or aesthetic preference, and that CES evaluation should shift toward a perception-based, nonlinear, and spatially differentiated understanding of heritage-related services.

title: Generalist taxa shape microbial community responses to riverine pollution and contribute to multi-element biogeochemical cycling
abstract: River pollution can reshape microbial community organization and alter biogeochemical functioning, yet how microorganisms with different niche strategies respond to pollution stress and relate to multi-element functional patterns remains poorly understood. Here, we selected different first-order tributaries of the Yangtze River as research targets and integrated high-resolution third-generation sequencing with QMEC functional gene chips to comprehensively evaluate, for the first time at the species level in riverine ecosystems, the niche characteristics, diversity dynamics, co-occurrence network roles, community assembly mechanisms, and contributions to CNPS cycling of generalist and specialist taxa. Results indicated that generalists had broader resource use and greater environmental tolerance, and that network cohesion and robustness were more strongly associated with the cross-module connectivity of generalist taxa. Community assembly in polluted rivers was generally dominated by stochastic processes, whereas in more severely polluted rivers the relative contribution of deterministic processes increased markedly and imposed stronger homogenizing selection on generalists, indicating that elevated pollution levels intensify environmental filtering. Generalists also showed tighter associations with CNPS functional genes and more integrated links to multi-element biogeochemical functions, whereas specialists were more strongly constrained by local environmental conditions and displayed more heterogeneous functional associations. Collectively, our findings indicate that generalist taxa can serve as priority indicators for river pollution management and ecological restoration assessment, providing actionable information for ecological risk early warning and the evaluation of restoration effectiveness.

title: Corrigendum to “Fish communities and diversity in river ecosystems on the Qinghai–Tibet plateau revealed by environmental DNA (eDNA) method” [Ecol. Indic. 156 (2023) 111185]
abstract: The authors wish to clarify and correct the species-level taxonomic assignments reported in our article.In particular, the original article reported environmental DNA (eDNA) sequence assignments corresponding to several non-native marine fish taxa, including Thunnus sp. and Xiphias gladius, from freshwater river samples collected on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP).Following reader feedback, we reexamined these taxonomic assignments and their underlying bioinformatic classification.In the original study, several marine fish taxa are indeed detected with very low abundance by eDNA, in specific river sections in the southern and downstream of the Yarlung Zangbo River.Although these detections were generated using an eDNA metabarcoding approach, eDNA detections represent sequence-based signals rather than direct observations of organisms (Goldberg et al., 2016;Valentini et al., 2016; Polanco F. et al., 2021).These detections should not be interpreted as evidence that these marine fishes occur in the sampled rivers, nor should they be regarded as evidence of biological invasion.We consider the following mechanisms that could have contributed to these anomalous detections.

title: Linking aboveground and belowground attributes to soil nutrient status during early-stage restoration of pika-induced bare patches in alpine grasslands
abstract: Grassland degradation compromises ecosystem integrity and stability, thereby reducing the capacity of grasslands to sustain multiple ecological functions. Rodent-induced bare patches are prominent manifestations of patchy degradation that accelerate soil erosion, nutrient loss, and vegetation fragmentation. However, ecological attributes associated with soil nutrient status during early-stage restoration of pika-induced bare patches remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated potential indicators of soil nutrient status in pika-induced bare patches of alpine grasslands using a soil nutrient composite index (SNCI) to characterize soil nutrient status. We conducted a site-specific two-year field assessment involving wood fiber, coconut fiber, and their combination, and assessed soil physicochemical properties, vegetation attributes, and bacterial and fungal communities to identify candidate indicators of soil nutrient status. Sampling-group differences were more apparent for soil properties than for vegetation attributes during early-stage patch restoration. Although vegetation attributes showed limited differences among the bare-patch sampling groups, vegetation cover and species richness were positively associated with soil nutrient status. Bacterial and fungal communities exhibited compositional variation among sampling groups, with fungal community composition providing complementary information on soil nutrient variation. Mixed-effects models and an AreaYear-level robustness assessment provided the most consistent support for vegetation cover, species richness, soil water content (SWC), and fungal community composition as candidate indicators of soil nutrient status, while piecewise SEM revealed conditional associations among these variables and SNCI. The integration of aboveground, abiotic, and belowground indicators may improve evaluation of early-stage soil nutrient status and provide a basis for future restoration assessment in degraded alpine grasslands.

title: Using Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS) to estimate surface soil properties in a mixed conifer forest
abstract: Mapping soil properties is critical to understanding ecosystem function and response to disturbance. Previous approaches rely on either cost-prohibitive and spatially/temporally limited direct sampling and measurement, or direct views of the soil from remote platforms for estimation from reflectance spectra. Here, we use an exploratory dataset to leverage the relationship between ecosystem structure and soil properties, providing the first demonstration that a number of important surface soil properties, including Soil Temperature (R 2 = 0.89), Dissolved Organic Carbon (DOC, R 2 = 0.75) and Total Nitrogen (R 2 = 0.77), can be well estimated using covariates derived from terrestrial laser scanning (TLS). This approach offers the benefits of remote estimation without the need for direct line of sight of the soil, enabling rapid monitoring in vegetated systems. The relationship between these covariates and relevant soil properties is explored using both dimension reduction and simple linear relationships with a small number of covariates. Our data driven approach supports the use of TLS in estimation of surface soil properties, while our simple models reveal correlations for further study of possible mechanisms linking forest structure and soil properties. This ecosystem-specific proof-of-concept requires further validation to verify transferability to other regions or forest types beyond our Southwest U.S. mixed conifer testbed. Our preliminary findings provide instigation for follow-on work to validate the mechanistic underpinnings and approach through more comprehensive soil sampling across spatial and temporal scales.

title: Diagnosing potential ecological externalities to support preliminary ecological compensation screening
abstract: Designing watershed ecological compensation schemes requires an assessment framework that can jointly characterize ecological contributions and human-induced pressures in a spatially explicit manner. To address this need, we develop an externality-informed assessment framework that integrates positive ecosystem functions and anthropogenic pressures within a unified, spatially explicit indicator structure. Net primary productivity, water yield, and habitat quality were used to represent ecological functioning, while nitrogen export, phosphorus export, and nighttime light were employed to capture environmental pressures. Indicators were standardized and aggregated to construct positive, negative, and net ecological externality indices. Using Jiangxi Province (China) as an illustrative application (1985–2023), we examined the spatial and temporal evolution of ecological externalities at both grid and municipal scales. Results show persistent spatial differentiation, with ecologically dominant regions maintaining positive net externalities despite increasing anthropogenic pressures. Habitat quality and net primary productivity contributed most to positive externalities, while nutrient export dominated negative externalities and nighttime light represented a smaller human-activity pressure component. Geographical detector analysis was retained as an exploratory spatial association analysis, with 2023 q values of 0.550 for DEM, 0.544 for land use, and 0.518 for NDVI. Structural patterns showed limited temporal reordering across the selected diagnostic years, suggesting that regional ecological roles were associated with relatively persistent biophysical and socio-economic configurations. By embedding ecosystem service-derived indicators within an externality-based diagnostic logic, the framework moves beyond single-metric ecosystem service assessments and provides a preliminary diagnostic basis for ecological compensation screening. The approach enhances interpretability and policy relevance, but final compensation design still requires source-receptor tracing, beneficiary identification, opportunity-cost estimation, and institutional rules.

title: Tree-tree interactions revisited – A refined approach to quantify spatial complementarity in tree crowns
abstract: Local tree-tree interactions are crucial for understanding biodiversity-ecosystem functioning relationships in forests. The complementary use of the canopy space increases canopy packing, thereby promoting community productivity. Several studies have measured theoretical volumetric complementarity using the crown complementarity index (CCI). Despite its effectiveness in quantifying vertical stratification, CCI does not account for tree distance and interacting crown volume. Here, we present the crown overlap index (COI). Based on the concepts of crown overlap and distance weighting, the COI quantifies the interacting crown volume within a distance threshold from 3D laser scanning data. We calculated CCI and COI for 136 tree pairs of the BEF-China experiment and found a negative correlation between the two indices. At high CCI values, COI was consistently low; at lower CCI values, however, COI varied greatly, suggesting that the COI complements the CCI in describing complementarity holistically. Dissimilarity in leaf functional traits and tree structural complexity increased CCI and decreased COI, indicating increased vertical stratification, but limited crown overlap. Similar patterns were observable in a dataset of mature, unmanaged beech forests. We attribute these patterns to differences in crown plasticity, which to some extent, were correlated with leaf trait dissimilarity and a more variable crown organization. Crown shyness, a phenomenon closely related to crown plasticity might also have affected the observed effects. Overall, the COI in conjunction with the CCI provide a more detailed characterisation of physical tree-tree interactions. Thereby, the COI could serve as a promising index for deepening our understanding of forest spatial structure.

title: Landscape spatial configuration determines seasonal nitrate transport rather than land-use proportions in mountainous rivers
abstract: Identifying seasonal nitrate (NO 3 − ) transport pathways remains a challenge in complex mountainous watersheds. This study integrated hydrogeochemistry, dual isotopes (δ 15 N-NO₃ − and δ 18 O-NO₃ − ), and the MixSIAR model with landscape metrics to investigate nitrate dynamics in the Chao River Basin. Spatial analysis categorized the watershed into upstream, midstream, and downstream zones. Source apportionment demonstrated that manure and sewage (M&S) was the dominant nitrate source across all sections and seasons, accounting for 71.4%–86.8% in the dry season and 69.2%–82.1% in the wet season. Soil nitrogen (SON) was the secondary source (11.1%–20.7%), primarily maintaining the low-nitrogen background in the upstream headwaters. The narrow spatial variation of δ 18 O-NO₃ − and highly oxygenated water column ruled out significant watershed-scale denitrification. Crucially, stepwise multiple regressions revealed that riverine nitrogen concentrations were dictated by landscape configurations rather than land-use proportions, showing a pronounced seasonal threshold effect. In the dry season, stagnant flows restricted transport to near-shore interfaces, where nitrate positively correlated with the patch shape complexity of forest and built-up lands. In the wet season, precipitation activated global hydrological connectivity, shifting landscape regulation to watershed-scale isolation distances and topological configurations. These findings indicate that optimizing landscape spatial structures is more effective than altering land-use proportions for mitigating seasonal non-point source pollution.

title: The widening biophysical divide in urban systems: Evidence from a 24-year study in Europe
abstract: As most cities in Europe face increasing population concentration, rapid urbanization oftentimes poses a threat to the environment. Due to constantly changing human-environment dynamics, studying the biophysical properties of urban areas becomes a complex task. We studied 690 Functional Urban Areas (FUAs) in Europe and analyzed four biophysical indicators: Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI), Leaf Area Index (LAI), Land Surface Temperature (LST), and Evapotranspiration (ET) in Urban Cores (UCs) and Commuting Zones (CZs). CZ-UC differences were also assessed utilizing monthly satellite images over 24 years. Our findings suggest that in the majority of FUAs EVI and LAI are increasing in both CZs and UCs, but the increase rates are faster in CZs, leading to a growing difference. UCs showed a tendency to experience faster LST rise compared to CZs, pointing to the urban heat island effect, particularly in the Mediterranean region, whereas the Mid-Europe/Alps region diverged from this pattern. ET revealed little year-over-year changes, with scarce instances of increases found in Turkey. Random Forest models followed by Shapley analysis revealed that urban and forest land cover fractions had the largest impact on explaining CZ-UC differences. Our results indicate that as urban land expands, it hinders vegetation expansion and increases LST. However, rising temperatures can be potentially mitigated by the increase of forest areas. Furthermore, increases in air temperatures and water surfaces were shown to drive faster increases of ET in CZs relative to UCs. This study provides a comprehensive view of environmental trends in European urban areas, and can act as a guide for finer scale research in the future.

title: Multidimensional vegetation stability and its associations with climate and permafrost degradation in the source region of the Yellow River
abstract: Alpine headwater ecosystems are increasingly affected by climate extremes and frozen-ground change, but their stability responses differ among ecosystem types and stability dimensions. Here, we assessed EVI-based trend-related temporal stability (TS), resistance (RES), resilience (RSL), and mean recovery time (MRT) in the Source Region of the Yellow River (SRYR) during 2001-2020. Climate-extreme indicators, terrain, and temperature-at-the-top-of-permafrost (TTOP)-derived permafrost change were integrated using ecosystem-specific structural equation models and spatial coupling analysis. The stability metrics showed strong spatial heterogeneity. TS was higher in several western-to-northern patches of the watershed, whereas higher RES, higher RSL, and shorter MRT occurred mainly in many central-eastern and southeastern areas. Alpine wetland showed a recovery-oriented pattern, with the highest median RES (0.478) and RSL (0.00447) and the shortest median MRT (21.6 days), whereas alpine steppe showed higher trend-related TS but weaker disturbance buffering. Permafrost degradation was detected mainly in alpine meadow (11.1%) and alpine steppe (5.0%) pixels within the classified samples. In alpine meadow, degradation was associated with higher TS but lower RES and RSL; in alpine steppe, it was mainly associated with lower TS and weaker direct links to recovery metrics. Spatial coupling identified approximately 3,969 km² of thaw-related low-resistance hotspots and approximately 5,966 km² of thaw-related long-recovery hotspots. These results provide a watershed-scale diagnosis of ecosystem-specific stability pathways and identify thaw-related risk hotspots for targeted monitoring and restoration in the SRYR.

title: Climate change shapes habitat suitability of the Asiatic black bear in the northwestern Himalaya
abstract: Climate change and increasing anthropogenic pressures pose significant threats to the suitability of wildlife habitats, particularly in montane ecosystems. This study evaluated the current and future habitat suitability of the Asiatic black bear in and around Dachigam National Park in the northwestern Himalaya. Habitat suitability was modeled using the maximum entropy approach based on species occurrence records, bioclimatic variables, and biophysical factors, including topography, vegetation, proximity to anthropogenic land use, and water sources, for the period 1980–2100. A total of 115 presence points, obtained through field surveys and camera traps, were used to train the model. Temperature- and precipitation-related variables, particularly the mean temperature of the warmest quarter, isothermality, and the precipitation of the driest month, emerged as the most influential predictors, highlighting the sensitivity of the species to climatic variability. Under current climatic conditions (1980–2011), 41% of the study area was classified as highly to very highly suitable habitat, while about 37% fell within low to medium suitability categories. Future projections for 2071–2100 indicated potential bidirectional range shifts across the elevational gradient. With the elevational range of 1551–3044 m asl, the number of grid cells under highly suitable habitats was projected to increase by ∼22% under SSP3–7.0, whereas SSP5–8.5 indicated a modest increase of ∼8% when compared with the baseline scenario. The model showed high predictive performance, with an area under the curve of ≥0.96. Overall, the findings suggest that the species may exhibit resilience through climate-driven range reorganization, although adaptive conservation planning will be essential to safeguard suitable habitats under future warming. The results also highlight the need to regulate anthropogenic encroachment in high suitability zones to reduce human-bear interactions and support the long-term conservation of the species amid climate change.

title: Dynamic cost-benefit assessment framework for ecological restoration in coalfield fire zones
abstract: Ecological restoration has emerged as a critical component of contemporary ecological governance. Nonetheless, conventional static assessment methodologies often fall short in adequately capturing the long-term economic viability and inherent uncertainties associated with ecological restoration initiatives. This study examines the Nanshan coalfield fire zone in Urumqi, Xinjiang, and develops a dynamic cost-benefit assessment framework tailored to the ecological restoration of coalfield fire zones. This framework integrates Gross Ecosystem Product (GEP) with the localized Equivalent Factor Method (EFM) to calculate ecological value. By incorporating the time value of money and combining Response Surface Methodology (RSM), single-factor sensitivity analysis, multi-scenario analysis, and Monte Carlo simulation, it systematically evaluates the economic feasibility of the ecological restoration project for the period 2025–2034. The results indicate that: (1) The static benefit-cost ratio (BCR) in the first year of restoration was only 0.22, with soil conservation value accounting for as much as 71.53%, significantly higher than the economic value of forage grass at 13.89%. This suggests that the core benefits of restoring extreme habitats primarily stem from ecological regulation services rather than direct economic output. (2) After incorporating the time value of money ( r = 3%, g = 0.5%), the project first reached BCR > 1 in the sixth year. The dynamic cumulative BCR rose to 1.68 by the tenth year, exhibiting a nonlinear pattern characterized by “high initial investment and cumulative returns in later stages.” (3) Response surface and sensitivity analyses indicate that the discount rate is a key factor influencing changes in the dynamic cumulative BCR. Multi-scenario analysis shows that even under an extremely pessimistic scenario of “high discount rate and zero ecological value growth” ( r = 5%, g = 0%), the 10-year dynamic cumulative BCR still reaches 1.51. (4) Monte Carlo simulation (10,000 iterations) showed that the mean dynamic cumulative BCR was 1.65, with a 95% uncertainty interval of 1.18–2.12. The dynamic evaluation framework developed in this study provides a quantifiable theoretical reference for investment decision-making and risk management in similar coalfield fire zones and other ecological restoration projects.

title: Natural and anthropogenic factors shaping old tree diversity and conservation in Central-South China
abstract: Old trees are important components of natural and cultural heritage. Although the influences of environmental conditions and human activity are widely recognized, their combined impact on species composition and multidimensional diversity remains poorly understood in topographically complex regions of central-south China. This study focuses on Hunan Province, a representative subtropical region with complex, basin-like topography. Using a database of 234,090 old trees (556 species), we investigated species composition, spatial diversity patterns, and the relative importance of environmental and anthropogenic factors by integrating species richness (SR), phylogenetic diversity (PD), and phylogenetic endemism (PE). Old tree diversity concentrated in the mountainous regions of western and southern Hunan. SR and PD showed highly congruent spatial patterns, whereas PE revealed a more fragmented distribution of evolutionarily unique lineages. Climate factors dominated, with precipitation seasonality as the strongest driver of species composition and climate stability as the predictor driver of spatial diversity. Different types of human activities showed contrasting associations with old trees. While economic development and agricultural land use were negatively associated with old tree diversity, traditional village networks showed positive associations with old tree persistence and conservation. This pattern is consistent with human preferences for the practical and cultural values of trees. Hotspot analysis showed that relying solely on SR may overlook evolutionarily valuable areas identified by PE. This study demonstrates the importance of integrating taxonomic and phylogenetic dimensions of biodiversity and provides a spatially explicit framework for old tree conservation in Hunan and other topographically complex regions of central-south China.

title: Nonlinear responses of watershed resilience to extreme climate events and grazing pressure in a semi-arid grassland watershed
abstract: Semi-arid grassland watersheds are increasingly affected by extreme climate events and grazing disturbance. Understanding the responses of watershed resilience (WR) to extreme climate events and grazing disturbance is critical for maintaining ecosystem stability in semi-arid grassland watersheds. This study developed a grid-based WR assessment framework for the upper Xilin River Basin (UXB), Inner Mongolia, by integrating resistance, restoration, and adaptability to characterize the capacity of the watershed to withstand disturbances, recover from their impacts, and adapt to changing conditions. Partial correlation analysis, generalized additive model (GAM), contribution analysis, and statistics across grazing gradients were applied to examine nonlinear climate-WR relationships, threshold responses, and grazing effects on WR vulnerability from 2000 to 2019. The results showed that WR exhibited strong spatial heterogeneity, with higher values in upstream mountainous and tributary headwater areas and lower values near reservoirs and confluence zones. Extreme climate indicators affected WR nonlinearly, with the multivariable GAM explaining approximately 60% of WR variation. Prolonged heat extremes generally weakened WR, whereas moisture conditions and drought duration elicited non-monotonic responses, indicating that resilience sensitivity changed across levels of climatic stress. Climate-WR relationships also varied significantly along the grazing intensity (GI) gradient. Compound drought-heat events identified using GAM-derived response thresholds consistently reduced WR relative to normal conditions, with the greatest losses occurring under moderate-to-high grazing pressure. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating climate response thresholds, grazing effects on WR vulnerability, and compound drought-heat risks into watershed resilience assessment. The proposed framework may help identify areas potentially vulnerable to climate and grazing pressures and could inform the future development of site-specific, resilience-oriented grazing strategies in semi-arid grassland watersheds.

title: Functional diversity is predominantly shaped by historical climate and is valuable for maintaining phytoplankton community uniqueness across seasons
abstract: Understanding the spatio-temporal dynamics of riverine algal communities and their driving influences is crucial for riverine biodiversity and functioning. Previous studies have yielded findings mostly based on single-time taxonomic surveys, frequently overlooking the role of functional traits in capturing seasonal variations. Here, we investigated phytoplankton in the upper reaches of Han River, a subtropical zone in China, across four seasons. Both α- and β- diversity were analyzed across taxonomic and functional dimensions, and functional communities were further divided into different functional groups to facilitate a trait-based analysis of community assembly. We found divergent seasonal patterns and drivers for functional and taxonomic diversity. Specifically, functional α-diversity (FRic) was significantly higher in winter (dry season) than in summer (wet season), whereas taxonomic α-diversity showed no significant difference between the two seasons. While taxonomic LCBD (local contribution to beta diversity) varied significantly across seasons, functional LCBD remained stable, highlighting the role of functional redundancy in maintaining the stability and uniqueness of community compositions. Importantly, functional diversity was predominantly shaped by historical climatic factors, while taxonomic diversity responded more strongly to local environmental conditions. This study further identified the influences of seasonal shifts on entire phytoplankton assemblages: local environmental processes prevailed in dry season, while spatial processes dominated community dynamics in wet season. Moreover, partitioning phytoplankton communities into distinct functional groups revealed that historical climatic factors dominated all functional groups in wet season, reflecting long-term evolutionary adaptations of functional traits to flood regimes. Our findings emphasize the importance of combining functional and taxonomic diversity to holistically assess river ecosystems by integrating long-term climatic adaptation with short-term environmental changes. We also suggest that partitioning functional traits into distinct groups provides an integrated perspective on understanding phytoplankton community assembly processes.

title: Construction of atmospheric security pattern under the goal of pollution and carbon reduction synergy: a case study of Tianjin, China
abstract: To address the limitations of traditional ecological security patterns (ESP) in representing atmospheric environments, this study developed a theoretical framework and technical pathway for an atmospheric security pattern (ASP) oriented toward synergistic pollution and carbon reduction, using Tianjin, China, as a case study. At the source identification stage, the focus was shifted from conventional ecological source functions to the synergistic sink capacities of pollutant deposition and carbon sequestration, yielding 33 ecological sources covering 1354.34 km 2 , or 11.38% of the municipal area. At the resistance surface construction stage, ventilation attributes were incorporated to couple ecological expansion resistance with atmospheric process resistance, revealing a spatial gradient decreasing outward from the Tianjin–Binhai core area. At the corridor extraction stage, ventilation corridors and ecological corridors were overlaid, both classified into two levels, jointly forming a dual corridor network for pollutant dispersion and ecological process maintenance. Furthermore, a dual minimum cumulative resistance game model integrating ecological expansion and urban construction expansion was applied to delineate three ASP zones: baseline, buffer, and optimal. Independent pollution, carbon emission, and WRF wind field data validated the rationality of ASP zoning: the baseline security pattern corresponded to the lowest PM 2.5 and O 3 concentrations and relatively low CO 2 emissions, and the orientations of major ventilation corridors were generally consistent with the simulated prevailing wind directions. Comparison with the territorial spatial master plan further indicated that ASP integrates well, and differentiated optimization recommendations were proposed accordingly. This study extends the theoretical scope of ESP to the atmospheric domain, providing a replicable planning paradigm for synergistic pollution and carbon reduction in rapidly urbanizing regions.

title: Impact of the forest chief system on biodiversity: Evidence from bird monitoring data in China
abstract: Based on the Social-Ecological Systems (SES) framework, this study integrates long-term bird monitoring data at the urban scale in China from 2010 to 2023, constructs a multi-period difference-in-differences model, systematically evaluates the impact of the Forest Chief System (FCS) on bird biodiversity, and examines its underlying mechanisms and heterogeneity. The main findings are as follows: (1) The implementation of the FCS significantly increases both bird abundance and species richness, indicating that an administratively driven forest governance system grounded in accountability can generate measurable biodiversity gains in bird communities. (2) The biodiversity-enhancing effect of the FCS operates through three main pathways: industrial ecological transformation, increased ecological conservation investment, and improved forest coverage, consistent with an SES-based transmission pathway linking institutional governance, behavioral responses, ecological conditions, and biodiversity outcomes. (3) The biodiversity effects of the FCS exhibit marked contextual heterogeneity, with the effects varying by species' habitat dependence, local development and governance foundations, and regional ecological conditions. By providing species-level evidence on the ecological consequences of forest governance institutions, this study extends the evaluation of ecological governance beyond conventional resource-based indicators toward biodiversity outcomes and offers new insights into the role of institutional arrangements in biodiversity conservation.

title: Performance of drought indices in capturing spatiotemporal drought dynamics in the Horn of Africa
abstract: Successful identification and characterization of drought are vital steps in drought risk assessment and management, requiring improved characterization approaches and suitable indices that capture different drought features. Although many drought indices have been developed, their broader suitability is often limited because local conditions frequently play a dominant role. Furthermore, multiple aggregation timescales for standardized indices make selecting the most appropriate timescale challenging. This study aims to identify suitable drought indices for the Horn of Africa (HoA) by evaluating 15 configurations of 6 drought indices with varying complexity. Employing a recently proposed combined cluster filtering mechanism, the performance of the indices in capturing spatial and temporal characteristics of droughts was evaluated against past drought records, specifically the 2010/11 and 2016/17 droughts. Results show that indices incorporating potential evapotranspiration (PET), particularly the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) and Multivariate Standardized Drought Index (MSDI), performed better. SPEI9 and MSDI9 showed strong performance in identifying drought-affected areas, with Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) values of 0.66 and 0.60 for the 2010/11 drought and 0.64 and 0.65 for the 2016/17 drought, respectively, while showing moderate temporal performance. In contrast, SPEI6 and MSDI6 effectively captured temporal characteristics while showing moderate spatial performance, with MCC values of 0.56 and 0.56 for 2010/11 and 0.58 and 0.53 for 2016/17, respectively. No individual index consistently outperformed across all aspects. Considering performance and computational complexity, SPEI6 and SPEI9 are recommended in parallel as complementary timescales for drought monitoring and to support related planning and management actions in the HoA, where droughts are frequent, prolonged, and widespread.

title: `Simulating land-use change and prioritizing zoned governance to restore ecological resilience in lake-region urban agglomerations
abstract: Rapid urban expansion in the lake domain urban agglomeration (LRUA) is profoundly reshaping regional land use patterns and ecological networks while also driving declines in ecological resilience. Yet where and how land use regulation and ecological restoration should be spatially prioritized remains insufficiently understood. Focusing on the urban agglomeration around Poyang Lake (UAPL), this study develops an integrated framework of “resilience assessment–multi-scenario simulation–zoning regulation” that couples the PLUS, Zonation, and MCR models. The framework is applied to analyze the co-evolution of land use change and ecological resilience (ER) in UAPL from 1980 to 2020 and to simulate future ER trends and optimal spatial optimization plans under five development scenarios from 2030 to 2060. Results indicate that the average ER of UAPL declined by 2.05% over the past 40 years, with a spatial pattern of “higher in the periphery and lower in the center” and a negative correlation with construction land expansion. In future simulations of UAPL, this negative correlation can be alleviated through ecological restoration, and ER levels in major cities of the region can be maintained between 0.4508 and 0.5222. Further scenario comparisons show that the sustainable development scenario (SDS) most effectively enhances ecological resilience. Under the optimal SDS scenario, the Zonation model is therefore used to delineate four levels of ecological resilience restoration zones, and the Minimum Cumulative Resistance Model (MCR) is used to construct an ecological restoration network comprising 33 first-level ecological corridors, 46 s-level ecological corridors, 59 third-level ecological corridors, and 141 key nodes, forming a “source–corridor–node” structure. This study can provide scientific support for resilience-oriented land governance and sustainable development in lake domain urban agglomerations.

title: Projecting ecological niche trajectories of the endangered large flying-fox (Pteropus vampyrus) under future climate change: Environmental interactions and spatial uncertainty for transboundary conservation
abstract: Climate change and anthropogenic pressures unpredictably alter ecological niches, exacerbating the extinction risk for threatened species. However, spatial projections often suffer from limited transferability and inadequate uncertainty quantification, hindering their application in dynamic conservation planning. Here, utilizing nine bioclimatic, topographic, and land cover variables, we developed an ensemble modeling framework integrating ten machine learning algorithms (AUC: 0.9099 ± 0.0130, TSS: 0.6432 ± 0.0428, and BI: 0.9370 ± 0.0352) to evaluate habitat suitability and climate-driven range shifts for the endangered large flying-fox ( Pteropus vampyrus ), a keystone umbrella species in Southeast Asia. Model interpretability revealed that slope aspect is strongly associated with predicted suitability, reflecting its role in shaping microclimatic exposure, moisture dynamics, and wind shelter, whereas temperature seasonality and precipitation of the driest month support population persistence across fragmented landscapes. Projecting spatial trajectories and mapping explicit uncertainties across three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1–2.6, SSP3–7.0, and SSP5–8.5) spanning three future time horizons (2011–2040, 2041–2070, and 2071–2100) indicated severe contraction and fragmentation of suitable ecological niches, with the area classified as General Decrease (29.13%) being more than threefold larger than the area classified as General Increase (9.29%) under the highest emission scenario SSP5–8.5. Beyond emphasizing the critical necessity of uncertainty quantification in transferability across climate scenarios and rendering ecological interactions transparent through model interpretability techniques, monitoring the current status and changes of the Pteropus vampyrus ecological niche provides valuable scientific evidence, serving as a critical foundation for formulating robust conservation strategies.

title: Driving mechanisms of vegetation evolution in the Mu Us Sandy Land considering the lag effects of climate and human activities
abstract: Vegetation dynamics in the Mu Us Sandy Land are influenced by the complex interplay of climate change and human activities, with response processes often characterized by temporal lag. Studies have insufficiently addressed these lag effects, which limits the accuracy of assessments of ecological restoration outcomes and hinders the formulation of sustainable management strategies. On the basis of long-term Landsat NDVI data, meteorological records, and land use data spanning 1989–2024, this study integrated Theil–Sen trend analysis, the Mann–Kendall test, partial correlation analysis, and residual analysis to identify the effects of various factors on the vegetation NDVI and quantitatively decomposed the relative contributions of climate and human activities while explicitly incorporating lag effects. The results reveal a distinct stagewise pattern of vegetation coverage in the Mu Us Sandy Land: stable fluctuation (1989–2001), slow recovery (2001−2012), accelerated improvement (2012–2017), and maintenance of stability (2017–2024). Temperature increase exerted a predominantly promoting effect in the early period (1989–1999), with significant positive correlations between temperature and the NDVI accounting for 79.09% of the area; this area expanded to 84.14% during 2000–2024, indicating a continuously strengthening positive impact of warming on vegetation growth. The positive effect of increased precipitation intensified over time, and the vegetation response to precipitation exhibited a pronounced annual lag. Precipitation with lags of one and two years provided dominant explanatory power for vegetation growth in a given year, with the affected area (68.07%) far exceeding that of current-year precipitation (lag-0 accounting for only 21.49%). The relative contribution of human activities increased steadily from 36.78% during 1989–1999 to more than 50% after 2000 and was revised to 58.91% for 2000–2024 when lag effects were considered, indicating that human activities were the dominant driver of vegetation greening. However, this contribution was 3.79 percentage points lower than that estimated without considering lags.
