Consequently, the intrinsic scaling relationships of UB&GS and the potential of NBS integration to improve accessibility and spatial equity of access across scales remain insufficiently explored. To address this gap, this study develops a scale-invariant framework based on Universal Multifractal (UM) theory to support the integration of NBS into existing UB&GS across various spatial scales, using Paris as a case study. Then, the fractal dimension ( D F ) and Gini index are employed as indicators to assess the effectiveness of NBS in enhancing accessibility and spatial equity of access to UB&GS, respectively. The results demonstrate that the developed scale-invariant framework can effectively support the optimal integration of NBS into the current UB&GS. With NBS integration, the D F increases by up to 0.07, while the Gini index decreases by a maximum of 0.27 across the study areas, indicating improved accessibility and enhanced spatial equity of access. Overall, the scale-invariant framework developed in this study provides quantitative recommendations to support the sustainable deployment of NBS in highly urbanised areas.

title: Scenario-based ecological zoning by coupling ecosystem service value and landscape ecological risk indicators in a rapidly urbanizing river–lake city
abstract: Rapid urbanization is restructuring land systems and intensifying tensions between ecosystem service provision and landscape ecological risk. Yet integrated frameworks that connect historical diagnosis, spatial association, future scenario, and zoning-oriented governance remain limited, particularly in river–lake cities with sensitive water–land interfaces. Taking Nanchang, China, as a representative case, this study developed a scenario-based ecological zoning framework integrating ecosystem service value (ESV) and landscape ecological risk (LER). Land-use changes from 2000 to 2025 were quantified, ESV and LER were assessed at a 2 km grid, and bivariate spatial autocorrelation was used to characterize their spatial association. Future land-use, ESV, LER, and ecological zones were then evaluated under four scenarios for 2030 and 2035. From 2000 to 2025, construction land expanded rapidly while cultivated land and water body declined. The proportion of high-ESV areas fell from 4.14% to 2.04%. Although high-LER areas declined from 26.92% to 15.47%, upper-middle and high-risk areas still accounted for 69.05% of the study area in 2025. Bivariate analysis showed a significant but weak-to-moderate positive spatial association, with high-ESV focal cells tending to occur in neighborhoods with relatively high LER, particularly along major river–lake corridors. Future simulations showed that the economic development scenario intensified construction land expansion and reduced Ecological Prevention Zones, whereas the sustainable development scenario better constrained urban growth and maintained key ecological spaces. The proposed framework supports the identification of priority function–risk areas, comparison of alternative land-use futures, and differentiated ecological zoning in rapidly urbanizing river–lake cities.

title: Rivers unchained: A spatial optimization approach for prioritizing river barrier removal
abstract: River fragmentation is a major constraint on ecological status and biodiversity in freshwater systems, creating a need for robust and operational tools to prioritize restoration. We develop a spatially explicit framework for prioritizing river barrier removal that integrates ecological indicators, river network connectivity, and economic constraints within a unified optimization approach. The framework combines a composite ecological benefit index with a dynamic, state-dependent representation of river network connectivity, allowing ecological gains from barrier removal to evolve as downstream and upstream conditions change. By linking connectivity, water quality, and species-specific habitat accessibility, the approach captures how restoration benefits depend on both local conditions and network structure. Applied at a national scale, the model reveals that ecological gains are highly non-linear and strongly shaped by network topology. Optimal restoration strategies form spatially coherent restoration corridors, where removing key bottlenecks unlocks extensive upstream habitats and guides subsequent removals within the same catchments. Restoration priorities vary with budget levels, hydropower opportunity costs, and policy objectives. Incorporating hydropower opportunity costs substantially alters restoration priorities, whereas alternative barrier-hydropower linkage formulations yield broadly similar aggregate outcomes once major hydropower assets are excluded from restoration portfolios. Sensitivity analyses demonstrate that restoration outcomes are influenced by alternative ecological-response formulations and parameterizations but remain primarily driven by river-network structure and dynamic connectivity processes. The results highlight the importance of integrating ecological indicators with dynamic network processes in restoration planning and provide a generalizable framework for supporting large-scale river restoration under competing environmental and economic objectives.

title: Combined effects of heatwaves and pollution on freshwater invertebrates: a scoping review of experimental approaches
abstract: Freshwater ecosystems are highly vulnerable to climate change and anthropogenic pollution. Climate change is characterized particularly by an increase in average temperatures, with more intense, longer, and more frequent heatwaves (HWs). While the effects of contaminants are well documented, sometimes in the context of global warming, the impact of HWs, either alone or in combination with pollution, remains poorly studied in freshwater invertebrates. A scoping review based on 68 studies was conducted to assess the current state of research. The objectives are to: (1) describe annual publication trends and geographic distribution, (2) analyze the diversity of heatwave (HW) scenarios used in experimental protocols, (3) assess the distribution of experimental approaches and model species, and (4) identify the outcome indicators most studied by authors. The analysis of this corpus showed the scientific community's growing interest in HW effects on freshwater invertebrates. However, only 5 of the 68 studies examined naturally occurring HWs, the rest relying on simulated exposures. Moreover, experimental HW intensities often exceeded those documented in natural lake HWs. Despite the use of robust models such as Daphnia or Lymnaea stagnalis , and the emergence of multi-stress approaches in semi-natural environments, most studies were conducted under laboratory conditions measuring individual-level indicators without necessarily considering the interactions between HWs and pollution. This review highlights the need for more realistic thermal scenarios, multi-stress approaches, and molecular analyses to better predict the resilience of freshwater ecosystems to global changes, particularly in sensitive regions such as the Arctic.

title: Spatial and temporal modelling of pastoral value in the Eastern Alps using Sentinel-2 and satellite embeddings
abstract: Semi-natural mountain pastures are multifunctional systems that provide key ecosystem services, including forage for livestock. Their long-term preservation depends on appropriate grazing management, a condition increasingly challenged in the European Alps by declining stocking rates and the resulting undergrazing of pastoral areas. In this context, we tested a remote sensing-based approach to spatially and temporally model pastoral value (PV), a comprehensive indicator of pasture quality and applicable for determining grasslands carrying capacity, in two alpages located in the Italian Eastern Alps. Using 111 botanical field observations, we applied Partial Least Squares regression to temporal composites of Sentinel-2 and Google Embeddings data to predict PV at 10 m spatial resolution. We then compared predictions for recent conditions (2023–2025 imagery) with those obtained by applying the same models to 2017–2018 imagery, examining their relationship with slope and distance from night barns as proxies of management intensity. Models achieved R 2 values between 0.53 and 0.75, with RMSE ranging from 9.11 to 12.08, and were able to spatially distinguish lower-quality pastures (PV around 15) from more productive grasslands (PV > 25). Temporal comparisons indicated a reduction in predicted PV at one of the two sites, detected only by the embeddings-based models, while Sentinel-2 predictions showed no change. A stronger decline was predicted in steeper areas, whereas no clear relationship emerged with distance from night barns. Overall, the results show that remote sensing is a promising approach for mapping PV and supporting grazing management in mountain grasslands, while detecting changes over time requires further improvements before operational use.

title: Evidence for potential top-down control of meso- and micro-copepods during jellyfish blooms revealed by eDNA metabarcoding
abstract: The limitation of traditional survey methods has catalyzed the rapid development and widespread application of eDNA metabarcoding. By collecting water samples from coastal waters off the Shandong Peninsula across the key blooming phase (May and August) of jellyfish, this study reveals the environmental drivers of jellyfish blooms and the potential top-down control exerted by jellyfish on meso- and micro-copepods. The results indicate that Aurelia coerulea is predominantly distributed in the northern Laizhou Bay, while Nemopilema nomurai is mainly found in the transition zone of Bohai and Yellow Seas. This distribution pattern may be attributed to different habitat selectivity during the polyp stage as well as environmental adaptability and ocean current effect during the medusa stage. The relative read abundance (RRA) of A. coerulea was significantly negatively correlated with that of meso- and micro-copepods, a pattern consistent with a potential top-down effect; however, under potentially phosphorus-limiting conditions, this inverse association did not cascade into an increase in phytoplankton biomass reflected by Chl a variation. Instead, elevated jellyfish RRA was associated with increased water turbidity. Our study provides a methodological paradigm for applying eDNA approach to elucidate the ecological consequences of regional jellyfish blooms, with future potential for scaling up to ecosystem-level investigations.

title: An integrated basin-scale indicator framework for assessing spatial imbalance in water availability and use: Evidence from India
abstract: Understanding basin-scale water-resource dynamics is essential for sustainable water-resources planning and management. However, existing national-scale assessments often evaluate rainfall, surface water, groundwater, storage infrastructure, and land-use dynamics separately, limiting a comprehensive understanding of basin-development status and water-resource conditions. Therefore, this study developed an integrated basin-scale indicator framework to assess water availability, utilization, groundwater stress, residual water, and basin-development status across 22 major river basins of India using nationally reported datasets on rainfall, surface water, groundwater, reservoir storage, sedimentation, and land use. The proposed framework integrates rainfall partitioning, groundwater processes, storage infrastructure, water utilization, land-use dynamics, and environmental-flow sensitivity within a common water-accounting structure. At the national scale, average annual rainfall of 1141 mm generates about 611 mm of basin water resources, of which 211 mm and 86 mm are utilized as surface water and groundwater, respectively, while approximately 314 mm (51.4%) remains as residual water. Considerable heterogeneity was observed across river basins. High-rainfall basins such as the Brahmaputra, Barak, and west-flowing river systems of the Western Ghats exhibited large residual-water fractions (>75%, reaching nearly 100% in some basins) and relatively low utilization, whereas basins such as Krishna, Cauvery, Pennar, and Indus showed intensive utilization, elevated groundwater stress, and limited residual-water availability. The Ganga basin, despite receiving moderate rainfall (∼1020 mm), was identified as a closing basin characterized by intensive conjunctive use of surface water and groundwater.The analysis further demonstrated that India's water resources are increasingly influenced by long-term human interventions in addition to hydro-climatic variability. Progressive reservoir sedimentation increased cumulative storage losses from 9.5% in 2000 to 16.6% in 2023, while expansion of irrigated agriculture has relied increasingly on groundwater development. The area-based assessment indicated that approximately 85% (range ∼ 78–86% across sensitivity and threshold scenarios) of the national river-basin area falls under critical to very critical water-stress conditions, whereas only about 15% remains under safe to very safe conditions. The study demonstrates that basin conditions are governed not only by hydrological availability but also by groundwater development, storage infrastructure, land-use change, and water-utilization patterns. The proposed framework provides a transparent and operationally relevant approach for integrated basin-scale water assessment and can support evidence-based water-resources planning and prioritization in India and other regions facing fragmented water-information systems and increasing pressure on water resources.

title: Remote sensing and the EU nature restoration Regulation: monitoring biodiversity indicators for integrated forest management
abstract: Implementing the EU Nature Restoration Regulation (EU NRR) requires Member States to monitor multiple indicators of forest biodiversity, yet the role of remote sensing (RS) in this process remains unclear. This review synthesises current evidence on the use of RS for monitoring forest biodiversity indicators defined in the NRR and identifies methodological gaps and operational priorities. Following a systematic review of 222 studies, we evaluate the suitability of different platforms, sensors, and scales of observation. Our results show that RS capabilities are strongly indicator and scale dependent, with no single approach suitable across all indicators. Airborne laser scanning is most effective for capturing forest structural attributes, including uneven-aged forest structure, while satellite multispectral imagery provides consistent, large-scale monitoring of forest connectivity. Tree species composition and diversity can be assessed using multi-sensor approaches, though accuracy declines in mixed and structurally complex forests. In contrast, the common forest bird index cannot currently be monitored using remote sensing, and deadwood indicators are limited by the resolution required for national monitoring. Key challenges include limited availability of repeated high-resolution data, difficulties in detecting high-resolution features, and reduced classification accuracy in complex forest systems. Overall, RS has strong potential to support monitoring when integrated with National Forest Inventories and multi-sensor data streams. Advancing towards operational implementation of RS within the NRR will require harmonised products, improved methods for complex forest conditions, and greater emphasis on temporal monitoring.

title: Decadal dynamics of surface water extent and quality in Fujian Province, China: An integrated optical-SAR remote sensing analysis using Landsat and Sentinel-1 time series (2015–2024)
abstract: Surface water resources are essential for ecosystem services, human welfare and climate regulation, yet face increasing pressure from climate variability and human activity. This study examined surface water extent, relative water-quality proxies and thermal regulation in Fujian Province, China, during 2015–2024 using Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-1 SAR. Optical water was mapped with a majority-voting ensemble of NDWI, MNDWI and AWEI (threshold >0) and fused with Sentinel-1 detections constrained by MNDWI > −0.15. A − 0.85 dB shift in Sentinel-1 VV backscatter between 2015 and 2016, coinciding with the start of Sentinel-1B acquisitions, was identified; it produced a spurious +577 km 2 increase in SAR-only water area, so SAR was used only as an MNDWI-constrained complement to the optical mask. Against the JRC Global Surface Water occurrence layer (>80%), used as a Landsat-derived consistency benchmark, the optical ensemble achieved F1 = 0.70, Kappa = 0.70 and IoU = 0.54. Fused water area ranged from 1476.76 to 1729.26 km 2 (mean 1573.95 km 2 , 1.27% of the land area). After a two-year persistence filter, net change was −106.63 ± 32.80 km 2 in 2015–2020, +65.05 ± 23.40 km 2 in 2020–2024 and − 41.58 ± 35.72 km 2 over the decade. On pixels that were water in all ten years, turbidity and total suspended matter proxies declined by 5.64% and 15.84% (Mann–Kendall p < 0.05), whereas the CDOM proxy showed no significant trend. In summer, water bodies were 2.45 ± 0.44 °C cooler than land within 1 km and 1.60 ± 0.52 °C cooler than land within 2 km ( p < 0.001), whereas a province-wide comparison reversed the sign because of elevation effects. These results provide a baseline for water-resource management and heat mitigation in rapidly developing coastal regions.

title: Compound indicators for vulnerable ecosystems (CIVE v1.0) framework
abstract: Terrestrial ecosystem risk is shaped by compound extremes that monthly indices can miss. We introduce the Compound Indicators for Vulnerable Ecosystems (CIVE), an 8-day, 0.125-degree framework separating hazard exposure from ecosystem vulnerability across the conterminous United States during 2000–2024. Fixed NLDAS-2 thresholds define a five-hazard catalogue. A target-year-excluded Dynamic-local reference built from up to ten nearest eligible non-hazard years defines expected GOSIF GPP. Exposure combines normalized event frequency and duration; vulnerability integrates impact magnitude, response time, recovery time, and relative resilience; risk is their geometric mean on joint support. GOSIF tracks 8-day AmeriFlux GPP ( r = 0.83, n = 8924), and event-scale losses agree between tower and grid estimates ( r = 0.78, n = 12). Across 25 annual records, national EI, VI, and RI average 0.023, 0.086, and 0.037. Their Sen slopes are +0.0024, −0.0018, and − 0.0002 decade −1 (Hamed–Rao p = 0.306, 0.870, and 0.981), providing no evidence of national trends. Sixteen overlapping 10-year windows show a modest positive EI direction and negative VI and RI directions, but these diagnostics are not independent because adjacent windows share nine years. Spatial contrasts persist: heatwave vulnerability and risk center on the Southwest and Southern Great Plains, flash-drought impacts extend through the Plains and upper Midwest, and cold-wave vulnerability is restricted to winter-active warm margins. Fixed-reference and alternative-window analyses show that temporal direction depends on method. CIVE supports hazard-specific spatial diagnosis, while national VI and RI trends remain unresolved.

title: When does rural population decline improve ecological quality? Evidence from population-density thresholds and spatial heterogeneity across Chinese counties
abstract: While a reduction in rural population density is commonly believed to alleviate human-land pressure and enhance ecological quality, this relationship may be far more complex when nonlinear dynamics are taken into account. Focusing on rural China, this study examines, whether the ecological effects of declining population density vary across different population density levels by employing county-level data from 2000 to 2020. The results show that ecological quality has generally improved across rural China, while pressures persist in developed and densely populated areas. More importantly, a clear double-threshold in rural population density is identified: one is an “Effect Intensification Threshold”, below which the ecological benefits of rural depopulation accelerate markedly, and an “Effect Reversal Threshold”, beyond which continued population loss reverses these benefits and leads to ecological degradation. Furthermore, regional disparities are pronounced, with ecological carrying capacities corresponding to differentiated threshold points: the Eastern region exhibits higher threshold levels, whereas the central and western regions generally follow the national pattern. Overall, this study advances a dynamic framework for understanding human-land interactions in depopulating rural systems and provides critical evidence for designing spatially tailored ecological policies.

title: Spatiotemporal patterns and nonlinear correlates of coordination between the digital economy and tourism ecological security in Chinese cities
abstract: Tourism ecological security (TES) is essential for sustaining destination resilience, ecological quality, and long-term tourism development. The digital economy (DE) plays a crucial role in improving TES by enabling smart monitoring, efficient resource allocation, and precision governance. Conversely, enhanced TES creates green demand and application scenarios for digital technologies, thereby facilitating DE upgrading. However, existing studies have mainly examined the one-way effects of DE on tourism or ecological performance, with limited attention to the bidirectional coupling coordination between DE and TES and its nonlinear correlates. Using panel data for 206 Chinese cities from 2006 to 2023, this study measures DE and TES using CRITIC and entropy-weighted TOPSIS, respectively; calculates the DE–TES coupling coordination degree (CCD); and combines kernel density estimation, Jenks natural breaks, and XGBoost–SHAP to examine its spatiotemporal evolution and associations with influencing factors. The results show that DE–TES CCD increased continuously, shifting from incoordination toward coordination, while displaying high values in eastern coastal urban agglomerations and lower values in central and western regions. Its influencing factors exhibit nonlinear associations, threshold patterns, and interactions in the model. Residents' educational attainment, tourism resource attractiveness, industrial structure upgrading, and population density are the key influencing factors, with educational attainment showing the strongest explanatory power. The interaction between tourism resource attractiveness and industrial structure upgrading is particularly prominent, indicating that higher tourism resource attractiveness is more positively associated with DE–TES CCD at higher levels of industrial structure upgrading. This study advances the theoretical understanding of DE–TES synergistic evolution and provides evidence for differentiated digital transformation and TES governance in tourism destinations.

title: Long-term evolution and climatic associations of dry and warm snow droughts across the Tibetan plateau
abstract: Seasonal snowpack on the Tibetan Plateau (TP) is an important store of water, yet long-term changes in snow drought types and their value for monitoring snow-water deficits remain unclear. Using multi-source data for 1982–2025, we classified dry (SWEI-3 ≤ −0.5; SPI-3 ≤ −0.5) and warm (SWEI-3 ≤ −0.5; SPI-3 > −0.5) snow droughts and assessed their trends, regional patterns, drought burden, and statistical climatic associations. Here, “warm” identifies an SWE deficit without a concurrent precipitation deficit, not a temperature-defined event. Total snow drought area increased by 0.595 percentage points yr −1 ( p < 0.001), mainly reflecting warm snow drought expansion (0.687 percentage points yr −1 ). Warm snow droughts accounted for 72.8% of snow drought occurrence, including 69%, 75%, and 72% in the western, south-central, and southeastern TP, respectively; the south-central TP showed the fastest historical increase. The positive warm-drought trend persisted when the product-transition years were excluded and under two alternative fixed seasonal windows, although trend magnitudes varied. Mean drought intensity changed little, and the increasing snow drought burden index largely reflected spatial expansion. XGBoost–SHAP identified precipitation as an important statistical discriminator (30.9% for dry and 23.1% for warm snow droughts), but the warm-drought model showed limited temporal discrimination (ROC-AUC = 0.548). No lagged climate-mode correlations survived false discovery rate correction, and composite NDVI differences were not significant. These results support monitoring seasonal SWE deficits without establishing specific physical mechanisms or downstream hydrological and ecological impacts.

title: Modelling future collapse risk of aapa mires across a boreal climate gradient
abstract: Northern peatlands provide critical ecosystem services, including carbon sequestration that mitigates climate change. Warming and land use threaten many peatlands, but a unique subclass of peatlands called aapa mires are currently listed as Least Concern in Europe. We aimed to evaluate risk for aapa mires in Finland using newly available datasets. We developed a new remote sensing-based indicator of aapa mire degradation and used forecasting models integrating climate change, hydrology, and peat mining scenarios to estimate trajectories of degradation in mire ecosystems to 2099. We modelled 120 Finnish aapa mires across three climate zones and used our results to assess risk against the global standard IUCN Red List of Ecosystems (RLE) criteria. We found substantial historical degradation, although this has slowed with the cessation of unsustainable land use practices since the late 1900s. Projected climate change produced moderately elevated risk; however, risk increased rapidly under intensifying peat mining scenarios. Aapa mires in the south boreal region had the highest risk of collapse, with a mean probability of collapse of 20.3% over a 50-year period (2025 to 2075), compared to 5.0% in the middle boreal and 1.6% in the northern boreal zones. Under the RLE criteria, northern and middle-boreal mires were Vulnerable and southern mires were Critically Endangered under Criterion C3 (historical environmental degradation). Conservation of core areas, refraining from mining, and restoration of degraded sites are essential, as remaining aapa mires provide critical wildlife refugia, and those undergoing natural succession processes offer climate mitigation potential.

title: Identifying land use thresholds for ecosystem service balance through supply-demand assessment in Hainan Island
abstract: Against the backdrop of accelerating urbanization, the imbalance between ecosystem services (ESs) supply and demand has become a major concern for regional sustainable development, particularly in geographically isolated islands, where spatially confined land resources limit the self-regulatory capacity of terrestrial ESs and amplify their vulnerability to supply-demand imbalance. Using Hainan Island as a case study, we integrated the InVEST model, random forest algorithm, and weighted linear regression to quantify the spatiotemporal supply-demand dynamics of five core ESs from 2010 to 2020, identified key land-use thresholds governing ESs balance, and established a dual-scale analytical framework at county and grid levels. The results revealed a pronounced spatial dichotomy of “coastal degradation versus central stability”. Central forests sustained surpluses in regulating services (Habitat Quality (HQ), Soil Retention (SR) and Carbon Sequestration (CS)), while deficit zones clustered in coastal towns. Contribution analysis of land-use types to the ecological supply-demand ratio (ESDR) identified built-up land as the primary negative driver of imbalance. Built-up expansion contributed to supply-demand deficits in Water Retention (WR), with mean ESDR values of − 0.0090 in 2020 and induced imbalance risks for Grain Production (GP) in half of the counties at the county scale. At the 500 m grid scale, 87.71% of the island maintained simultaneous supply-demand balance across all five services. Threshold analysis identified a structural land-use dilemma: attempting to achieve GP balance through forest-to-cropland conversion triggers a “denominator effect”, mechanically increasing built-up land proportions and pushing locally bound regulating services beyond their critical thresholds. This reflects an asymmetry in compensability, as GP deficits can be mitigated via external trade networks whereas regulating services are difficult to compensate externally. At the county scale, five management zones (“maintained zone”, “GP promoted zone”, “CS promoted zone”, “GP-CS promoted zone”, and “GP-CS-WR promoted zone”) were delineated to safeguard ecological cores and address spatially differentiated deficits; at the grid scale, 87.71% of the study area currently maintains ESs balance across all five services, with the identified land-use thresholds serving as early-warning indicators to guide timely regulation of built-up expansion. The integrated analytical framework established in this study is potentially transferable to other tropical islands facing land resource constraints, while the empirical threshold values necessitate site-specific calibration for regional adaptation. This threshold-based governance paradigm offers a practical and quantitative reference for alleviating structural trade-offs in ESs and optimizing ecological management strategies for land constrained island regions.

title: Developing an ecological indicator framework for anthropogenic underwater noise: a multi-level cascade from sensory disruption to ecosystem service impairment
abstract: Anthropogenic underwater noise is an increasingly pervasive environmental pressure affecting marine and freshwater ecosystems, yet its ecological consequences are rarely incorporated into operational indicator-based assessment frameworks. Although behavioral, physiological, and population-level responses to underwater noise have been extensively documented, a major challenge remains in translating this fragmented evidence into a mechanistically coherent and decision-oriented assessment system. This review synthesizes current evidence on acoustic characteristics, sensory detection mechanisms, biological responses, and ecological consequences of underwater noise and develops an evidence-informed, multi-level ecological indicator framework linking acoustic exposure to ecosystem-level impairment. The framework integrates six hierarchical levels—acoustic exposure, sensory disruption, behavioral modification, energetic and physiological reallocation, population-level consequences, and ecosystem function alteration—and links each level to measurable ecological indicators and corresponding assessment endpoints. Candidate indicators include acoustic exposure metrics, stress and physiological biomarkers, behavioral thresholds, recruitment and population responses, and changes in ecosystem functions and services. We further integrate hazard characterization, exposure assessment, dose–response relationships, indicator selection, and ecological risk characterization into a decision-oriented assessment pathway, with particular emphasis on chronic sub-lethal exposure and cumulative stressor interactions. By organizing mechanistic evidence across biological scales and translating it into measurable indicators and management-relevant assessment endpoints, the proposed framework provides a structured basis for incorporating underwater noise into ecological monitoring, environmental impact assessment, and ecosystem-based management. The framework also highlights key uncertainties, including species-specific sensitivity, threshold variability, and the limited standardization of acoustic–ecological response relationships, thereby identifying priorities for future validation and application.

title: Opposite spatiotemporal sensitivity of terrestrial vegetation to intensified extreme precipitation across China's aridity gradients
abstract: Extreme precipitation has intensified in many regions under global warming, yet how vegetation sensitivity to extreme precipitation varies along aridity gradients and changes over time remains poorly understood. Here we quantified vegetation sensitivity to extreme precipitation ( β EP ) across China during 1982–2020 using a Bayesian dynamic linear model (DLM) based on long-term NDVI and precipitation datasets, and disentangled its spatiotemporal drivers using Random Forest and SHAP attribution. Vegetation exhibited significantly positive β EP values across 72% of dryland grids (mean = 0.03), with grasslands contributing the largest positive β EP values, whereas only 37% of humid grids had positive β EP and 43% showed negative values (mean = −0.005), with forests exhibiting weak negative responses. Temporally, β EP increased significantly in arid and semi-arid regions but declined in humid ecosystems, with widespread directional turning of sensitivity observed after 1999 across all aridity zones. The long-term mean β EP was primarily controlled by water availability in drylands and solar radiation in humid regions. In contrast, elevated CO 2 exerted positive effects on the interannual fluctuations of β EP in dry regions but negative effects in humid regions. These gradient-driven contrasting responses require differentiated ecological policies for vegetation dynamics projection and extreme precipitation risk mitigation.

title: Soil properties shape nematode communities more than vegetation in Robinia pseudoacacia plantations on the Loess Plateau
abstract: Soil nematodes are often used as indicators of soil ecosystem health due to their large population, diverse species, ease of acquisition and identification, and sensitivity to disturbances. Black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia) has been widely planted in the Loess Plateau due to its rapid growth and high tolerance to environmental stress. Compared to the above-ground plant communities and soil microorganisms, little research has been conducted on how black locust plantation ecosystems affect soil nematodes. To fill this knowledge gap, we investigated understory vegetation and soil nematode communities in mature black locust plantations across three vegetation zones (steppe, forest-steppe, and forest) in the Yanhe River catchment along environmental gradient. The primary objective was to understand how soil nematode communities respond to the introduction of black locust along environmental gradient, thereby providing insights into the complex interactions within black locust plantation ecosystems. Our results found that: (1) Black locust growth increased understory vegetation richness and enhanced leaf photosynthetic traits (LPT) but indirectly reduced understory aboveground biomass, with limited effects on root functional traits; (2) The steppe zone exhibited superior soil nematode community structure and functionality compared to the forest-steppe and forest zones, with distinct differences in trophic group composition among the three zones; (3) Soil total nitrogen, total phosphorus, and organic carbon were identified as primary determinants of soil nematode community structure and function, whereas the growth of black locust and the structure and functional traits of understory vegetation had no significant influence on nematode communities. Our findings revealed the regulatory mechanism of environmental factors on understory soil nematode communities in black locust plantations, with the development of black locust plantations acting as a mediating variable, regulating the effects of meteorological factors on understory vegetation structure and functional traits, while soil nematode communities were predominantly governed by the direct regulation of climatic factors and soil properties.

title: Spatiotemporal variations and persistence of water storage in the Shendong mining area accounting for mining-induced mass changees
abstract: Groundwater and terrestrial water storage in mining-affected regions are subject to complex variations, making it essential to accurately characterize their dynamics for sustainable water resource management. This study integrates high-resolution observations from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and its successor, the GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO), the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS), and coal-production data to analyze the spatiotemporal variations of terrestrial water storage anomalies (TWSA), soil moisture anomalies (SMA), and groundwater storage anomalies (GWSA) in the relatively small-scale Shendong mining area of the Yellow River Basin, China, during 2002–2024, and quantitatively evaluates their stability and persistence using the coefficient of variation and the Hurst index. Results indicate a persistent decline in TWSA and GWSA across the study area, with strong temporal consistency and spatial continuity, with GWSA depletion identified as the primary contributor to long-term water storage loss, while SMA remains relatively stable with weaker variability. Accounting for mining-induced mass changes and examining stability and persistence at a localized scale, the results further reveal that GWSA exhibits low stability but strong persistence, indicating a sustained downward trajectory of groundwater storage. These findings provide new insights into the co-evolution of water storage components in mining-affected regions and emphasize the need to consider human-induced effects when interpreting GRACE-based water storage changes.

title: Nonlinear dynamics and driving mechanisms of precipitation and soil water use efficiency in the Three-North Region of China
abstract: The Three-North Shelterbelt Program region is an important ecological security barrier in the arid and semi-arid ecologically fragile zone of northern China, where the carbon-water coupling mechanisms under water limitation urgently need to be quantitatively identified. Using the Three-North Shelterbelt Program region as the study area, this study constructed precipitation use efficiency (PUE) and soil water use efficiency (SWUE) based on remote-sensing productivity products and reanalysis hydrometeorological data. We further compared two CEDAR-GPP scenarios with different representations of CO 2 -related processes to characterize the spatiotemporal variations and driving mechanisms of PUE and SWUE during 1982–2018. CatBoost-SHAP was further employed to reveal the nonlinear effects of key driving factors and the modulation effects of aridity gradients, and a partial least squares structural equation model was used to construct a cascading pathway framework linking geography, climate, vegetation, and human activities, so as to comprehensively analyze the underlying mechanisms. The results showed that PUE and SWUE under the scenarios with and without the CO 2 fertilization effect generally exhibited increasing trends at both monthly and annual scales, accompanied by significant interannual fluctuations. Spatially, the trend patterns under the two scenarios were generally consistent, with differences mainly reflected in the intensity of local changes. PUE was mainly controlled by evapotranspiration and showed significant threshold and saturation characteristics in the low evapotranspiration range; SWUE was mainly controlled by leaf area index and jointly modulated by factors such as radiation, air temperature, and latitude, while exhibiting diminishing marginal effects at high leaf area index levels, and aridity significantly regulated the strength and direction of the contributions of key driving factors. Topography constituted the main indirect pathway by influencing climate and regulating vegetation, while human activities exerted direct effects on both indicators as well as vegetation-mediated indirect effects, leading to differences in the composition of the pathways of PUE and SWUE. These results provide a new analytical framework for ecological restoration and carbon–water coupling mechanisms in the Three-North Shelterbelt Program region.

title: The multi-scale heterogeneity of habitat quality changes in the Heihe River basin
abstract: Habitat heterogeneity in inland river basins constitutes a dynamic and structured ecological pattern governed by hydrological processes and expressed across multiple temporal and spatial scales. Understanding and conserving this heterogeneity is crucial for ensuring ecological security and promoting sustainable socio-economic development in the arid regions of northwestern China. Drawing upon the general characteristics of inland river basins, this study establishes a theoretical analytical framework to examine habitat quality differentiation across mountainous, oasis, and desert ecosystems. And based on the spatial heterogeneity of oases, they are classified into three geomorphic zones: the Higher Position Oasis (HPO), the Middle Position Oasis (MPO), and the Lower Position Oasis (LPO). This study employs the Habitat Quality module of the InVEST model to conduct a systematic spatiotemporal assessment of habitat quality dynamics across two nested ecological scales: the entire inland river basin and its constituent oasis systems. Key findings are as follows: (1) Habitat quality exhibits a consistent spatial gradient at the basin scale—mountainous areas > oases > desert—while within the oasis system, it declines along a gradient from HPOs to MPOs and LPOs. (2) Although habitat quality remains relatively stable over time, localized degradation is observed, with mild, moderate, and severe deterioration predominantly concentrated in medium-productivity oases. Collectively, this research advances methodological rigor in habitat quality assessment for arid inland river basins and offers empirically grounded insights to inform ecosystem conservation strategies and early-warning frameworks for basin–oasis coupled systems.

title: Optimizing vegetation restoration strategies based on pre-mining soil ecosystem quality in coal mining areas
abstract: Mining-induced subsidence areas require restoration strategies that support long-term ecosystem development. A key challenge is rebuilding self-sustaining soil–plant feedbacks. Vegetation configuration is critical because unsuitable assemblages may constrain microbial recovery, enzyme-mediated nutrient cycling, and the persistence of soil improvement below the surface layer. Based on 840 pre-mining vegetation–soil sampling plots, we examined the associations of eight vegetation configurations with soil physicochemical properties, enzyme activities, and microbial attributes in the 0–10 cm surface and 30–40 cm subsurface layers， aiming to identify vegetation configurations capable of sustaining soil quality improvement and supporting ecological restoration. Shrub-dominated mixed forests (VT6 and VT7) had a notably lower relative decrease from surface to subsurface rate of enzyme activity (48–52%) compared to pure shrub systems (VT2: 71%). Microbial community α-diversity exhibited a homogenization pattern, while fungal α-diversity showed significant positive correlations with nitrification enzyme activity and dehydrogenase activity. By integrating the Surface-Subsurface Response Index (SSRI) and microbial community α-diversity metrics through correlation analysis and principal component analysis, a modified soil quality index (SQI′) was developed. The large-sample dataset was then used to evaluate soil quality stability and the probability of high-quality soil occurrence among vegetation types, identifying VT6 as the optimal mixed-forest restoration configuration. The LEfSe analysis identified Pseudomonas as a genus-level bacterial indicator signal enriched in VT6. Structural equation modeling revealed that dehydrogenase activity (total effect: 0.36) and maximum water-holding capacity (0.23) were the most influential factors driving microbial diversity. Nitrification enzymes, urease, and dehydrogenase are commonly used as key indicators for assessing soil ecological functions. These findings provide a scientific basis for selecting effective vegetation types in ecological restoration efforts targeting arid, mining-induced subsidence areas.

title: Waterbird beta-diversity responses to disturbance in afrotropical wetlands: Implications for conservation policy and sustainability
abstract: Gaining insights into how disturbance shapes biodiversity patterns and overall ecosystem functioning is fundamental for guiding meaningful conservation and policy-driven sustainability strategies in rapidly transforming tropical wetlands. Our research evaluated the extent to which anthropogenic disturbance influences waterbird beta-diversity (β-diversity) and indicator species across 29 Afrotropical wetlands in the Niger delta region of Nigeria. We delineated our wetlands into lowly and highly disturbed classes using a constrained ordination technique, while waterbird presence-absence dataset sampled between 2019 and 2021 were analyzed to partition total β-diversity into its components of turnover (species replacement) and nestedness-resultant dissimilarity associated with richness differences. We used PERMDISP, PERMANOVA, and Welch's t -test to evaluate spatial variations and compositional differences between our disturbance classes. To identify specific taxa associated with each anthropogenic disturbance class, we employed the indicator species analysis technique. The compositional dissimilarity between lowly and highly disturbed classes was primarily driven by the turnover component of β-diversity, with nestedness contributing comparatively little. Nestedness richness difference was greater in lowly-disturbed wetlands, whereas the highly-disturbed wetlands - characterized by high richness difference – exhibited low nested patterns or high species turnover, which is indicative of species filtering. Our indicator species analyses identified four waterbird taxa associated with anthropogenic disturbance extents, with three indicative of highly disturbed wetlands and one indicative of lowly disturbed wetlands. Our results indicate that increase in disturbance shifts waterbird assemblages toward disturbance-tolerant species, leading to lower ecological heterogeneity and potentially limiting wetland recovery and resilience over time, since these species acts as vital ecosystem engineers. Overall, our findings advance wetland conservation policy and environmental sustainability, highlighting the urgent need to reduce disturbance, improve habitat protection strategies, as well as incorporating indicator species into adaptive monitoring frameworks as meaningful mechanisms for long-term ecological sustainability in Afrotropical systems.

title: Environmental DNA-derived indicators reveal species turnover and connectivity-related ecological patterns across patch-corridor-matrix framework
abstract: Habitat fragmentation alters biodiversity patterns and ecological connectivity across agricultural landscapes. Here, we investigated how Patch-Corridor-Matrix (PCM) landscape components influence animal community structure within a vineyard-dominated landscape in Southern Italy. Biodiversity was assessed using leaf-surface environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding, integrating arthropod and vertebrate detections with multivariate analyses, beta-diversity partitioning, indicator species analysis, and co-occurrence networks. A total of 27 sampling units (9 per PCM element) were surveyed using a stratified grid-based design. Patches supported significantly higher observed taxon richness than corridors and matrix habitats. Community composition was significantly structured by both elevation and landscape element, whereas precipitation and temperature did not show significant effects. The dbRDA model explained approximately 24.3% of the total variation, and landscape element remained significantly associated with community composition after controlling for elevationand spatial structure. Beta-diversity partitioning revealed that differences among PCM elements were overwhelmingly driven by species turnover (βJTU = 0.962) rather than nestedness (βJNE = 0.009), indicating strong species replacement and limited compositional redundancy among landscape components. Corridors shared taxa with both patches and matrix habitats, suggesting a potential dual role as connective elements and distinct habitat units. Co-occurrence networks exhibited clear modularity, reflecting habitat filtering and landscape structure rather than direct ecological interactions. Overall, our findings demonstrate that eDNA-derived metrics, including species turnover, modularity, and indicator taxa, can serve as ecological indicators of habitat differentiation in complex landscapes.

title: A bias-aware indicator framework for prioritizing surveys of data-deficient freshwater leeches in China
abstract: Sparse and spatially biased occurrence records complicate survey planning for freshwater invertebrates. We evaluated a bias-aware indicator framework linking taxon documentation with a fixed 40:40:20 ranking of environmental similarity to documented occurrence contexts, documentation gap and freshwater support. Contemporary accessibility was evaluated separately to characterize documentation associations and inform survey logistics. Habitat-scope and coordinate audits retained 198 records representing 44 freshwater leech taxa in China; 88.6% of taxa had fewer than ten records. Using 197 predictor-eligible records and 4907 freshwater-background points, random-record validation indicated repeatable environmental structure within the compiled dataset (median background-rank AUC = 0.753). Geographically blocked transfer was weak (AUC = 0.511) but exceeded a randomized-reference median of 0.293 ( p = 0.005). At 50 two-degree cells selected nationally within each fold, the reference recovered 55.3% of held-out records but none in two folds. Environmental similarity plus documentation gap recovered 57.9%; relative performance changed with budget. A 75:25 acquisition–exploration portfolio recovered 56.3% with a smaller environmental coverage gap (1.048 versus 1.364); a 50:50 portfolio retained 52.0%. An external retrospective cell-level adaptation using 158 filtered Procambarus clarkii records recovered 22/36 held-out record-containing cells versus a random median of six ( p = 0.001). Environmental transfer was heterogeneous, and the aggregate randomized-reference comparison was inconclusive (weighted AUC = 0.629; null median = 0.564; p = 0.0939). National mapping identified 985 freshwater-background points meeting both environmental-similarity and documentation-gap criteria. These comparisons expose budget-dependent indicator value and acquisition–coverage trade-offs, not validated field priorities or ecological learning. Standardized prospective surveys are required.

title: Geographic gradient interactions reveal non-additive organization of aboveground carbon density in mountain forests
abstract: Classical geographic zonality describes latitudinal, longitudinal, and elevational differentiation in forest vegetation, but these dimensions are commonly treated as separable gradients. In mountain regions, however, horizontal geographic position and elevation jointly define the environmental context in which forest carbon accumulates. Whether mountain forest aboveground carbon density (AGCD) follows uniform geographic belts or exhibits context-dependent three-dimensional organization remains unresolved. Here, we evaluated whether mountain forest AGCD is better represented by additive geographic effects or by interactions among longitude, latitude, and elevation. Using an inventory-derived AGCD dataset for Yunnan, southwestern China, we fitted nested generalized additive models (GAMs) with additive effects (M1), additive and pairwise terms (M2), and additive, pairwise, and three-way terms (M3). The same model hierarchy was fitted separately in six global mountain systems for independent regional replication. In Yunnan, full-data deviance explained increased from 10.80% (M1) to 13.94% (M2) and 14.18% (M3). Full-data RMSE declined from 23.71 to 23.00 and 22.86 Mg/ha, respectively. Pairwise interactions accounted for approximately 93% of the interaction-related improvement. The three-way interaction provided only a small additional refinement in full-data fit. M3 had the lowest full-data AIC, but this reflects in-sample fit rather than spatial predictive performance. Five-fold spatial block cross-validation showed low predictive R 2 and no consistent predictive advantage of M2 or M3 over M1. High AGCD in the fitted response surface was concentrated within restricted longitude–latitude–elevation combinations rather than continuous single-axis geographic belts. Across the six mountain systems, marginal geographic responses differed substantially, yet interaction models generally improved full-data fit, with pairwise interactions accounting for most of the improvement beyond additive effects. These results suggest a recurrent non-additive geographic organization of mountain forest AGCD, in which AGCD associations along each geographic axis depend on the broader geographic context. These descriptive associations provide a framework for comparing mountain forest carbon patterns but do not establish causal ecological mechanisms. A major limitation is that uncertainty in inventory measurements and conversion parameters was not propagated through the AGCD estimation chain and geographic modeling.

title: Corrigendum to “Are greener forests stronger carbon sinks? Rising vapour pressure deficit instigates greening-productivity decoupling in a tropical biodiversity hotspot in India” [Ecol. Indic. 191 (2026) 115663]
Impact of hydropower construction on vegetation NPP in the Yarlung Zangbo River, Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
abstract: Vegetation net primary production (NPP) is integral to the global carbon cycle, especially in the alpine ecosystems of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. However, hydropower construction can profoundly disrupt ecosystem health and carbon sequestration capacity, particularly along the Yarlung Zangbo River. Therefore, there is an urgent need to understand the impacts of hydropower construction on riparian vegetation NPP through precise, engineering-scale assessments of long-term changes. Changes in NPP may alter soil carbon inputs and turnover, with potential feedbacks on ecosystem carbon balance. Such assessments are essential for comprehensive ecological evaluations of hydropower projects. In this study, we downscaled MODIS NPP data to 30 m resolution using a convolutional neural network-based model to examine the spatiotemporal dynamics of NPP changes at the engineering scale across disturbance zones (DZs) and influence zones (IZs). We further applied a structural equation model (SEM) and a generalized linear model (GLM) to enable process-based attribution of dam- and climate-driven changes in NPP from the pre-construction, during-construction, to post-construction stages. The results showed that hydropower construction caused persistent NPP reductions in DZs due to engineered surface expansion and vegetation loss, whereas IZs experienced a sharp NPP decline during construction (88.6%), followed by widespread recovery in the post-construction stage (93.9%). The SEM–GLM framework identified dam construction as the predominant driver of NPP variations (standardized path coefficient: −0.35 in DZs; mean relative importance: 38.6% in IZs), exceeding the combined effects of precipitation and temperature. These findings provide critical insights for ecological risk assessment, sustainable ecosystem management, and the coordinated development of engineering infrastructure and the natural environment in future hydropower projects in environmentally sensitive alpine regions.

title: Indicator-based diagnosis of carbon metabolism in production–living–ecological spaces: Land-use transitions, ecological network relationships, and terrain-constrained carbon flows in the Nanling Mountains, China
abstract: Land-use changes among production–living–ecological (PLE) spaces are critical drivers of regional carbon metabolism. Although these changes have been extensively examined in urban agglomerations and plains, their carbon metabolic mechanisms in mountainous areas remain inadequately explored. In this study, ecological network analysis (ENA) was used to identify ecological interactions among PLE spatial categories and evaluate the utility of the carbon metabolism network. In addition, the topographic constraints on major negative carbon flow pathways were examined. The results reveal the following. (1) Ecological spaces continuously dominated the Nanling Mountains during the full study period. From 2000 to 2020, total carbon emissions increased from 14.46 million t C to 25.18 million t C, whereas total carbon sinks remained relatively stable. (2) The carbon metabolism network was dominated by competitive and control/exploitation relationships. The overall utility values for 2000–2010 and 2010–2020 were 0.690 and 0.815, respectively, both below 1.0. In the latter period, competitive relationships decreased, whereas mutualistic relationships increased; this indicates a slight improvement in network relationships, although negative network effects still predominated. (3) The conversion of forest ecological spaces and agricultural production spaces into manufacturing production spaces, particularly F → M and C → M transitions, was the main driver of negative carbon flows. These flows were spatially concentrated in low-elevation, gentle-slope, and low-relief areas, suggesting that terrain suitability constrains carbon source expansion. The 52 counties in the study region were classified into four categories. This study demonstrates that, in ecologically dominant mountainous regions, stable carbon sinks do not automatically offset the rapid growth in carbon emissions caused by localized development. The spatial clustering of negative carbon flows along topographically suitable corridors provides a clear direction for differentiated, low-carbon territorial spatial management.

title: Evaluating the multi-phase evolution of social-ecological system coordinated adaptability under water environmental constraints: A case study of Xiamen Island
abstract: During urban evolution, complex dynamic interactions occur both between the water-environmental system (WES) and the social-ecological system (SES) and between the human-socioeconomic subsystem (HSS) and the ecological-environmental subsystem (EES) within the SES. However, their evolutionary characteristics and feedback relationships remain insufficiently explored, limiting the clarity and effectiveness of environmental governance strategies. This study constructs a comprehensive dynamic evaluation framework that integrates methods such as cloud model, adaptive cycle theory model, and catastrophe theory models. It can identify the development phases of various subdistricts in the city, their phase-specific feedback and synergies, and reveal the nonlinear dynamic changes in coordinated adaptability. The results indicate that: (1) During the study period, the overall coordination adaptability followed the phase sequence of κ > γ > α > Ω, exhibiting significant spatial linkage and clustering, with a pattern of high peripheral and low central areas coexisting with high southern and low northern areas; (2) Based on the three-dimensional characteristics of coordinated adaptability, three types of subdistircts are identified, with their differing characteristics influenced by the interplay of internal and external systems; (3) Type A subdistricts mainly have insufficient per capita ecological resources, Type B subdistricts have low environmental efficiency and poor pollution control, and Type C subdistricts have limited ecological space, low environmental quality, and pollution accumulation; (4) Accordingly, identified key obstacle factors and proposed differentiated governance strategies, providing a reference for the refined formulation of sustainable development policies appropriate for Xiamen Island.

title: Corridor–barrier effects of urban road networks on native spontaneous plant richness: Nonlinear thresholds and regulation by green space patterns
abstract: Urban road networks can function as either dispersal corridors or ecological barriers, but existing studies have not fully elucidated the complex effects of road networks on plant diversity. On one hand, many studies assume linear relationships, neglecting nonlinear responses and ecological thresholds; on the other hand, research typically focuses on road morphology while insufficiently considering the ecological significance of road network topology. Moreover, road networks and green space patterns are often analyzed independently, without fully revealing the regulatory role of green spaces in the ecological effects of roads. Currently, there is a lack of a framework capable of quantitatively integrating the nonlinear effects of road networks, the interactions of green space patterns, and their ecological significance. This study, using Shenzhen, China, as a high-density urban case, constructed an XGBoost model and integrated SHAP, interaction analysis, segmented regression, and individual conditional expectation curves to investigate the nonlinear effects of road network characteristics on native spontaneous plant richness and explore how green space coverage and cohesion regulate these effects. On this basis, an indicator, total effect of road network (TRSHAP) was developed to represent the net contributions of road metrics, thereby diagnosing corridor-like and barrier-like tendencies of road effects. In the Shenzhen case, when arterial road density exceeds 2.83 km/km 2 ; intersection density exceeds 63.18 intersections per km 2 , and mean road width exceeds 5.35 m, their effects on spontaneous plant species richness turn from positive to negative, while road mean connectivity must exceed 2.94 to maintain its positive effect. Segmented regression analysis identified marginal-response breakpoints reflecting shifts in response intensity, including 5.64 km/km 2 for arterial road density, 5.01 m for mean road width, and 2.48 for road mean connectivity. Together, these values indicate that the nonlinear effect of road networks on native spontaneous plant richness involves both directional transitions and changes in marginal response intensity. Furthermore, green space patterns regulated the direction and magnitude of road effects. Green space coverage primarily determined whether roads showed corridor-like or barrier-like tendencies, while green space cohesion regulated the strength of these tendencies in a coverage-dependent manner. This study developed a quantitative framework centered on TRSHAP for diagnosing the corridor-like and barrier-like tendencies of road networks and provided actionable evidence for biodiversity-oriented coordinated planning of roads and green spaces, with applicability to new road planning, urban renewal, and ecological corridor design. • Road metrics showed nonlinear threshold effects on native species richness. • TRSHAP diagnosed net corridor-like or barrier-like road contributions. • Roads shifted between corridor or barrier roles across green space contexts. • Green space coverage determined total road corridor–barriers tendencies. • Green space cohesion regulated road effects in a coverage-dependent manner.

title: Quantifying blue–green space degradation dynamics and associated thermal responses across urban expansion patterns: Insights from interpretable machine learning
abstract: Urban expansion areas have emerged as critical hotspots of blue–green space degradation and thermal intensification during rapid urbanization. However, nonlinear relationships between multidimensional blue–green space degradation and thermal intensification, including their variation across expansion patterns, remain insufficiently understood. Using 26 cities in the Yangtze River Delta Urban Agglomeration, this study characterizes urban-expansion-area blue–green spaces (UEBGSs) and their degradation from 2000 to 2020, while identifying urban expansion patterns (UEPs). By integrating TabPFN with SHAP, the study reveals nonlinear relationships between UEBGS degradation and changes in relative land surface temperature (ΔrLST), as well as pattern-specific heterogeneity. The results indicate that: (1) edge-expansion was the dominant UEP in the Yangtze River Delta, with the intensity and pathways of UEBGS degradation varying across UEPs; (2) UEBGS degradation exhibited nonlinear relationships with ΔrLST, where green-space quantity loss and biophysical-condition degradation were the dominant contributors to thermal intensification, while structural degradation played a significant role at the early stage; and (3) the relative importance of degradation indicators, sensitive response intervals, and marginal effects differed among UEPs. Specifically, edge-expansion was more sensitive to quantity degradation, infilling-expansion responded more strongly to biophysical-condition degradation, and outlying-expansion showed buffering effects at low levels of degradation but accelerated thermal intensification at higher levels. Overall, the UEBGS degradation–ΔrLST relationship is strongly pattern-dependent, with distinct response intensities and sensitive intervals across UEPs. This finding underscores the need for pattern-specific blue–green space interventions across UEPs. This study provides a framework for understanding heat-risk formation and supports targeted thermal governance in rapidly urbanizing regions.

title: Environmental controls on shallow water benthic foraminifera along Singapore's equatorial urban coastlines
abstract: Foraminifera are valuable bioindicators that can help assess the ecological impacts of nutrient enrichment and organic matter loading in rapidly urbanising coastal environments, particularly in Southeast Asia where baseline environmental data remain sparse. Singapore provides a pertinent site to address this gap because its compact coastline encompasses pronounced environmental gradients within an equatorial setting. Monthly water quality and seabed investigation of Singapore's coastal environment from November 2023 – October 2024 identified four environmental regimes, ranging from relatively marine-influenced to persistently eutrophic environments. Notably, while water quality showed pronounced seasonal variability, sediment characteristics and foraminiferal communities exhibit stronger spatial variation, suggesting that they primarily record persistent environmental conditions rather than shorter-term fluctuations. Multivariate analyses show that foraminiferal communities are spatially structured, and are primarily driven by nutrient availability, organic matter enrichment and degree of marine influence. Specifically, increasing nutrient and organic loading are associated with declining diversity, greater dominance of stress-tolerant taxa (e.g., Ammonia veneta ), and disappearance of sensitive taxa (e.g., Elphidium somaense) . This is also evident in the community metrics, where foraminiferal diversity (H′) and Foram Stress Index (FSI) were significantly correlated with water trophic status (TRIX) and sediment total organic carbon. Random Forest modelling further identified organic matter enrichment as primary drivers for Ammonia confertitesta and Elphidium somaense abundance, highlighting their potential as bioindicators for this change. Our findings establish the first modern living foraminiferal baseline record for Singapore, and demonstrate the value of integrating community metrics and taxon-environment relationships to support long-term monitoring of equatorial urban coastal systems.

title: Integrating ecological resilience assessment and machine learning for ecological security patterns in Guangdong Province, China
abstract: Ecological security patterns (ESPs) provide an important framework for coordinating ecological conservation and urban development in rapidly urbanizing regions. However, conventional approaches to ecological source identification often emphasize current ecosystem functions while paying limited attention to ecological resilience under ongoing urbanization and environmental uncertainty. Meanwhile, the application of machine learning to resistance-surface construction in such contexts remains limited. To address these gaps, this study develops an integrated framework that combines ecological resilience assessment, machine learning, and circuit theory to construct an ESP for Guangdong Province, China. Ecological resilience was first assessed to identify potential ecological sources, while Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) was then used to construct a resistance surface by capturing nonlinear relationships between human activities and ecological resistance. Circuit theory was subsequently applied to identify ecological corridors and key ecological nodes. The results show that ecological sources are unevenly distributed across Guangdong, with higher resilience concentrated in mountainous and forested areas. The LightGBM model achieved the highest test-set AUC among six candidate algorithms. The resulting resistance surface further reveals substantial spatial variation in ecological pressure, with intensive human activities concentrated around major urban agglomerations. Ecological corridors and pinch points identified through circuit theory highlight critical areas for maintaining regional connectivity. The findings demonstrate that integrating ecological resilience with machine learning can provide a more adaptive basis for ESP construction in rapidly urbanizing regions and offer practical support for targeted ecological conservation and connectivity management.

title: Beach litter footprint: indicator design and operational testing across Iberia, the Balearics, and Macaronesia
abstract: Citizens, scientists, and governmental agencies are generating vast datasets on beach macrolitter, generally reported as litter item inventories. Despite this richness of information, most assessments of coastal environmental status rely on total item counts, underutilizing data on item size and type. Here, we introduce the Beach Litter Footprint, a multidimensional indicator comprising seven source-related sub-indicators that account for both litter size and potential origins. By leveraging the full structure of beach-litter datasets, this multi-source indicator provides a more nuanced diagnostic of coastal conditions, offering more targeted guidance for management. In this manuscript, we first present the design, calculation, and interpretation of the indicator, which can be represented in the form of footprint visualizations, fine-resolution maps, or litter curves, depending on the purpose and scale of analysis. Utilizing routine beach-litter monitoring data, we demonstrate the indicator's applicability through an operational test conducted across the region extending from the Macaronesian Islands (Atlantic Ocean), the Iberian Peninsula, and the Balearic Archipelago (Mediterranean Sea). Additionally, we offer a suite of automated tools to facilitate the application of the Beach Litter Footprint to other shores worldwide.

title: Hydrological-state reorganization of eutrophication risk in temperate monsoon coastal rivers revealed by interpretable machine learning and structural path analysis
abstract: Hydrological-state variability strongly shapes eutrophication risk in small coastal catchments, but the transition from low-flow source accumulation to rainfall-driven transport remains poorly quantified. We analysed monthly eutrophication index (EI) patterns for 30 coastal rivers on the Shandong Peninsula, China, from 2020 to 2024 using an integrated interpretable machine-learning and observed-variable structural path-analysis framework. The EI, derived from TN, TP, DO, and COD Mn , was evaluated against terrain, hydroclimate, hydrology, human activity, point-source pollution, and anthropogenic-pressure proxies derived from annual wastewater and fertilizer inventories. EI was significantly higher under high-flow conditions than under low- and transition-flow conditions, accompanied by marked changes in the relative contributions of the individual EI components. Predictor associations also varied across hydrological states. Low-flow conditions were more closely associated with river discharge (Q), human pressure, and downstream catchment setting, whereas transition-flow conditions showed a stronger terrain-related association structure. Under high-flow conditions, human-activity, terrain, precipitation, and Q signals were more broadly represented. Structural path analysis further showed that precipitation was positively associated with Q and the TP- and COD Mn -related components under high-flow conditions, whereas temperature- and HFI-related associations were more evident under transition- and low-flow conditions. Overall, the results reveal a hydrological-state-dependent reorganization of eutrophication risk and its environmental associations, providing a basis for flow-state-specific water-quality monitoring.

title: Spatio-temporal evolution and prediction of desertification sensitivity in the Hulun Buir grassland under future climate scenarios
abstract: Desertification ranks among the most serious environmental problems facing human society. What drives desertification in the Hulun Buir grassland? To answer that and improve how we manage it, this study used two tools: the MEDALUS model and the Geodetector method. These helped analyze changes in space and time, plus the factors behind them. Looking ahead, the same MEDALUS model was run with three CMIP6 forcing scenarios (low, medium, high). That gave projections for two future windows: mid-century (2030–2050) and late century (2070–2100). Desertification sensitivity exhibited a decrease–increase–decrease trend during 2001–2020, with a spatial pattern of “low in the east and high in the west”. Precipitation has the strongest inhibitory effect on desertification (β = −0.468), primarily by promoting vegetation growth (β = 0.577) and increasing soil moisture (β = 0.439). Vegetation cover directly inhibits desertification (β = −0.351) and mitigates soil erosion. Temperature affects desertification in two opposite ways: it worsens soil erosion (β = 0.293) on one side, yet also shows a slight direct restraining effect (β = −0.108) on the other. Soil sandification is a key process that intensifies desertification (β = 0.156). How sensitive the land will be in the future depends heavily on which emission path is taken. Under SSP1–2.6 and SSP2–4.5, it goes down, but under SSP5–8.5 it goes up, and the change speeds up over time. This work offers a scientific foundation for stopping desertification and protecting ecosystems in semi-dry areas.

title: Ecological-state and modeled ecosystem-service trajectories of persistent cropland-to-forest transitions across policy-context windows in Hunan, China
abstract: Assessments of cropland-to-forest transitions often rely on vegetation greenness or composite indices, obscuring whether structural greening reflects functional recovery and how initial conditions shape post-transition trajectories. We examined remotely detected persistent cropland-to-forest transitions across three policy-context windows (2000–2006, 2007–2013, and 2014–2020) in Hunan Province, China. The Grain for Green Program provided the institutional context for these windows rather than verified treatment assignment. Six component indicators—greenness (EVI), wetness (WET), bare-surface exposure (NDBSI), modeled water yield, modeled soil retention, and an NPP-based productivity proxy—were evaluated using balanced event-time alignment, multivariable covariate adjustment, directional synchrony, and spatially validated XGBoost-SHAP. Canopy greenness increased (0.0033–0.0037 yr −1 ) and surface exposure declined (−0.0034 to −0.0039 yr −1 ) consistently across all windows. By contrast, directional agreement between EVI changes and modeled service-indicator changes was generally around or below 50%, and WET showed a near-flat trend in the latest window. After covariate adjustment, between-window differences in EVI and NDBSI were no longer statistically significant, whereas differences in WET and modeled services remained significant. Pre-transition baselines and climate/topography accounted for 50%–96% of model-explained variance. County-level socioeconomic context generally accounted for a small share of model-explained variance, with indicator- and window-specific exceptions. Out-of-sample predictive performance varied across indicators and windows under the two spatial validation strategies, with baseline state and precipitation generally dominating predictions. Because the detected transitions were not administratively verified program parcels, the results describe land-transition dynamics under evolving policy contexts rather than causal program impacts. These findings show that structural greening does not ensure synchronous functional improvement and support component-level, service-specific monitoring.

title: Agroforestry's ecological promise: A global meta-analysis reveals context dependence, temporal decline, and policy implications
abstract: Balancing the demand for agricultural production with the maintenance of ecosystem services, climate mitigation and adaptation, and biodiversity conservation will be a major challenge of this century. Crop production in agroforestry systems is being widely practiced with the expectation that it can simultaneously meet all of these goals. This study conducts a global meta-analysis of peer-reviewed literature on agroforestry outcomes. By synthesizing 1328 matched data pairs from 42 studies across 14 countries, using indicators that encompass biodiversity, soil properties, and carbon-related metrics, we find that agroforestry has a positive impact, improving overall environmental performance by 13.0%. After accounting for the influence of the replaced land-use type, agroforestry shows a 44.5% improvement in environmental performance relative to monoculture plantations. However, in contrast to reference native forests, its effect on environmental performance is not significant (RR = −0.02, 95%CIs = −0.12 to 0.09). Furthermore, the likelihood of agroforestry systems delivering simultaneous benefits across the assessed ecological indicators declined with increasing implementation duration. These findings demonstrate that the ecological value of agroforestry is fundamentally context-dependent, underscoring the necessity of incorporating baseline land-use history into policy design and environmental assessment frameworks for sustainable land management.

title: Traditional markets as indicators of wild plant diversity and availability under land use change in Central Sumatra
abstract: Wild plants play an important role in the daily practices of local communities. However, modernisation and rapid habitat alteration in Central Sumatra (Indonesia) threaten local knowledge associated with these resources.
